*Chan yuan yao lin zhu*, Scroll One.
Written by Chan Master Chuo’an Zhiming of Shaolin, Songshan; courtesy name Bohun, with the refined sobriquet Lezhenzi (Son of Joyful Truth);
from Anzhou. Annotated by Wuzheng and Dejian at Dawan Shou Temple in Yanjing.
Recorded by Lezhenzi. Composed by Zhiming. Chan Master Zhiming of Shaolin, Songshan, whose courtesy name was Bohun and refined sobriquet Lezhenzi, was a native of Anzhou.
The son of the Hao family was by nature indifferent to conventional restraints; outwardly simple and plain, yet inwardly refined and compassionate.

Initially practicing the "husk-like Chan" under the Fourth Patriarch, he compiled the *Guānhuá Biāoyuè jí* (Anthology of Stringing Flowers and Pointing to the Moon). Encouraged and sharpened by the head monk Jie, he shaved his head and received full ordination from Master Jing of Xianglin.
Day and night, he sought instruction and inquiry at the chambers of Shengjing and Fuzhi. Later, he attained thorough realization at Donglin.
He once hung a wooden mallet and used it to wipe his hands, calling it a "mallet-towel. He leaned on a single staff as he went, leaving or staying according to his own ease;
no one could judge him as either intimate or distant. When Donglin moved to Chao-hua, the assembly requested that he fill the vacancy at Shaolin.

The Master struck the tally-sticks to swear his oath and departed with a long song. The song said: "A tavern opens before Wuru Peak; Steamed buns are as large as buckets, and cakes are like sieves. Luoyang..."

Within the city, there were many lay devotees; vying with one another, they offered vegetarian feasts with fallen earrings and discarded hairpins. As for the impoverished cripple—his talent was as profound as a still pool—why did he break into the "Three Terraces" dance in his old age?
Leaning on his staff, he walked directly onto the path of Songyang; laughing, he pointed toward the green mountains and said, "Come, let us return home.
Though they sought to detain him, it could not be done; everywhere, all admired his lofty character.
Preface to the *Commentary on the Jade Forest of the Zen Garden* by Master Xuetang:
My teacher, Wansong, possessed the unsurpassed faculty; having read every book under heaven, he once said to me:
"Those who record events must extract their essentials; those who compile statements must probe their mysteries. What Han Yu said is indeed well-founded.
The successor, Zen Master Xuedang Jian, took pleasure in the True Chan Garden of Old Yuxi and desired to have this work carved into woodblocks for circulation.
He composed a commentary on it, totaling nearly sixty thousand words. Some were surprised by its prolixity, but when they reported this to the Master, he exclaimed:
"The east wind blows down the apricot branches; where does the red fragrance reside within?"
Written on the second day of the second month of the Year of Yi-mao by the Layman of Longshan, Lü Bopi of Yanmen.
This *Canyuan Mengqiu* was composed by Cuocan. As for Cuocan, he was Li Han and Wang Ling among the bhikṣus.
This book comprises two thousand words and elucidates five hundred matters. Its language is lucid and its record is comprehensive; its learning is profound and its scope is vast.

It may serve as a manual for the seasonal rites of the Chan school and a thematic compendium for the ocean of Dharma, enabling later students to save themselves the labor of ten years and achieve a record equivalent to half a Tripitaka.
The Master’s compassion is fully evident herein. As for this "Cuo-an," who else could it be? It is none other than [the Master].

on the fifth day before the end of the twelfth month in the year Wuyou of the Zhengda era, following the preface to the *Chan Garden Primer* (Chanyuan Mengqiu),
which was brushed with the sleeves of Hongfen at Xiao Lin.
Master Yuezheng composed this for the sake of beginners and junior students.
Using the Eye of the True Dharma to compose "literary Chan," he employed parallel couplets and harmonious verse, totaling over five hundred stanzas, intended for scholars to contemplate and observe.
I was reading and laughing, saying, "The Master has firmly grasped the essential ford; he does not admit ordinary people or sages.

Why concern yourself with this book? Is it not like adding legs to a snake? The Master said, "What you say is indeed true. Nevertheless, children lack discernment and have not yet been able to inquire and seek instruction.
If they can commit this to memory and gain a rough understanding of how to ask for the way, then my book will serve as an aid."

It was like instructing a deaf-mute great official to perform a dance; though not his true vocation, it was simply to ensure that his descendants would not let their ancestral profession fall into ruin.
Thereupon, he smiled in thanks and composed the preface.

*Chan yuan meng qiu*, Scroll One:
Śākyamuni’s Seven Steps (*Puyao jing*). When the World-Honored One was born, he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward the earth. He circled...
He took seven steps and looked toward the west, saying: "In the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am the most honored. ○ Supplement:

The *Puyao jing* (Sutra of the Universal Radiance) states that when the Buddha was first born into the family of the Kṣatriyas, he emitted a great light of wisdom that illuminated the worlds of the ten directions.
The earth surged forth golden lotus flowers, which he held beneath his two feet as he walked east and west, as well as north and south.
He took seven steps, pointed his fingers toward heaven and earth, and let out a lion’s roar, saying: "In the realms above, below, and in the four intermediate directions, whoever can surpass me...
(From *The Transmission of the Lamp*, Vol. 3). The First Patriarch sat facing a wall for nine years at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song. People...
No one could fathom him; at that time, he was called the "Wall-gazing Brahmin. [Huìbǔ adds: The *Chuándēng lù*, fascicle three, states:
"The Master traveled from Liáng to Wèi and reached Shàolín in Luòyáng, where he sat facing the wall for nine years before the Second Patriarch finally received the transmission of the Dharma."
The Secret Transmission at Vulture Peak (Huìyuán 1): At the assembly on Vulture Peak, the World-Honored One held up a flower to show the multitude.
At that time, everyone remained silent; only the Venerable Kāśyapa broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said:
"I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, the reality-phenomenon which is signless—the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate that does not rely on words or letters."

The Outer Separate Transmission. It was entrusted to Mahākāśyapa. When the World-Honored One arrived before the Many-Sons Stūpa, he commanded Mahākāśyapa to share his seat and sit with him; he then encircled him with his *saṃghāṭī* robe and said:
"I have secretly entrusted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to you. You must protect and uphold it, and transmit it to future generations."
The Single Transmission of Shaoshi (Chuan Deng III): Regarding the various patriarchs who transmitted the Dharma, initially the teachings of the Tripitaka were practiced concurrently.
Later, the Patriarch Bodhidharma transmitted the mind-seal alone, shattering attachments and manifesting the essential doctrine.

This is what is known as the "Separate Transmission Outside the Teachings," which does not rely on words and letters, but directly points to the human mind so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha. [Supplementary Note by He]: Chuan Deng III.
It is said: At Shaolin, Bodhidharma looked toward Huike and told him, "In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to Kāśyapa;
it has been passed down through successive generations until it reached me. I now entrust it to you."
Qingyuan and the Hatchet (The Dharma Heir of the Sixth Patriarch, *Huiyuan* 5): Master Qingyuan Xingsi of Qiyuan, Jizhou, dispatched Shitou to visit Master Huairang of Nanyue with a letter.
[Shitou] said, "When you return, I will give you back your worn-out hatchet."
When Shitou arrived there, he asked, "What is it like when one does not admire the various sages and does not prize one's own spiritual nature?
Yuezhou said, "Your question is far too lofty; why not ask about things below? Shitou said, "I would rather sink into the depths for eternal kalpas than seek the liberation of the various sages.
He then turned back. Yuezhou remarked, "Why have you returned so quickly? Shitou replied, "The letter has not even been delivered."
Faith was likewise not yet established. When he departed, he had been granted permission to dwell in the mountains with his "rusty axe.
He then invited [the Master] to descend one foot, whereupon he prostrated himself at the head of the steps. He returned to Mount Nanyue and dwelt in a hermitage.
**Nanyue Polishing a Brick (Huìyuán III)** When Chan Master Huairang was residing at Mount Nanyue, Mazu was staying there in a hermitage, where he spent his days solely in seated meditation.

One day, Huairang went to him and asked, "What are you doing here? Mazu replied, "I am practicing seated meditation. Huairang asked, "What do you hope to achieve by this? Mazu said, "I hope to become a Buddha.
One day, Huairang took a brick and began polishing it in front of the hermitage. Mazu asked, "What are you polishing that brick for?"
"What is this for? Hué asked. "I want to make a mirror," the Master replied. "How can you make a mirror by polishing a tile? asked Hué.
"How can one become a Buddha by sitting in meditation? asked the Master. "What else would it be? asked Hué. "It is like a person driving a cart; if the cart does not move..."

"Striking the cart is it; striking the ox is it. Thereupon, the Patriarch attained realization of the essential meaning beneath these words, whereupon he was sealed in mind and transmitted the Dharma.
This fulfilled the prophecy of the Western Patriarch that "a colt shall trample the people of the world," and the Southern School was established in Jiangxi.

The Founding of Baizhang Monastery (The Sixth Lamp in the Dharma-lineage of Mazu): One day, Zen Master Baizhang Huaihai of Hongzhou remarked that since the inception of the Chan school at Shaoshi until its arrival at Caoxi, practitioners had mostly resided in monasteries following the Vinaya.
Although these were called "separate cloisters," they remained within the confines of the established monastic system.

The Cloth Bag Monk of Fenghua County in Mingzhou was of unknown clan or surname; he called himself Qici. His physical form was stout and heavy, with a furrowed brow and a protruding belly.
His speech was unpredictable, and he would sleep wherever he happened to be. He constantly carried a cloth bag slung over a staff. All...

Whether it was thin wine, fish sauce, or pickled fish, as soon as he took even a small portion into his mouth, he would divide it and throw a little back into the sack. At that time, he was known as Master Bùdài (Sack) of Chángtīng.

Xiangyan Strikes the Bamboo (Chuan Deng Lu, Case 11). When Chan Master Xiangyan Zhixian of Dengzhou first visited Mount Guishan, he did not attain realization. He took his leave and traveled to Nanyang, where he stayed at the site of National Teacher Huizhong’s former residence.

One day, while clearing weeds and brush in the mountains, he struck a bamboo with a piece of tile, and as it made a sound, he suddenly burst into laughter. In that moment, he attained a vast and clear self-awakening. Thereupon, he composed [this verse]: A single word, and the thousand-year-old dead tree sprouts anew; A single phrase, and the ten-thousand-year-old withered stump blooms in spring.

The myriad phenomena are all complete within the mind-ground; The three vehicles are entirely contained within the single vehicle. If you wish to know the source of the Buddhas and patriarchs, Look directly at the tip of the staff. (Note: This is the famous verse attributed to Xiangyan Zhixian.)

The verse says: A single blow causes all that was known to be forgotten, requiring no further cultivation or refinement. Leaving no trace anywhere, it transcends both sound and form as well as outward deportment.
Those who have realized the Way in all directions all declare this to be the highest capacity.

Regarding the "Seeking Lodging" (from *Huiyuan I*): Master Hongren, the Fifth Patriarch, was a native of Huangmei in Qizhou.

The woman said, "I have parents and brothers; you may go seek them out. He replied, "Very well, I shall do so immediately.
The woman nodded her head in agreement, and he turned his horse and departed. This woman was Zhou Shi’s younger daughter. Upon returning home, she conceived at once.
Her parents, being greatly repulsed by her, cast her out. Having nowhere to turn, she hired herself out as a spinner in the village during the day and stayed beneath a public inn at night.
After some time, she gave birth to a son; deeming him an ill omen, she threw him into a muddy harbor.
The next day, seeing him swimming upstream against the current with a radiant countenance, she was greatly astonished. She then took him up, and he grew to boyhood under his mother’s care.

He begged for alms, and the villagers called him "The Child Without Surname. Meeting a man of wisdom, the latter marveled, saying, "This child lacks seven physical marks and thus does not equal the Tathāgata.
Later, he encountered Master Xìn and became his Dharma heir, whereupon he transformed beings on Mount Pòtóu.
Chaoqie Chuimao (Dachin’s Dharma Heir; *Huiyuan* 2). Chan Master Daolin of Chaoqie in Hangzhou was known as "Nest-in-a-Tree" because he lived perched upon a tree.

upon arriving, I see only a pool for soaking hemp. The Master said, "You see only the pool for soaking hemp."
[The Master] did not see Guankui. A monk asked, "What is Guankui? The Master said, "As swift as a split arrow.

Shushan [once] bit down on the arrowhead (*Chuan deng lu* 17). Chan Master Kuangren Yuanzhao of Shushan in Fuzhou was short and unimposing in physical appearance, yet his refined discernment was preeminent among the masses.
During his time under Dongshan, he possessed the "biting the arrowhead" mechanism, vigorously expounding the profound mysteries.
All consider benevolence to be that which can define and measure [the Dharma]. Regarding the various samādhis, one may consult the "Shorter Uncle" (Ācārya).
When the celestial bowl flowers bloom and the wheat ripens on the Nine Peaks—[the successor of Yanshou]—Dhyāna Master Jiufeng Daoquan. A monk asked: "I have heard, Master, that you yourself..."
When Yan-shou arrived, [the Master] asked, "Is it so? Quan replied, "Has the wheat ripened before the mountain?
Yan-shou then invited monks;
this was the matter of Empress Wu Zetian of the Tang bestowing a bath (Shi-yuan 1). Empress Wu Zetian of the Tang dynasty, the Elder An of Mount Song, and Shen of the Northern School.

Xiu entered [the water] with his robe tucked into his chest to offer worship. During the course of the bathing, palace ladies attended him; he remained alone, peaceful and serene, without any other concern.
Later, the Empress sighed and said, "Only upon entering the water does one truly know there is a tall man here. (And so forth.)
The Prefectural Secretary Plays Ball (From *Chanlin Leiju*, Vol. 1). Supplement: Wang, the Attendant, and Chan Master Muzhou Zong.
One day, the Master asked, "Why have you come to the monastery today? Wang replied, "I came because I was watching people play ball.
The Master asked, "Are the people playing ball or the horses playing ball? Wang said, "The people are playing ball. The Master said, "Then the people are exhausted."
[The Master] asked, "Are you tired? [Wang] said, "I am tired. The Master said, "Is the horse tired? The Master said, "Is the pillar tired? Wang was taken aback and had no reply.
Upon returning to his private residence, he suddenly attained realization during the night. The next day, he saw the Master and said, "I have understood the matter from yesterday.
The Master said, "Is the pillar tired? Wang said, "It is tired. The Master then granted him approval.
The Official Shuanglu (Chuan Deng Lu 8). When Grand Master Lu Xun of the Tang dynasty and Nanquan saw someone playing *shuanglu* (double-six), he picked up the dice and said:
"Whether it is thus or not thus—if one simply follows the roll of the dice like this, what then?"
Quán said, "A stinking bone, eighteen.

The practitioner lost his laughter (Míng’ān was a successor of Xuánfǎ; this is recorded in the *Sēngbǎozhuàn*). When Xuědò first served as the guest prefect in the Chan assembly of Dàyáng Xuán, he engaged in a monk in nocturnal discourse, critiquing the past and present with the impartiality of "vermilion and yellow.
This led to a dispute over the karmic cause concerning Zhàozhōu’s "Cypress Tree."

He could not resolve the matter. A practitioner standing nearby laughed and departed. After the guest had withdrawn, Xuedou called him back and reprimanded him, saying, "How dare you laugh in the presence of a guest?
He replied, "I know that the Guest Master possesses the ability to distinguish between the ancient and the modern, yet lacks the eye to discern what is truly ancient or modern;
therefore, I dared to laugh. Xuedou asked, "Furthermore, how do you understand Zhaozhou’s meaning? Because of this...
He replied with a verse: "A single rabbit lies across the ancient road; The blue hawk, upon seeing it, seizes it instantly. Later hunters' dogs lack spiritual nature;
They vainly search for it at the old spot where the withered stump stood. Xuedou was greatly amazed and subsequently became friends with him.
Some say he was Chan Master Zong of Chengtian. I believe that by hearing this, one can gain insight into his character.
At that time, the assembly at the Dharma seat was so magnificent.
Lu Xun Weeps (from *Chuan Deng Lu* 10): Grand Master Lu Xun wept upon the passing of Nanquan. The head of the monastery asked, "Grand Master, why do you not weep for the late Master?
Lu Xun replied, "If you can speak the Way, then I shall weep. The head of the monastery was speechless. Changqing spoke on his behalf.
The Master said, "It is appropriate to laugh, not to weep.

Daji blew into [Lengqie] Jian’s ear (the third volume of *Huiyuan*, among the Dharma-heirs of Mazu). One day, Chan Master Wejian of Letan in Hongzhou was sitting in meditation behind Mazu’s Dharma Hall.
When Mazu saw him, he blew into Jian’s ear; after being blown twice, Jian arose from his concentration and looked.
The Preceptor then returned to his meditative absorption. When the Patriarch returned to the abbot’s quarters, he instructed an attendant to bring a bowl of tea for Jian;
Jian, however, paid him no heed and simply returned to the hall himself.
Venerable Baimi (from *Chuandeng lu*, fascicle 7): When Venerable Piṇḍola went to the great assembly at King Aśoka’s palace, the King asked, "I have heard that you personally saw the Buddha;
is this true? The Venerable one brushed his eyebrows aside with his hand and said, "Do you understand?
The King replied, "I do not understand. The Venerable one said, "The Dragon King of Lake Anavatapta has invited the Buddha for a meal."
At that time, this poor monk was also included among their number. Piṇḍola pointed to my body and asked, "What is this? (Huìyuán 2). Regarding the Elder Hanshan of Mount Tiantai:

once, while the assembly of monks were roasting eggplants, Hanshan took an eggplant skewer and struck one monk on the back with it. When the monk turned his head, Hanshan held up the skewer and said: "An eggplant skewer.

(Huìyuán 2) Hanshan of Mount Tiantai, while the monks were roasting eggplants, took an eggplant skewer and struck one monk on the back. The monk turned his head; Hanshan held up the skewer and said: "An eggplant skewer. (Huìyuán 2)
“What is it? The monk said, “This madman. Shan turned to a bystander and said, “Tell me, how much salt and vinegar has this monk cost me?

[This concludes] the *Jietuo zhoubi* (The Rice-Paddle of Liberation), by Niu Tou Zhong’s successor, from the *Huìyuán* (Compendium of the Source), volume two. From the *Gǔqīngliáng zhuàn* (Record of the Ancient Qingliang), the Shao Temple in Wutai County during the Great Sui Dynasty.
After Master Jietuo of Guo Temple had been shown the mind-seal by Mañjuśrī, he humbled himself and practiced self-restraint, devoting himself exclusively to serving the assembly.

Later, Mañjuśrī personally came to test him. Whenever Jietuo prepared congee for the assembly at dawn, Mañjuśrī would suddenly appear before him; yet Jietuo did not look back at all. Mañjuśrī warned him, saying: "I..."
Wen-shu was there. Deyi took the rice-paddle used for stirring the porridge and struck him, saying, "Wen-shu is Wen-shu;
liberation is liberation. Wen-shu then spoke this verse: "The bitter gourd is bitter from root to tip; The sweet melon is sweet from stem to end.
Having practiced for three great kalpas, I am yet despised by this old monk."
Chan Master Daotong of Longxing Temple in Muzhou, known as "Old Chen of the Reed Sandals" (a dharma successor of Huangbo), was the Venerable Chen himself.
Having attained enlightenment upon meeting Huangbo, he resided at Mishan Temple in Gaoyang. Later, because his mother grew old, he returned to the east;
there he sold straw sandals to provide for her. Subsequently, he took up residence at Longxing Temple.
Pang Yun’s Bamboo Strainer (from the *Biographies of the Lamp*, Disciples of Mazu): The layman Pang Yun of Xiangzhou had a daughter named Lingzhao.
She would often accompany him in making bamboo strainers to sell them, providing for their daily needs.
Wuben’s "Paper Wick" (Yunyan Cheng’s successor; *Huiyuan* 15). The supplementary commentary states: Master Dongshan Shouchu was asked by a monk, "What is the Eye of the True Dharma?
The Master replied, "A paper wick without oil. Initially, he was a successor of Yunmen;
however, the account of the "paper wick" does not appear in the *Dongshan Wuben Chuan*.

Fayan Xiangchi (Dharma Successor of Guichen; *Chuan Deng Lu*, Case 24). Chan Master Wenyi, the Great Fayan of Qingliang Monastery in Shengzhou, was warming his hands by the fire with Chan Master Wugong when he picked up an incense spoon and asked Wugong, "One must not call this an incense spoon.
What would you call it, brother? Wugong replied, "An incense spoon. The Master did not approve. Later, Wugong...
It was only after more than twenty days that this statement became clear.
Regarding Guangren’s Daughter (Liangjia’s Dharma heir; *Chuan Deng Lu* 17): Shushan held a wooden snake in his hand. A monk asked, "What is this in your hand?
The Master raised it up and said, "A daughter of the Cao family."
**Master Xuanze of Jinling Baoyuan (Dharma successor of Tianyi; *Chuan deng lu*, Case 24)** When Master Xuanze first questioned Qingfeng, "What is the Buddha?
Qingfeng replied, "The child Bingding comes seeking fire. The Master took these words to heart.
Later, upon visiting Jinghui, he was questioned regarding his realization of the essential meaning. The Master responded, "Bingding is..."
It is like seeking fire while already amidst fire; it is as if one were asking a Buddha about a Buddha. Jinghui said, "How many times have you missed the mark? You have fundamentally misunderstood.
Although the Master had received this instruction, he still harbored some hesitation. He withdrew to reflect further, yet remained unable to comprehend the profound principle.
Thereupon, he offered his heart with sincerity and requested further guidance. Jinghui said, "Ask me, and I will explain it to you. The Master then—
A question was asked: "What is the Buddha? Jinghui replied, "The child of the Bing and Ding trunks comes seeking fire. The Master (Zhimen) suddenly realized his true home.
Later, he resided at Baoyuan Temple. Regarding this, the Elder Qin of Jiufeng said:
"Yangqi is plowing with an ox. (From the *Monk-Treasure Chronicle*, Vol. Lower, on Zhimen Zu). The Elder Jiufeng Qinfu said: "Yangqi is pulling the plow."
Jiufeng drags the handle;
Baofu supports the plow. (Xuefeng’s Dharma heir; *Chuan Deng Lu*, Case 10). Chan Master Congzhan of Baofu Monastery in Tanzhou once raised the question:
"Panshan said that when light and objects are both forgotten, what is it then? Dongshan said, 'When light and objects are not yet forgotten...'"
"What is this? the Master asked. The Venerable said, "According to these two venerable elders' deliberations, they have still not reached a definitive conclusion.
He then asked Changqing, "How would you express it now so as to reach a definitive conclusion? Changqing remained silent for a long while.
The Master said, "I knew the Master was making his living inside a ghost cave. Changqing then asked, "What about you? The Master replied, "Supporting with both hands."
His plow handle reached down past his knees.
Xuantai the Patched-Robe Monk (from *The Lamp of the Succession of Shishuang Zhu*, volume 16): The senior monk Xuantai of Mount Nanyue was a man of unknown origins.
He was profound, serene, and spoke little; he never wore silk garments. The assembly called him "Xuantai the Patched-Robe Monk."
Heshang Zhiyi Kefu (Dharma Heir of Linji; *Lingji Lu*, Case 11): Heshang Zhiyi Kefu was from Zhuozhou and wore paper robes.
Anzhu (Dharma Heir of Linji; *Chuan Deng Lu*, Case 12): Anzhu Xiang of Lotus Peak held up his staff and addressed the assembly, saying, "When ancients reached this point, why did they refuse to stay?
The assembly was silent. [The Master] spoke on their behalf, saying: "Because..."
He found no efficacy on other paths. He spoke again, asking, "Ultimately, how is it? Then he said himself: "Carrying my staff slung across my shoulder, I pay no heed to others;
I go straight into a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks. (The *jìlì* is a walking staff.)
Liangsui, who possessed complete knowledge (Huìyuán 4), was the Preceptor Liangsui of Shouzhou. Having received the seal of approval from Magu, he returned to the lecture halls in the capital.
Upon concluding his session, he addressed his disciples, saying: "What you all know, Liangsui knows entirely;
what Liangsui knows, you all do not know."
The Attendant Throws Down His Brush (Huishan’s Disciple Huiyuan, Volume Nine). While the Attendant Wang Jingchu of Xiangzhou was attending to his official duties, Master Mi arrived.
The Attendant then took up his brush. Master Mi asked, "Can you issue a decree for empty space? The Attendant threw down his brush, entered the hall, and did not come out again.
Master Mi harbored doubts. On the following day, he sent Drum Mountain’s Master of Offerings to enter [the hall].
He sought to fathom his meaning. Mi followed him, secretly standing behind a screen to observe.
As soon as the Master of Offerings sat down, he asked, "Yesterday, what words did Master Mi say that you were not permitted to see?
The Attendant replied, "A lion bites a man; a hunting dog chases a clod of earth. Upon hearing this, Master Mi immediately realized his former error. He came out at once and laughed.
Miaoyan said, "I understand! I understand! The Attendant said, "Understanding is not non-existent; try to say something. Miaoyan said, "Please, Attendant, bring it forth.
The Attendant then held up a single chopstick. Miaoyan said, "This wild fox spirit! Gong said, "This man has penetrated through to the bottom."
Taifu Guoni (Huayuan 9) adds in his commentary: Once, while Wuyue Shan was plastering a wall, Li Junrong arrived, fully dressed in official robes.
He went directly behind the Master and stood there holding his ceremonial tablet upright.
When the Master turned his head and saw him, he tilted his mud tray as if to receive the mud. Li then turned his tablet as if to offer the mud. Thereupon, the Master threw the mud down.
The tray was returned to the abbot’s quarters.

Yu Ti turned pale (Huìyuán III). When Minister Yu Ti questioned Chan Master Daotong of Ziyu Mountain, "What is it that black winds blow their ships and cause them to drift down into the realm of the rākṣasa demons? The Master said, "Yu Ti, you guest."
Zuowen asked, "Such a matter is like this. Master Yu turned pale with fear. The Master then pointed and said, "This is drifting and falling into the land of the rākṣasa demons.
Yu asked again, "What is the Buddha? The Master called out, "Yu Di! Yu responded, "Yes.
The Master said, "Do not seek anything else."
Li Bo’s Doubts (Chuan Deng Lu 7): Li Bo, the Regional Inspector of Jiangzhou, questioned Guizong:
"I have often heard that Mount Sumeru can contain a mustard seed, so I do not doubt that. But as for a mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru—is this not mere idle talk?
Guizong said, "People say you, the Prefectural Lord, possess ten thousand scrolls; is this true? Li Bo replied, "I dare not say so. Guizong then rubbed Li Bo’s head with his hand down to his heels.
He then said, "It is about the size of a coconut. Where would one place ten thousand scrolls of poetry and books? Ziming lowered his head in submission.
(Recorded in *Chuan Deng Lu*, Case 14) Shigong Huizang Chan Master of Fuzhou constantly used bows and arrows to receive [students]. (Recorded in *Chuan Deng Lu*, Case 14)
When Sanping arrived, the Master made a gesture of drawing a bow and said, "Behold the arrow! Sanping made a gesture of dodging.
The Master said, "In my entire life, I have set up but one bow and one arrow; I have only been able to shoot half a sage."
Heoshan Beats the Drum (The Ninth Case of Biyan; Dharma Heir of Jiufeng Qian). Master Chengyuan Wuyin of Heoshan gave this instruction:
"To study is called 'hearing'; to cease studying is called 'neighboring. To transcend these two is to truly transcend."
A monk came forward and asked, "What is the true transgression? The Master said, "Know how to beat the drum. He asked again, "What is the absolute truth?
The Master said, "Know how to beat the drum. He asked again, "I do not ask about 'this very mind is Buddha'; what is 'neither mind nor Buddha'? The Master said, "Know how to beat the drum.
He asked again, "When a superior man arrives, how do you receive him? The Master said, "Know how to beat the drum."
Beating the drum.
Guizong drags a stone (a dharma heir of Mazu; *Chuan deng lu*; *Shi yuan*, vol. 2). This is what Yunmen meant by "Xuefeng rolling a ball" and "Guizong dragging a stone."

**Muping Bantu (Disciple of Panlong Kewen; *Chanzhong*)** Master Muping Shandao of Biao Prefecture would not permit any newly arrived monk to pay his respects before first ordering him to carry three loads of earth.
He would then present this verse to him: "The eastern mountain road slopes down by the western hill;
You who have newly arrived, do not refuse these three loads of mud. Alas, you have traveled for many days upon the road."
Clearly facing the Way, yet one becomes lost.
Xuánjiàn’s Chopping of the Plaque (Huìyuán 7): Dēngshān set up his plaque in the bustling marketplace. On the plaque he wrote: "If a Buddha comes, I will beat him;
if a Patriarch comes, I will beat him. *Chuándēng*: Yàntóu set up his plaque. After Yàntóu had abolished the teaching, he... [was in]... the marketplace.
While serving as a ferryman by the lakeside at Ezhou, he erected a wooden signboard on both banks inscribed with these words:
"If there are those who wish to cross, please strike this board once. Whenever anyone struck it, the Master would dance with his oar and ferry them across.

However, the source for Deshan’s setting up of the signboard has not yet been identified. ○ Hebu (Ando) added: The *Zuting shiyuan* (Garden of Affairs from the Patriarchal Hall) and the *Huiyuan* (Compendium of the Source) state: [text continues].
One day, when Xuansha approached Xuefeng, Xuefeng rolled three wooden balls at once.
Xuansha immediately made a gesture as if brandishing a sword-blade. Xuefeng deeply approved of this; thus, Xuanjian acted as Xuansha.
White Clouds Rocking the Oars;
Daowu Rises to Bow (Guannan Dao was once a Dharma heir; *Chuan Deng Lu*, Case 11). The Monk Daowu of Guannan in Xiangzhou.
A monk asked, "What is the Master’s profound depth? The Master descended from his meditation seat, performed a woman’s bow, and said, "Thank you."
"You have come from afar; there is nothing with which to receive you.
Kāśyapa performed a dance (*Huìyuán 1*). Because the Gandharva King presented music to the World-Honored One, at that time the mountains, rivers, and great earth all became the sound of a lute.
Kāśyapa rose and performed a dance. The King asked Kāśyapa, "Is this not [the work of] A..."
The Arhat has exhausted all outflows; how could there still be residual habits? The Buddha said, "In truth, there are no residual habits. Do not slander the Dharma.
The King played the lute three times, and Kāśyapa likewise performed a dance three times. The King said, "Did Kāśyapa not perform a dance?
The Buddha said, "In truth, he never performed a dance. The King said, "How can the World-Honored One speak falsely?"
The Buddha said, "I do not speak falsely. When you play the lute, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all wood and stone become the sound of the lute;
is this not so? The King replied, "It is. The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa was also like this. Therefore, he truly never performed a dance.
Thereupon, the King believed and accepted it.
Yongquan Riding an Ox (Shishuang Zhu’s Successors, *Lamp History* 16). Chan Master Jingxin of Yongquan in Taizhou was visited by two Zen guests, Jiang and De.
On the road, they saw the Master riding an ox; not recognizing him, they said, "The hooves and horns are very distinct;
what can we do? We simply cannot recognize the rider. The Master spurred the ox away, and the two Zen guests rested beneath a tree.
Tea was being brewed. The Master returned and went down to the ox-stable. [The guests] approached him; he inquired after their well-being, invited them to sit, and they drank tea together.
The Master asked the two Chan practitioners, "Where have you recently come from? They replied, "We have come from over there. The Master said, "What is the matter with 'over there'?
One of them lifted up his tea cup. The Master said, "This is still 'this side. What is the matter with 'over there'? The two were speechless.
"Correct. The Master said, "Do not say that only the rider does not recognize the good.
This was Muan of Huanglong (Fayan's successor; *Pudeng lu*, vol. 16), Chan Master Fazhong of Muan at Huanglong in Longxing Prefecture. He rode a tiger.
He resided at Mount Nanyue. Whenever he went out riding a tiger, Confucians and Buddhists alike would bow upon seeing its dust.
Jing Mountain (Jingshan Fazhi, successor of Guishan, *Chuan deng lu* 11). Chan Master Hongyin of Jing Mountain, Hangzhou (the third patriarch of Jing Mountain).

A monk asked, "What is long? The Master said, "Even the thousand sages cannot measure it. The monk asked, "What is short? The Master said, "It will not even fill the eye of a gnat. The monk did not accept this and departed. He went to report this to Shishuang, who said, "It was simply because you were too close to the literal reality. The monk asked, "What is long? Shishuang said, "Without being crooked. The monk asked again. Shishuang said, "Without being crooked. The monk asked, "What is short? Shishuang said, "Without being crooked. The monk asked, "Why do you say 'without being crooked' for both? Shishuang said, "Because there is nothing that can be measured. The monk said, "I still do not understand. Shishuang said, "If you wish to understand, go ask the old monk over there. The monk went to find the other monk, who said, "If you wish to understand, go ask the old monk over there. The monk returned to Shishuang and reported this. Shishuang said, "That fellow is a man of great capacity; he has truly understood the meaning. The monk asked, "How is it that he has understood? Shishuang said, "He has understood that there is no such thing as long or short. The monk said, "I still do not understand. Shishuang said, "If you wish to understand, go ask the old monk over there. "What is short? [The Master replied: "In the midst of the double-six game, there is no shouting for a roll.
This was Chan Master Guichen of Luohan Temple in Zhangzhou (a dharma heir of Xuansha; *Huiyuan*, vol. 8).
A royal official of Zhangzhou requested that he establish a vihāra called Dizang on Mount Shi to the west of the city of Min, and invited the Master to reside there.

He resided there for barely more than ten years. Later, he moved to Lohan Monastery in Zhangzhou, where he extensively expounded the profound essentials of the Way, attracting a great multitude of disciples.
The Master asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Qinzhou. The Master said, "What have you brought with you?
The monk replied, "I have brought nothing. The Master said, "Why do you speak such nonsense before the assembly?"
The monk was speechless. The Master then asked, "Is it not true that Qinzhou produces parrots?
The monk replied, "Parrots come from Longxi. The Master said, "Not by much."

Shishuang served his master (the Dharma heir of Daowu; *Chuan deng lu*, fascicle 15). Chan Master Qingzhu of Shishuang in Tanzhou was designated by Daowu as his legitimate successor before Daowu passed away.
Daowu personally traveled to Shishuang to install him there. The Master attended upon him with diligent devotion, observing every ritual propriety due to a teacher.
When Daowu entered nirvana, disciples gathered like clouds, numbering five hundred in all.

Cijue’s foster mother, Guquan, was sentenced to penal labor (*Sengbaozhuan*). Zen Master Guquan of Mount Heng was sentenced to the prison guard corps of Chenzhou during the Jiayu era because a man named Qingliang falsely accused him, claiming that the Master had once administered a beating to Qing while he was staying at the hermitage. The sentence was severe.
Carrying earth on his back during the summer heat as he passed through a main thoroughfare, he set down his burden and recited a verse, saying: "Today is the sixth day of the sixth month;
the valley springs are choked by the heat. I am not ascending to heaven, but entering hell. Having finished speaking, he smiled and became motionless, like a cicada shedding its shell.

**Changxing (遭虜)** (Successor of Quanren; No. 13 in Huìyuán) *Supplementary Note:* Chan Master Zhìhuī of Chóngyún returned to his former residence at Guǐfēng on Zhōngnán Mountain and established a monastery there.
Later, Emperor Míngzōng of the Later Táng dynasty bestowed upon it the name Changxing.
A monk asked the Head Monk, "What is 'losing the source through following illumination'? The Master said, "My home has been ransacked by bandits."
**Chan Master Xuān of Guīzōng (Huíyuán 12)** Xuān was a native of Hànzhōu. He was a successor of Lángyá Guǎngzhào and maintained a close friendship with Guō Gōngfǔ.
One day, the Magistrate of Nánkāng arrived to deal with certain affairs.
Xuān sent a messenger with a letter to Gōngfǔ, instructing the messenger with these words: "Do not let the County Lady know."
Jian Gongfu was serving as the Commandant of Nanchang at that time. [The spirit] wrote: "I have six more years of worldly karmic ties remaining.
Today, unable to endure this oppression, I wish to take rebirth in your family; I hope you will look upon me with favor. Thereupon, it passed away.
Gongfu was filled with joy and surprise upon receiving the letter. In the middle of the night, his wife dreamed that Xuan entered her bedchamber;
she involuntarily cried out, "This is not the way for a monk to enter! Gongfu asked her the reason.
The wife reported what she had seen. Gongfu called for a lamp to illuminate the written characters and showed them to her; indeed, she was pregnant. When the child was born, he was named Xuanguang.
Upon reaching his first birthday, his memory and questioning were as they had been before. By the time he was three years old, Master Yuanwu Keqin (Heshang Baiyun) passed by their home.
Gongfu called him out to meet the master. As soon as he saw him from afar, the boy called out, "Master, you are my uncle! Yuanwu said, "Give him to the Master."
"How many years have passed since we parted? Xuanchang counted on his fingers and said, "Four years. Duan asked, "Where did we part? Xuanchang replied, "At Bailian Zhuang.
Duan asked, "What is the proof of this? Xuanchang said, "Father and Mother will invite the Master for a meal tomorrow.
Suddenly, a cart passed by outside the gate. Duan asked, "What is that sound outside the gate? Xuanchang acted it out.
[The Master] pushed his cart forward. Duan asked, "How is it when you have passed through? Xuang said, "A single ditch across level ground.
At only six years of age, he passed away without illness.
Master Xin composed this [eulogy]. (He was a Dharma heir of Emperor Tianshuang; *Chuan Deng Lu*, Case 14. Master Haiyin Xin succeeded Langya. He was a native of Gui Prefecture.
He resided at Dinghui Temple in Suzhou. At over eighty years of age, he had been receiving offerings from the household of Defense Commissioner Zhu and frequently visited his residence.
One day, Zhu asked, "Master, will you be able to come to your disciple's home to take rebirth in a future life?
The Master smiled slightly and gave his assent. Upon returning to the temple, he fell ill and passed away several days later. His...
On the day she passed away, a daughter was born to the Zhu family. At that time, Chan Master Yuanzhao Ben was residing at Rui Guang Temple.
Hearing of this matter, he went to visit them. She had just emerged from the birth-chamber; when he took her in his arms and looked at her, she smiled.
Yuanzhao said, "Haiyin, you have dissolved. The girl wept several times and then passed away.
The Four Worthies Ask About the Way (Huìyuán 19): Prime Minister Yú Dí met Zǐyù; State Councilor Péi Xiū questioned the eminent monk Huángbò;
Palace Secretary Yáng Yì penetrated through Guǎnghuì; and Grand Marshal Lǐ Zūnxū attained great enlightenment upon meeting Shímén.
The Three Buddhas’ Turn of Phrase (Huìyuán 19). When the Three Buddhas were with the Fifth Patriarch, they once conversed at night atop a pavilion.
Upon returning to the abbot’s quarters, the lamp had already been extinguished. The Fifth Patriarch then said from the darkness, "Each of you provide a turn of phrase.
Fojian replied, "A phoenix dances in the crimson sky. Foyan said, "An iron snake lies across the ancient road. Foguo said: [The text continues with his response].
"Look beneath your feet. The Fifth Patriarch said, "The one who will extinguish my lineage is Keqin (i.e., Yuanwu).

Regarding Zhenji Tingbo (Huayuan 4): Chan Master Congshen of Zhaozhou Guanyuan (also called Dongyuan), a native of Haoxiang in Caozhou, surnamed Hao, was posthumously titled Great Master Zhenji. A monk asked: "What is the Patriarch?"
Regarding "the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West," the Master said, "The cypress tree in the courtyard. A monk asked, "Master, do not point to external objects to instruct people.
The Master said, "I am not pointing to external objects. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "The cypress tree in the courtyard."
Shouchu Majin (Dharma heir of Yunmen; *Chuan deng lu*, fascicle 23). Zen Master Shouchu of Dongshan. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha?
The Master said, "Three pounds of flax."
Fushi Yuboku (The Successor of Zihu Zong; *Chuan Deng Lu*, Volume 11). Dharma Master Fushi of Zhangzhou once ascended the hall and said:
"I, this mountain monk, have opened a divination shop that can determine people's poverty or wealth and settle their life or death. At that time, a monk stepped forward and said:
"Setting aside life and death, and poverty and wealth, and not falling within the five elements—please, Master, speak directly. The Master replied: "Metal and Wood."
Water, fire, and earth.
Master Nánquán Wáng (Wáng Nánquán’s secular surname was transmitted in the *Lamp Records*, volume eight) of Chízhōu, Chán Master Pǔyuàn, addressed the assembly, saying:
"Master Wáng is selling himself; is there anyone who can buy him? A monk stepped forward and said, "I [will buy him]."
Jiashan bought some coins. Quan said, "Neither acting as if they were expensive nor acting as if they were cheap—how do you buy them?
The monk who offered the price had no reply. (Xiangyan Yuangong, *Chanzang Denglu* 9): While Guishan was lying down, Yangshan went to inquire after him.
Guishan turned his head to look behind him; Yangshan said, "I am your disciple, Master. Why do you need to be so formal? Guishan made a gesture as if to get up.
Yangshan stepped out. Guishan called him back, saying, "I just had a dream; try to interpret it for me.
Yangshan brought a basin of water and a hand towel and presented them to Guishan. Guishan then washed his face.
When Xiangyan arrived, Guishan said, "I have just engaged in a moment of Chan communication with Jizi (Yangshan); it was no ordinary matter."
Yan said, "I understand each point clearly. Guishan said, "Try to explain it then. Yan poured a cup of tea for Guishan.
Guishan said, "These two sons possess spiritual powers that surpass those of Śāriputra."
Puhua描真 (Huiyuan III): Master Puhua was a Dharma heir of Master Baoci of Mount Pan in Youzhou.
As he was about to pass away, he addressed the assembly, saying, "Is there anyone who can paint my true likeness? The assembly all produced their portraits for him to see, but he rebuked them all.
Puhua stepped forward and said, "I have painted it. The Master asked, "Why [do you not show it]?"
He presented it to the Old Monk. Puhua then performed a somersault and went out.
Yaoshan said, "This fellow will later go about like a madman, leading people away. Yaoshan then passed away.
The Old Lady Steals Bamboo Shoots (Huìyuán 4). While traveling on the road, Zhaozhou encountered an old woman who asked him, "Where are you going?
The woman replied, "I am going to steal Zhaozhou’s bamboo shoots. Zhaozhou said, "What will you do when you suddenly encounter an old monk like me? The woman then gave him a slap.

Zhouxiu departed. The practitioner Xi gave silver (Recorded Sayings 14). Yushan ordered the master of offerings to go out and convert people. When the practitioner Ganqi asked him, "Where have you come from?
the monk replied, "I have come from Yushan. Gan said, "What have you come for? The monk replied, "To convert people. Gan said:
"Did you bring the medicine back? The monk asked, "What illness does the attendant have? Gan replied, "If there is anyone [to deliver it], send it; if there is no one, then let it be.
The Master (Shan) was surprised that the monk returned so quickly. The monk said, "I obtained two ingots of silver because the Dharma and the matter were in accord.
The Master ordered him to repeat those words. Once he had finished, the Master told the monk to leave immediately.
He sent silver back to the practitioner’s house. When the practitioner saw the monk returning, he said, “You have come again! and subsequently added more silver as an offering.

Emperor Zhuangzong obtained this treasure (*Chuan Deng Lu*, Vol. 12). When Emperor Zhuangzong of the Later Tang traveled to Hebei and returned to his temporary palace at Weifeng, he issued an edict summoning Chan Master Xinghua Cunjian, asking him: “I have recovered the Central Plains and obtained a treasure.”
No one had ever offered a price for it. Xiang said, "I beg Your Majesty to examine this treasure. The Emperor extended the ends of his *baku-tō* (head-wrap) with both hands.
Xiang said, "Who would dare to offer a price for the treasure of a sovereign? (Xuánjué asked: "Tell me, did Xinghuà approve of Zhuāngzōng? If he approved of Zhuāngzōng, where was Xinghuà's eye?
If he did not approve of Zhuāngzōng, where did the fault lie? The Emperor’s countenance was greatly pleased, and he bestowed upon Xiang purple robes and a monastic title. Xiang...
He accepted neither. The Emperor then bestowed a horse upon the Master for him to ride. Suddenly, the horse bolted; the Master fell and injured his foot.
The Emperor again bestowed medicine for his treatment. The Master called to the head monk, saying, "Make me a wooden crutch.
Once the monk had finished it and brought it to him, the Master took it and walked around the monastery grounds. He asked the monks, "Do you recognize this old monk? They replied, "Yes."
Zheng asked, "I do not recognize you, Master. The Master said, "A 'leaping-foot' Dharma teacher can speak but cannot practice.

(This was the Dharma heir of Yaoshan Weiyan; *Huiyuan*, vol. 5. Chan Master Chuanzi Decheng of Tongzhou Huating. *Note: The term "leaping-foot" (跳-兆+戾) refers to a specific type of practitioner who possesses theoretical knowledge but lacks practical realization.*
His integrity was lofty and remote; his capacity for judgment was extraordinary. He attained the seal of realization at Yaoshan and formed a bond of spiritual comradeship with Daowu and Yunyan.
Upon leaving Yaoshan, he said to his two companions, "You gentlemen should each occupy a region and establish the fundamental principles of Yaoshan.
As for me, my nature is rustic and simple; I delight only in mountains and waters, and in following my natural inclinations."
"I shall depart on my own; I have no further abilities. Later, he learned of my whereabouts. If you encounter an intelligent and sharp presiding abbot (zuozhu), send one person to me.
Should there be someone capable of being refined, I shall take what I have attained throughout my life to repay the kindness of my former master.
Thereupon, they parted company and traveled to Huating in Tongzhou, where he took to a small boat to pass his days according to circumstances, in order to receive [the successor].
Those who traveled to and fro from the four quarters did not know of his lofty conduct at the time, and thus he was called the Boatman Monk.
One day, while mooring his boat by the shore and sitting idly, an official asked, "What is the Master’s daily activity?
The Master held up his oar and asked, "Do you understand? The official said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "The oar sweeps the clear [waters]."
"Golden-scaled fish are rarely encountered. The Master had a verse that said: "For thirty years I have sat upon the fishing platform;
Time and again, yellow eels are caught on the hook. Failing to meet the golden-scaled fish, my efforts are in vain; I shall gather in my line and return home.
Later, Daowu went to Jingkou and encountered Jiaoshan while he was presiding over the assembly. A monk asked, "What is the Dharma-body? Jiaoshan replied:
"The Dharma-body is without marks. [Daowu] asked, "What is the Dharma-eye? Shishuang said, "The Dharma-eye is without flaw.

Daowu could not help but laugh. Shishuang immediately descended from his seat and asked Daowu, "In my response to this monk just now, there must have been something incorrect, which caused you, Venerable Sir, to laugh. I hope you will not withhold your compassion and instruct me. Daowu said:
Xuefeng said, "Master, you are one who has emerged from the world; yet, there is still no teacher for me. Deshan said, "In what way am I not right?
I hope you will explain it to me through and through. Wuye said, "I shall certainly not say anything.
I ask that you, Master, instead go to Chuanzi at Huating. Deshan asked, "What is this man like? Wuye said, "This man has not a single tile above him and..."
"There is not even space for a awl to stand upon. "If you, Master, must go, you should change your robes before departing.
Deshan then dismissed his assembly, packed his belongings, and went straight to Huating. As soon as Chuanshi saw him, he asked, "Virtuous One, in what monastery do you reside?

Deshan replied, "I do not reside in a monastery; where I reside is not like [a monastery]. Chuanshi asked, "What is it that is not like [a monastery]? Deshan said, "It is not something seen by the eyes."
Regarding the previous case, the Master asked, "Where did you learn this? Shishuang said, "It is not where the ears or eyes can reach.
The Master said, "A single phrase that fits the head is a tethering stake for ten thousand kalpas. The Master asked again, "The line hangs down a thousand feet, its intent lies in the deep pool;
three inches away from the hook, why do you not speak? As Shishuang was about to open his mouth, he was struck with a single oar by the Master.
He fell into the water. As soon as Shanshan climbed back onto the boat, the Master said again, "Speak! Speak! Just as Shanshan was about to open his mouth, the Master struck him again.
Shanshan attained great enlightenment and nodded three times. The Master said, "The line on the tip of the pole is for you to play with;
it does not disturb the clear waves, yet its meaning is unique. Shanshan then asked, "Regarding casting the line and throwing the hook—what is your intention? The Master said:
A strand of silk hangs over the green water, floating with the sense of both existence and non-existence. Shanshan said, "The words carry the profound yet there is no path;
the tongue speaks, yet it does not speak. The Master said, "Having fished the entire river until the waves were spent, only then is the golden-scaled fish encountered. Shanshan then covered his ears.
The Master said, "So it is, so it is. He then added, "In the future, you must directly vanish from where you hide your body;
do not hide your body where there are no traces. For twenty years at Yaoshan, I have clarified nothing but this matter."
"Now that you have attained this, do not dwell in cities, capitals, or villages hereafter.

Go instead to the depths of the mountains and, by the side of your spade, seek out one or two [successors]. Do not allow the lineage to be severed. Shan then took his leave, looking back again and again.
The Master called out, "Acarya! Shan turned his head. The Master held up his oar and said, "Take this with you."
It is said that he departed separately, submerging his boat like an overturned vessel as it entered the water. *Hebu (Ando) says:* For thirty years I have roamed the seas;
The waters are clear, the fish appear, yet they do not swallow the hook. When the fishing pole is worn out, plant bamboo anew;
Without calculating the time or effort, attain rest upon finding the opportunity. (Chuanzi Chengzhi’s Verse)
Zhaozhou’s Dog (A Letter from Dahui to a Dharma Heir of Nanquan): A monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?
Zhaozhou said, "No. The monk asked again, "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; why then does the dog lack it?
Zhaozhou said, "Because it still possesses the consciousness of karmic affliction (*karmavijñāna*)."

Linji Zhenren (The Twelfth Lamp): Linji ascended the hall and said, "Upon this ball of red flesh dwells a True Person of No-Station who constantly enters and exits through the gate of the face of all of you. Those of you who have not yet realized it—look, look!
At that time, a monk asked, "What is the True Person of No-Station? The Master stepped down from his meditation seat, seized him, and said, "Speak! Speak!"
The monk hesitated to respond. The Master leaned forward and said, "What is the 'Unranked True Person'? He is nothing but a dried-up piece of shit!
He then returned to his quarters.
Huālín Èhǔ (Mazu’s Dharma heir; *Chúndēng lù*, Case 8): Chan Master Huālín Shànjué of Tánzhōu constantly carried a staff.
At night, he went out among the forest thickets. Every seven paces he shook his mendicant’s staff once and recited the name of Avalokiteśvara once.
One day, the Regional Inspector Pei Xiu visited him and asked, "Does the Master have any attendants?
The Master replied, "I have one or two. Pei asked, "Where are they? The Master then called out, "Dàkōng! Xiǎokōng! At that moment, two tigers emerged from the hermitage.
Later, as he was leaving, Pei Xiu saw them and was struck with alarm. The Master said to him, "There is a guest; please depart. The two tigers roared and left.
Pei asked, "What kind of practice did you cultivate to evoke such a response? After a long silence, the Master asked, "Do you understand? Pei replied, "I do not.
The Master said, "This mountain monk constantly recites the name of Avalokiteśvara."
Qingyuan Yilun (Fifth Patriarch of the Huayuan lineage). Shitou Xiqian asked Master Qingyuan Xingsi: "Does the Great Master of Caoxi still recognize you, Reverend?
Xingsi said: "Do you recognize me now? [Shitou] replied: "Even if one recognizes you, how could one possibly fully grasp it?
Xingsi said: "Though there may be many horns, a single qilin is sufficient."

When Daowu was dressing as a ghost for the Three Saints' visit, the Three Saints arrived at Daowu’s place. Daowu, having anticipated their arrival, stood at the gate wearing a red headband and holding a divine staff.
The Saints said, "Be careful and wait attentively. Daowu responded with an assent. After the Saints had completed their tour of the hall, they came again to pay their respects.
Daowu assumed a dignified posture and sat within the abbot's quarters. As soon as the Saints drew near, Daowu said, "I have a matter to discuss with you."
"May I ask if you have attained it? The Sage said, "That was also just now a wild fox spirit;
get out! (From the *Chuan Deng Lu*, Case 27). As for Shidi of Tiantai, his name and lineage were not recorded.
Once, while the Chan Master Fenggan was walking about in the mountains, he heard the sound of a child crying by the side of the path at Chicheng. He went to investigate and saw a—
The boy was several years old. At first, he was thought to be a shepherd’s child; however, when questioned, he said that he had been abandoned here alone.
Fenggan therefore named him Shide (拾得) and took him to Guoqing Temple, entrusting him to the head cook, saying, "If anyone comes to claim him, you must surely return him to them.
There was a guardian deity of the temple who would daily descend to eat in the monks' kitchen, whereupon it was disturbed by birds.
There was one who picked him up and supported him with a staff, saying, "If you cannot even protect your own food, how can you protect the monastery?
That night, a deity entered a dream of the monks of the entire temple and said, "Shide has struck me. At dawn, the various monks recounted their dreams, and they all matched.

The whole monastery was in an uproar, and a formal petition was submitted to the prefecture and county authorities. When the official messengers arrived, they declared, "This is a worthy man living in seclusion."
The response-body (nirmāṇakāya) of the Bodhisattva should be used to commemorate him; thus, Shi-de was titled "Worthy Man" (Xianshi).
He vanished while reclining upon a stone. Da-jue’s splashing of water (Lectan Dharma-heir; Huayuan, vol. 15). Chan Master Huai-lian of Mount Yuyang in Mingzhou, known as Da-jue.
He was the son of the Chen family of Longxi in Zhangzhou. On the evening of his birth, he dreamed that Śākyamuni descended into his chamber;

consequently, he was given the childhood name Sishou (Zhou of Sishui). As there were such extraordinary omens, everyone recognized them as auspicious signs. He left home to become a monk at the age of seven and received full ordination at the age of fourteen.

He devoted himself earnestly to the study of the Way, never neglecting his practice even for sleep or food. One day, while washing his face, he splashed water upon the ground and experienced a slight awakening.
He immediately set out in search [of the truth], traveling far to the Dharma seat at Letan. There he found his spiritual resonance and received formal certification (*kengyin*).

Regarding the phrase "dropping firewood" (*xingjiao duoxin*): Chan Master Hongshou of Xingjiao in Hangzhou, a dharma successor of National Teacher Huairang (as recorded in *Huiyuan*, fascicle 10), while engaged in communal labor with the National Teacher, attained realization upon hearing the sound of falling firewood.
He composed a verse, saying: "It falls—nothing other than this; Transverse and horizontal..."
"It is not dust. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—these fully reveal the body of the Dharma King.
Master Huanzhong of Daci Temple in Hangzhou (who succeeded Baizhang Hai), one of the Three Teachers, addressed the assembly, saying:
"A foot of practice is better than ten feet of talk; an inch of practice is better than a foot of talk. Dong...
Mount [Dongshan] said, "I do not speak in such a way. The monk asked, "How then? Dongshan said, "Speak that which cannot be practiced;
practice that which cannot be spoken. Yunju said, "When walking, there is no path of speech;
when speaking, there is no path of walking. When neither speaking nor walking, what path should one take?"

2. The Two Elders on Intimacy and Distance (*Chuan Deng Lu*, Case 7). While Jia Shan and Ding Shan were traveling together and engaged in conversation, Jia Shan said, "If there is a Buddha within birth and death, one is not deluded by birth and death.
Ding Shan said, "If there is no Buddha within birth and death, then there is no birth and death.
The two men exchanged views back and forth without reaching a resolution, so they went up the mountain to pay their respects to [Master] Shangshan. Jia Shan then brought up their previous discussion.
He asked Damei, "I do not yet know which of these two is the true one. Damei said, "One is close; one is distant. Jiashan asked, "Which one is the true one?
Damei replied, "Go away for now and come back tomorrow. The next day Jiashan went up again to ask.
Damei said, "The one who is true does not ask; the one who asks is not true."
Mañjuśrī struck the gavel (Recorded Sayings I). As the World-Honored One ascended the seat, Mañjuśrī struck the gavel and said: "Observe closely the Dharma of the Dharma-King;
the Dharma of the Dharma-King is thus. Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from the seat.

Baizhang Rolls Up the Mat (Huìyuán III). One day, while Baizhang Hai was strolling in the mountains with Mazu, they saw some wild ducks. Mazu asked, "What is that? Baizhang replied, "Wild ducks. Mazu asked, "Where have they gone? Baizhang said, "They flew away. Mazu then reached out and twisted Baizhang’s nose. Baizhang let out a cry of pain. Mazu said, "When did they ever go? Baizhang was suddenly enlightened. He rolled up his mat and left. Later, he went to Mount Dongting to see Huangbo. Huangbo asked, "Where have you come from? Baizhang replied, "I have come from Mazu. Huangbo said, "Did he have any instructions for you? Baizhang said, "He had none. Huangbo said, "Even so, he still has something. Baizhang said, "What is it? Huangbo twisted his nose. Baizhang cried out in pain. Huangbo said, "When did they ever go? At this, Baizhang was again enlightened. He bowed and withdrew. This is called "Baizhang Rolls Up the Mat. Dada Wangxiang (Mazu’s Dharma heir; *Chuan deng lu* 8): Chan Master Wuye of Fenzhou was posthumously titled National Teacher Dada.
Whenever a student came to pose a question, he would reply, "Do not engage in false conceptualization."
The Message of Luobou (Fifth Volume of the *Huiyuan*): Luobou went to Tianxian. The Immortal asked, "Where have you come from?
Luobou replied, "I have come from Nanxi. The Immortal said, "Have you brought back news from Nanxi? Luobou said, "'To extinguish'—the news has not yet been extinguished.
The Immortal said, "The most painful thing is that it has not yet been extinguished. Luobou said, "Tell me, what is it that has not yet been extinguished?"
The Immortal said, "Once we have met face-to-face, one will not forget the name for a thousand years. Baofu shook his sleeves and departed.
The Immortal said, "What limit is there to the hand that plays with a dead snake?
Yaoshan’s Melody (A Disciple of Shitou; *Chuan Deng Lu*, Case 14): After High Sāmanera resided in a hermitage, he came to visit during the rain.
Yaoshan said, "You have come. The Master said, "I have. Yaoshan said, "This is medicine. Yaoshan said, "It can indeed kill dampness.
The Master said, "One does not strike this drum and flute. Yunyan said, "There is no hide; what drum would one strike? Daowu said, "There is no drum; what hide would one strike?
Yaoshan said, "Today there is truly a magnificent melody."
Qingyuan’s Lineage (Fifth Generation of the *Chuan Deng Lu*): Qingyuan went to Caoxi, paid his respects, and asked, "What should one attend to so as not to fall into stages?
The Patriarch said, "What have you been doing? Qingyuan replied, "I do not even practice the Noble Truths;
what stages could there be? The Patriarch held him in high esteem, remarking, "In you, I see the spirit of the Second Patriarch at Shaolin."
Jiashan Wields the Sword (Dharma-heir of Huating; *Huayan Yuan* 5). A monk asked Jiashan, "When one brushes away the dust and sees the Buddha, what then?
The Master said, "You must wield the sword. If you do not wield the sword, the fisherman will nest in his hut. Later, the monk asked Shishuang about this.
When the dust is swept away and the Buddha is seen, what then? Shishuang said, "He has no land; where could he meet him?
A monk returned and reported this to the Master (Dongshan). After the Master ascended the hall and finished recounting the story, he said, "In the establishment of the gate, he is not my equal;
yet in the profound discourse on principle, he still falls short of Shishuang by a hundred paces."

Yinping Flies with His Staff (Dharma Heir of Mazu; *Chuan Deng Lu*, Volume 8). Chan Master Yinping of Mount Wutai, surnamed Deng (commonly known as Deng Yinping), ascended Mount Wutai during the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty.
On his journey, he passed through Huaisi, where Wu Yuanji had mobilized troops to defy royal decrees.
As government forces and rebels were locked in combat with neither side yet victorious, the Master said, "I shall—"

To dispel their distress, he tossed his monk’s staff into the air and passed over them by flying through the sky. As the soldiers of both armies looked up in awe, the events corresponded with their prior dream, and their desire for combat was instantly extinguished.
Dongshan on Cold and Heat (Chuan Deng Lu, Case 8). A monk asked Dongshan, "When cold and heat arrive, how can one avoid them?
Dongshan said, "Why not go to a place where there is no cold or heat to avoid them? The monk asked, "What is this place where there is no cold or heat?"
Shan said, "When it is cold, it kills you, O Ācārya; when it is hot, it kills you, O Ācārya.
(From *Chuandeng lu*, fascicle 8) Gushan asked Master Touxi, "When sound and form are pure and true, what is the Way?
Touxi said, "Why do you disturb the Way? Gushan then walked from the east over to the west and stood there. Touxi—
Xuyun said, "If it were not so, it would be a disaster. Gushan then stepped over to the east side. Xuanxi descended from his meditation seat;
just as he had taken two steps, Gushan seized him and asked, "What is the reality of sound and form being pure and true?"
Xixian then took hold of Gushan. Gushan said, "In ten years, will there even be someone here to serve tea?
Xixian said, "What do you want with this old fellow Gushan? Gushan laughed heartily three times.

Yuanyou’s Reply (Huanglong Nan’s Dharma Heir; *Biographies of Buddhist Monks*, Vol. 2): When Chan Master Yunju Yuanyou was residing at Yujian Temple, Prince Xu heard of his reputation and memorialized the throne to grant him a purple robe.
The Master composed a verse to decline the offer, saying: "Sixty years as a monk, my hair has long been white;
Failing to benefit the Empty Gate, I am ashamed to have left home. I pray you grant me a return of the Ministry of Rites’ official decree."
The old monk Mugulu’s cassock;

"The year is spent and the end of the month has come; there is nothing with which to share this year-end feast with you all. For now, let us cook a head of ox from the open field."
[The Master] said, "A white ox. Cooked millet rice. Boiled wild vegetable soup. Singing 'Village Fields' by the fire of wood blocks. Why?
To avoid leaning on others' doorways or huddling by others' walls; otherwise, one would inevitably be called a 'lord' by the people of this age.
