The official was tall. Xian asked, "What are you doing? Yu said, "I am collecting leather and horn for the Master.

Xian took off his head-cloth and cap, threw them on the ground, and Yu immediately went to pick them up. Xian stepped down from his meditation seat, seized him, and said, "Catch the thief! Catch the thief!"
Fayu encountered [Zhao]zhou, who wrapped his head-cloth around Xian’s head and said, “The weather is cold;
let us return, Master. Xian laughed heartily. Fayu then departed.
Sanjiao shouted, “Thief! (A successor of Weishan Yuanzhuo; *Chuan deng lu*, Volume 18). This concerns the Hermit Master Fayu of Sanjiao Mountain in Qizhou. Because...
A bandit leader entered the mountains during a time of chaos and, brandishing a blade, asked the Master, "What treasures or wealth does the Venerable One possess?
The Master replied, "The treasures of a monk are not suitable for you. The bandit asked, "What kind of treasure is it? The Master let out a single, resonant shout.
The bandit did not realize its significance and struck him with his sword.
Baoning slaps his own mouth (the fourth entry in the *Fulampu*, a successor of Yangqi). The supplement states: Zen Master Renyong of Baoning accepted a second invitation from Baoning.
He ascended the hall, clapped his hands three times, slapped his own mouth and shook his hand three times, and then descended from the seat.
Hongying pinched his knee (from the *Linjian Lu*, upper volume; a successor of Huanglong Nan). Cuiyan Zhen pointed to his chest and asked a monk:
"Mañjuśrī is the teacher of the seven Buddhas; for what reason was he unable to emerge from the woman’s samādhi?
Wangming came from the lower regions; for what reason was he able to emerge from the woman’s samādhi? No one could answer. Only Hongying of Shaowu responded to the question.
At that time, he pinched his knee with his hand and departed. Zhen laughed and said, "The customer who buys chopsticks has not yet arrived.
Huanglong Nan was the successor of this master; see *Zongmen Wuku Shiyi*. When the head seat Huanglong Gong took up residence at Chanlin Temple, he visited Master Yu of Fachang.
Master Yu asked him, "I have heard it said that you burn incense for Huanglong."
"Is it so? Cong replied, "I dare not. Yun said, "A dragon gives birth to a dragon; it must be able to raise clouds and spit mist before it can succeed.
Cong said, "It is according to one's own means, whether abundant or frugal. Yun said, "Before you have even lifted the incense, you have already failed Huanglong.
Cong said, "Do not be so talkative. Yun said, "Tell me then: what is the 'real head' of Huanglong?"
When Huigong rose to leave, he lifted his sitting mat (niṣīdana). A monastery attendant happened to call out for the sitting mat to be brought;
as the attendant held it in his hand, Huigong struck him and said, "Thirty years from now, you too will say you have seen this old monk.

Later, Huigong resided at Huaguang Temple in Hengzhou, where he possessed a straightforward and unpretentious manner. He was subsequently arrested by the local authorities, who stripped him of his robes. Once at Huaguang...
Though it encountered a fire, Master Gong’s *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings) remained with its characters undamaged amidst the ashes, while all other papers were completely consumed;
this is truly a manifest verification of the power of Prajñā.
*Xuán yán shàng shí* (From the *Língyān Yuàn guān sì sēng bǎo zhuàn*, concerning Zen Master Jǐng Xuán of Dàyáng Mountain in Yězhōu).
When Zen Master Jǐng Xuán first arrived at Língyān Mountain while traveling, he asked, "What is the formless place of practice (*wúxiàng dàochǎng*)?
The Master pointed to Guanyin and said, "This is it. A certain Mr. Wú, a painter, was about to offer a word [of response] when the Master hurriedly called out, "This has form!"
"What is that which is signless? The Master then attained realization and prostrated himself. Yunshan said, "Why do you not utter a single phrase?
The Master replied, "I would not decline to speak it, but I fear it would take up too much space on paper. Yunshan smiled and said, "These words shall be engraved upon a stone monument."
His full name was Yingshan Xiuming Tiebi (a successor of Tianyi Huai; in the lineage of the Sangbao); he was Chan Master Fayun Yuancong Fashou.
Within the monastic community, he was known as "Iron-Face Shou."
Longya Chanban (Wufeng’s Dharma heir; *Chuan Deng Lu*, Case 17). Chan Master Judo of Longya Mountain in Hunan, while at Cuiwei, asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarchs?
Cuiwei said, "Pass me the meditation board. The Master then passed the meditation board to him.
Cuiwei took it and struck him. The Master said, "I am willing to be struck, but..."
"It lacks the meaning of the Patriarchs. He asked again, "Linji, what is the meaning of the Patriarchs?
Linji said, "Pass me the meditation cushion. The Master then passed the cushion to Linji. Linji took it and struck him immediately. The Master said, "Strike as you will;
nevertheless, there is still no meaning of the Patriarchs. Later, a monk asked, "When you were traveling on pilgrimage, you asked [the masters] two—"
"The meaning of the venerable patriarchs—do you not know whether the two venerable masters’ Dharma-eye is clear or not? The Master said, "It is indeed clear;
however, it simply lacks the meaning of the patriarchs. Dongchan Qi said, "Among the assembly, some say that while the Buddha-dharma exists, there is merely no meaning of the patriarchs.
If one understands it in such a way, what connection could there be? How else should one understand it?"
There is no principle that lacks the meaning of the Patriarch.
Changqing’s Meditation Cushion (Sectarian Lineage: Dharma Heir of Xuefeng; *Huiyuan* 7). Chan Master Huiling of Changqing in Fuzhou had traveled through various Chan gardens.
Later, he visited Lingyun and asked, “What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? Lingyun replied, “The donkey’s business is not yet finished.”
The time for his training had arrived. For twelve years, the Master traveled back and forth between Xuefeng and Xuansha;
he sat through seven broken bundles of rush mats without clarifying this matter. One day, as he rolled up the curtain, he suddenly attained great enlightenment.
He then composed a verse which said: "How very mistaken! How very mistaken! Rolling up the curtain, one sees the whole world. If someone asks..."
"What school do you understand? [Xuefeng] raised his whisk and struck him on the mouth. Xuefeng exclaimed to Xuansha, "This boy has attained thorough penetration!
Xuansha said, "Not yet. This is merely a fabrication of the conscious mind; he must still be tested further before he is truly ready."
In the evening, when the assembly of monks came up to pay their respects, Feng said to the Master, "Tou-tou Bei has not yet consented to you remaining here.
If you truly possess correct realization, bring it forth before the assembly. The Master then offered this verse: "Amidst the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed;
Only when one consents within oneself does one become intimate with it. In the past, I mistakenly sought it along the road; Today, I look..."
"Come into the fire and enter the ice. Juefeng then looked at him and said, "Do not further engage in conceptualization or composition.

The Master asked Juefeng, "The single path transmitted by all the sages of antiquity—please grant me your instruction. Juefeng remained silent for a long while; the Master performed a prostration and withdrew. Juefeng then smiled.
The Master entered the abbot’s quarters to pay his respects. Juefeng asked, "What is it? The Master replied, "Right now..."
The weather was bright and fine as they went on public labor service (*fushō*).
From then on, their exchanges never failed to accord with the profound principle (*genji*). **Panshan’s Meat Stand** (A Dharma heir of Mazu; *Huìyuán*, Vol. 3).

One day, while Panshan was in the marketplace, he saw someone at a butcher shop buying meat and said, "Cut me a pound of the finest. The butcher set down his knife, folded his hands, and said, "Venerable Sir..."
"Which of these is not the essence? Upon hearing this, Shanshan was suddenly and greatly enlightened. He informed Mazu, who again certified his realization.
(Lianzi Taidan [Liangjia’s Dharma heir; *Chuan deng lu* 17). The Venerable Lianzi of Jingzhao Prefecture: his origins are unknown.)
He was a human being whose deeds were quite extraordinary. He had no fixed dwelling and, having received the seal of mind from Dongshan, lived among the common people in Minchuan.
He did not maintain ritual implements nor follow the monastic codes; throughout both winter and summer, he wore only a single robe.
Each day he would go to the riverbank to gather shrimp and clams to satisfy his hunger, and at night he would sleep amidst the paper money at the White Horse Temple on Mount Dong.
The residents called him the "Shrimp Monk. When Chan Master Jing of Huayan heard of this, wishing to determine whether he was genuine or false, he first hid himself among the paper money offerings.
At deep night, as the Master returned, Jing seized him and asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master immediately replied, "The wine table and dishes before the spirit altar. Jing let go of him and said, "It is not in vain that I have granted you [this encounter]."
I was born with the same roots as him. After Yan [Yanzhi] went to Chang’an at the summons of Emperor Zhuangzong, the Master also arrived there first.
Every day he sang and played his own lute, or else feigned madness; whether moving through deep snow or departing, he left no tracks behind.
Later, his final whereabouts remained unknown.
**Baling Yinyuan (Dharma Heir of Yunmen Wenyan; *Chuan Deng Lu*, Case 22)** Xinkai, the Chan Master of Baling, was asked by a monk, "What is the school of Deva?
The Master replied, "Snow in a silver bowl."
Yunyan Baoguan (Dharma Heir of Mazu; *Huìyuán* 3). Supplement: Chan Master Baoyun Luzu of Chizhou. A monk asked, "What is a Buddha?
The Master said, "One who has a crown on his head is not. The monk asked, "What then is it?
The Master said, "One who has no jeweled crown upon his head."

Jingmen Duni (Dharma heir of Beita Zhongguang; *Huìyuán*, volume 15). Master Chéng hào of Yùquán in Jingmén Commandery traveled to various regions to study under Beitā, where he realized the essential point of the mind and attained the Samādhi of Great Freedom (*mahāsvatantra-samādhi*).
He fashioned a loincloth (*vṛṣaṇasūtra*) and inscribed upon it the names of the successive patriarchs, saying: "Only Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are slightly superior. Furthermore—
He wrote [the characters] upon his waistband; thus, the monastic communities referred to it as "White Cloth Underpants" (Hào bùkùn).
During the Yuánfēng era, while leading the assembly at Gǔyǐn in Xiāngyáng, there was a monk named Qīng who also imitated him. Upon seeing this, the Master rebuked him, saying:
"What principles do you possess that you dare to treat this as a mere joke? It will be too late when you vomit blood. Shortly thereafter, at Lùmén, [Qīng] acted exactly as the Master had said.
He departed.
Shushan Pu Dan (Dharma heir of Liangjia; *Huiyuan* 13). Shushan heard that Master Daomian of Mount Maitreya in Fuzhou was addressing the assembly, saying:
"The phrase with a line and the phrase without a line are like a vine leaning against a tree. The Master specifically entered the mountain passes and arrived there just as Daomian was plastering mud.
Biyu asked, "I have heard the Master say that 'there is a phrase and there is no phrase, like a vine leaning against a tree. Is this so? Wuwei said, "Yes.
The Master said, "If suddenly the tree falls and the vine withers, where does the phrase return? Wuwei set down his mud-plastering tray, laughed heartily, and returned to his quarters.
The Master said, "I have traveled three thousand *li* and sold my cotton robe just to ask this."
"I have come for this very reason. How can you, Preceptor, deceive me? Baizhang called to his attendant, "Bring three hundred coins to give to this senior monk.
He then instructed him, saying, "In the future, there will be 'One-Eyed Dragon' who will pierce through the truth for you."
The next day, Guishan ascended the hall for the discourse. The Master came forward and asked: "The principle of the Dharmakāya is a principle beyond the profound and subtle;
not even the realm of 'is' and 'is not' can seize it, yet this is still merely a matter on the side of the Dharmakāya. What is the matter that transcends it? Guishan raised his whisk.
The Master said, "This is still merely a matter on the side of the Dharmakāya. Guishan asked, "What is the Dharmakāya?"
In the aforementioned matter, the Master snatched away the whisk, folded it, and threw it to the ground, then returned to the assembly. Guishan said, "Dragons and snakes are easy to distinguish;
a patch-robed monk is difficult to deceive. Later, hearing that Master Mingzhao Qian had appeared in the world at Wuzhou, he went straight there to pay his respects.
Mingzhao asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Min Province. Mingzhao asked, "Have you ever been to Great Baizhang?"
The Master said, "I have arrived. Zhao asked, "What words or phrases did you encounter? The Master recounted the previous story.
Zhao said, "Miaoyan can truly be called 'head straight and tail straight,' yet he simply did not meet a true connoisseur. The Master still did not understand.

He asked again, "If one suddenly encounters a tree falling and the vines withering, where do the words return? Zhao said, "This will only cause Miaoyan to laugh even more freshly. At these words, the Master was enlightened.
Having attained great enlightenment, he said, "It turns out that there was a blade within Huishan’s smile. He gazed afar, prostrated, and repented his error.

Baofu’s Mountain Excursion (Seventh in the *Huìyuán*, Dharma Successor of Xuefeng):

Hot and Idle Words.
Qianfeng’s Single Path (Dharma heir of Liangjie; *Huiyuan* 13). A monk asked Qianfeng, “The Buddhas of the ten directions all share this single path to the gate of nirvana.
I wonder, where does the beginning of this path lie? Qianfeng took up his staff, drew a line, and said:
Here, a monk requested instruction from Yunmen. Yunmen picked up his fan and said, "The fan leaps up to the Thirty-three Heavens and pokes the nostrils of Śakra;
a carp from the Eastern Sea receives a single blow, and the rain pours down like an overturned basin."
The Three Barriers of Tuṣita (True Purity Wen’s Dharma Heir; *Huìyuán* 17). Master Cóngyuè of Tuṣita established three barriers to question practitioners. First:

"One day you pull up weeds to investigate the profound, seeking only to see your nature. Right now, where does your original nature reside? Second: "Only when you recognize your own nature can you escape birth and death.

When the light of your eyes falls to the ground, what will you do? Third: "If you have not yet attained the Way, you must seek it. If you have already attained the Way, you must not lose it. Tell me, how can you avoid losing it?"

"How does one achieve liberation? The third [question] was: "Having attained liberation from birth and death, one knows the place of departure; when the four great elements separate, where does one go?
Guquan followed his circumstances (Fenyang Zhao’s Dharma heir; *Huìyuán*, vol. 12). This is the Chan of Guquan Daodao at the Bājiā Hermitage on Mount Nanyue.
The Master was leaning against a pillar when Layman Yu (later the abbot of Fachang Temple) came to visit. Layman Yu asked, "Is the hermitage master here?
The Master said, "Who is it? He replied, "A wandering monk. The Master asked, "What do you want? He said, "To pay my respects to the hermitage master.
The Master said, "It happens that the hermitage master is not here. He asked, "And what about you? The Master said, "I told you he was not here; why speak of 'you' and 'me'?"
He dragged him out by the neck. When the man came again the following day, the Master again drove him out. On another day, the man came once more and asked, "Is the hermitage master here?
The Master said, "Who is it? He replied, "A wandering monk. Without even lifting the curtain, he entered.
The Master grabbed him by the chest and pinned him down, saying, "Tigers and wolves roam here; you son of a dog, you have come to beg three or four times!"
"What is it? he asked. The Master replied, "People say that the Hermitage Master has personally seen Fenyang.
The Master took off his robe and shook it out, saying, "You say I have seen Fenyang; how extraordinary is that? He asked, "Who is the master of this hermitage?
The Master said, "One must discern him upon entering the gate. He asked, "Is it not simply this very thing? The Master said, "How many people have you deceived?"
[The monk] said, "Where were you just now? The Master said, "When listening is not true, one calls a bell a jar.
[The monk] said, "When the myriad dharmas are extinguished, the whole body is manifested; where the ruler and subject meet, the right departs from the center.

The Master said, "You ignorant fellow, stop being so ignorant! Why do you create such confusion? [The monk] asked, "I wonder, when a guest arrives, with what will you receive them? The Master said, "Yunmen."
"Stapled cakes and Zhaozhou’s tea. [The student] said, "If that is so, then I shall go to thank the Master for his offerings.
The Master rebuked him, saying, "I have not even planted the great seeds here yet; how can you already speak of thanking me for my offerings?"
Yuanzhao Xi (Sengbao Zhuan; successor of Tiantai Yihuai): During the early Yuanyou era, Chan Master Yuanzhao retired from Huilin Temple in the capital and returned to Gusu.
There he met Master Zi at Ganlu Temple and said, "Are you not Master Zi?
Zi replied, "I am. The Master teased him, saying, "You are merely a village lion. Zi responded immediately, "A village [lion]..."
Performing in the village of Siṃhapura, the tip of the brow and the eyes move in unison. Opening his mouth, he is straightforward from within;

though he is coarse and does not welcome people taking him by the fist, even if one were to perform such antics all the way to the imperial palace, it would still be nothing more than a hollow clamor.
Shisui Mei failed to realize the irony of this.
The Life of Master Baozhi (compiled by Huìyuán, vol. 2). Master Baozhi was originally the child of a woman of the Zhu family from Dongyang in Jinling.
On the Shangsi festival, she heard the crying of a child within an eagle’s nest; she climbed the tree and retrieved it, raising him as her own son.

At the age of seven, he entered the monastic life under the śramaṇa Sengjian at Mount Zhongshan and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of dhyāna and contemplation. This was during the second year of the Taishi era of the Song dynasty.

He had gray hair and walked barefoot, wearing a brocade robe. He traveled back and forth beneath Mount Xuan and the Jian River, carrying a pair of scissors, a fly-whisk, and a staff over his shoulder, with a literary text slung across his back.
In the second year of the Tianjian era, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty issued an imperial decree to inquire:

"Your disciple’s afflictions and delusions have not yet been eliminated; how may they be cured? He replied, "By the twelve [links of dependent origination]. The Emperor asked what the meaning of this was.
The answer was: "Even during the time spent on writing characters, he was all the more unintelligible within the measured intervals of the water-clock.
The Emperor once issued an edict for the painter Zhang Sengyou to paint the Master’s likeness. Whenever Sengyou set his brush to the work, he could not achieve a definitive result.

The Master then used his finger to incise his face, revealing eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara with distinct features of exquisite beauty, appearing sometimes compassionate and sometimes majestic. Sengyou—
In the end, he was unable to complete it.
The Sixth Patriarch’s Statue Was Difficult to Mold (*Chuan Deng Lu* 5). A monk from Shu named Fangbian came to visit the Patriarch and said, "I am skilled at molding statues.
The Patriarch assumed a stern expression and said, "Try molding one then. Fangbian did not grasp the meaning; he then proceeded to mold a likeness of the Patriarch.
It was seven inches high and executed with exquisite skill. When the Patriarch saw it, he said, "You are skilled in shaping clay, but not in understanding Buddha-nature.
He rewarded him with garments and other items, and the monk bowed in thanks before departing.
**Chan Master Huaiyun of Changjing Temple in Jingzhao Prefecture (Dharma Heir of Mazu;

*Chuan Deng Lu*, Case 7)** Someone asked the Chan Master, "The Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground that you transmit—is it the mind of True Suchness, the mind of deluded thought, or the mind that is neither true nor deluded?
Is it the mind transmitted outside the teachings of the Three Vehicles? The Master said, "Do you see what is before your eyes?"
"Is it empty space? [The monk] said, "I know it is always before one's eyes, yet people themselves do not see it.
The Master said, "Do not mistake a reflection for the reality. [The monk] asked, "How about you, Master? The Master struck the air three times with his hand.
[The monk] asked, "What is it, then? The Master said, "You shall understand it later."
Yunmen’s “Withdrawing the Gaze” (*Renyantenmoku*): Whenever Yunmen saw a monk, he would look at him and say, “Discern! Heh!
Those who recorded this referred to it as “Gazing, Discerning, and Heh. Chan Master Deshan Mi excised the word “gaze,” leaving only “Discern! Heh!
The monastic community came to call this the “Eulogy on Withdrawing the Gaze. Chan Master Beita Zu composed a verse on it, saying: “Yunmen’s gaze and discernment.”
Smiling broadly. To hesitate is to meet his "Gu-jian-yi. No matter how many clever stratagems Zhang Liang may possess, in the end they will be difficult to employ here.
Wuben called it extraordinary (Yunyan Cheng’s Dharma heir; Huayuan 13). Chan Master Wuben Liangjia of Dongshan in Ruizhou. He went to study under [Yunyan].
Guishan asked, "Recently I heard the story of National Teacher Nanyang Zhong regarding 'insentient things preaching the Dharma.
I have not yet fathomed its subtlety. Guishan said, "Does the Venerable One remember it? The Master replied, "I remember it. Guishan said, "Try to recite one passage for me. The Master then recited:
A monk asked, "What is the mind of the ancient Buddha? The National Teacher said: [The text continues with the National Teacher's response].
The monk pointed to a wall, a tile, and some rubble, saying, "Are these not insentient? The National Teacher said, "Yes. The monk asked, "Do they also understand how to preach the Dharma?
The National Teacher said, "They constantly preach; they preach with blazing intensity without interruption. The monk asked, "Why do I not hear it?
The National Teacher said, "It is you yourself who do not hear; it cannot be that they hinder others from hearing. The monk said:
The monk asked, "I do not yet understand who is able to hear this. The National Teacher replied, "All the sages are able to hear it.

The monk said, "Does the Master also hear it? The National Teacher said, "I do not hear it. The monk said, "If the Master does not hear it, how can you know that insentient things are capable of preaching the Dharma?
The National Teacher said, "It is fortunate that I do not hear it. If I were to hear it, I would be equal to all the sages; you [would then be unable to distinguish between them]."
[The Master] said, "Then they would not hear my preaching of the Dharma. The monk asked, "In that case, sentient beings have no share [in it].
The National Teacher said, "I preach for the sake of sentient beings; I do not preach for the sake of the various sages. The monk asked, "After sentient beings have heard it, what then?
The National Teacher said, "They are no longer sentient beings. The monk asked, "On what scriptural authority is there 'preaching by the insentient'? The National Teacher said...
The Master said, "It is evident that such words do not accord with the scriptures; they are not the talk of a gentleman.
Have you not seen it stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: 'The lands speak, sentient beings speak, and all things of the three periods of time speak'?

Having finished citing this, the Master said, "I also have this here, but it is rare to meet someone who can realize it. The student said, "I have not yet understood; I beg the Master to point it out to me."
[Zhaozhou] showed [him]. Guishan held up his whisk and asked, "Do you understand? The Master said, "I do not understand. He requested, "Please, Reverend, explain it to me.
Guishan said, "The mouth born of one's parents shall never speak for the sake of a son. The Master asked, "Are there others who, at the same time as you, aspire to the Way?
Guishan said, "From here, going toward Shiling Youxian, there are interconnected stone chambers where Yunyan Daoying resides."
"If a person can brush aside the grass to gaze at the wind, they will surely be held in high esteem by you, my son.
The Master asked, "I wonder, what kind of person is this? Baizhang said, "He once questioned me, saying: 'When a student wishes to go serve his teacher, how should it be?
I replied to him, 'One must completely cut off all leakage. He then said, 'Does this not accord with the teacher's intent?'"
"No," the old monk said. "First of all, you must not say that the old monk is here. The Master then took his leave and returned to Mount Gui.
He went directly to Yunyan, recounted the preceding circumstances, and then asked, "Who can hear the Dharma preached by the insentient?
Yunyan replied, "The insentient can hear it. The Master asked, "Does the Master hear it as well? Yunyan said, "If I were to hear it..."
"You have not heard me preach the Dharma. The Master asked, "Why have I not heard it? Yanguan held up his whisk and said, "Do you hear it now?
The Master replied, "I do not hear it. Yanguan said, "If you do not even hear me preaching the Dharma, how much less can you hear the insentient preaching the Dharma?
The Master asked, "In which scriptures does the preaching of the insentient appear? Yanguan...
He said: "Have you not seen it stated in the *Amitābha Sūtra* that 'the waterfowl and the trees and forests all recite the Buddha’s name and the Dharma'?
Upon this, I attained realization and composed a verse, saying: How wondrous! How truly wondrous! The insentient preach the Dharma; inconceivable indeed.
If one listens with the ears, it will ultimately be difficult to understand; Only when hearing through the faculty of sight can one truly know."
The Great Chan Master Fuzhi Tong of Mount Wutai (Successor of Guizong Chang; *Cueyuan* 4).

While serving under Master Guizong Chang at Mount Wutai, [there were two "Great Chan Masters" among the Buddhas of Chan: one named Jingtong, who succeeded Yangshan; the other was Zhitong, who succeeded Guizong Chang].
One night, he suddenly cried out, "I have attained great enlightenment! The assembly was startled by this. The following day, Guizong ascended the hall and gathered the monks.
The assembly said, "Last night he came forth having attained great enlightenment. Chanfo stepped forward and said, "I, [Name].
Zong asked, "What principle have you seen that you speak of 'great enlightenment'? Chanfo replied, "In the beginning, my teacher was originally a woman.
Zong remained silent, struck by this remark.
Yicun Returns to the Hermitage (Huìyuán 7). When Chan Master Yicun of Xuefeng was dwelling in a hermitage, two monks came to pay their respects.
Seeing them approach, he propped his hand against the hermitage door, leaned his body out, and asked, "What is this? The monks also said, "What is this?
Yicun lowered his head and returned to the hermitage.
Lao Guan Closes His Door (Dharma Heir of Huangbo; *Chuan Deng Lu*, Vol. 12). Chan Master Lingguan of Niaoyan Mountain in Fuzhou (commonly known as Lao Guan).
He usually kept his door bolted, and few people ever saw him; he would only open it when a lay believer arrived at mealtime to deliver offerings.
One day, Xuefeng waited for an opportunity and knocked on the door. When the Master opened the door, Xuefeng suddenly grabbed him by the chest and asked, "Are you an ordinary man or a sage?
The Master spat at him and said, "You wild fox spirit! He then pushed him out and shut the door. Xuefeng said, "So be it."
It only requires that you recognize this elder brother.
In the *Shàn-lín lèi-jù*, it is recorded that the Senior Seat (Shàngzuò) Guānyú was walking with two senior monks (*shàngzuò*) and saw them catching fish.
Seeing one fish leap out of the net, Guānyú said, "How magnificent! He is truly like a monk. Míng said, "How can he compare to the present [case]?"
At that time, he did not fall into another’s net. Yunmen said, "You still lack awakening. Mingxing realized this only after traveling thirty li.

Shibo Jiantu (Dharma heir of Yunyan Cheng): While Chan Master Sengmi of Shishan in Tanzhou was walking with Dongshan, they suddenly saw a white rabbit scurry past. The Master said, "How clever! Dongshan asked, "How so? The Master—
Yun said, "It is very much like a layman being appointed as a high minister. Dong said, "An old man like me making such remarks.
Yun asked, "What about you? Dong replied, "A family of generations of official rank, now temporarily fallen into obscurity."
**Mingjiao Jiangxing (Dongshan Cong’s Dharma Heir; *Cenlin Leiju* 9)** Chan Master Mingjiao Song initially traveled from Dongshan to Mount Kang and took up residence at the Dharma seat of Kaixian.
The abbot, perceiving that he was young and keen on literary pursuits, appointed him as the Secretary.
Mingjiao laughed and said, "Would I do this for you merely for a cup of ginger-and-apricot soup? Thereupon, he departed. (*Lin*)
[Record of Mazu]:
Regarding Mazu’s salt and vinegar—Mazu was propagating the Dharma in Jiangxi. Nanyue Huairang asked the assembly, "Does Daoyi preach the Dharma for the community?
The assembly replied, "He has already preached the Dharma for the community. Huairang said, "No one at all has brought [anything back] to me."
"A message has arrived. The assembly had no reply. Thereupon, he sent a monk away, instructing him: "When he ascends the hall, simply ask him, 'What is it?
and remember the words he speaks. The monk went and acted exactly according to Xuefeng's instructions.
Hui returned and said to Xiangruang, "Mazu said, 'Since the days of chaos, for thirty years I have never lacked salt and sauce.
Xiangruang agreed with this.
[This was] Zhulin Mazhuai.

Dizang of Muping Wearing Straw Sandals and Plowing the Fields (A Dharma Heir of Xuansha; *Huiyuan* 8). Chan Master Guichen Dizang of Fuzhou, while planting his hoe, saw a monk and asked, "Where have you come from?
The monk replied, "From the South. The Master said, "The Buddha of the South."
The monk asked, "What is the Dharma like? The Master said, "The assembly debates it in a great clamor. The Master said, "How can it compare to my way here:
planting fields and eating the rice I earn? The monk said, "But what about the three realms? The Master said, "What do you call the 'three realms'?"
The monk remained silent.
Lan Zan (a Dharma heir of the Fourth Patriarch) was roasting yams. Regarding Zen Master Mingzan of Mount Nanyue in the Tang dynasty: his clan and place of birth are unknown.
Initially, while traveling, he went to Mount Song to attend upon Chan Master Pujie, who was then widely propagating the Dharma. However...
Thus, he silently realized the mind of stillness and entered into a firm accord with the nature of man through profound contemplation.

He sought seclusion on Mount Heng, where while the assembly of monks engaged in construction work, he remained at ease. Even when subjected to slanderous words, he felt no shame whatsoever; at that time, people called him Làn Zàn.
Emperor Dezong of the Tang dynasty, having heard of his reputation, dispatched an envoy to summon him. When the envoy arrived at his dwelling, he proclaimed the imperial decree.
The Emperor issued a decree that the Venerable One should rise to express his gratitude. The Master was then just stirring up cow-dung fire to seek out roasted yams to eat;
with cold tears hanging from his chin, he did not respond. The messenger laughed and said, "Please, Venerable One, wipe your tears.
The Master replied, "How could I have the leisure to wipe away the tears of a worldly person? He ultimately did not rise. The messenger returned and reported this to the Emperor. De...
Zong deeply admired and sighed in praise of this.
(From *Huiyuan* 4): Once, when Zhaozhou was walking with Attendant Wenyuan, he pointed to a patch of ground.
Dizang said, "A good place here to establish a checkpoint. Wenyuan immediately went to stand by the roadside and said, "Bring out your official pass!
The Master then gave him a slap. Wenyuan said, "The pass is clear; you may pass."
Lao-shen’s Four Gates (Biyan Lu I). Zhaozhou ascended the hall and said: "When a person of integrity speaks of heterodox teachings, those heterodox teachings are entirely orthodox.
When a heterodox person speaks of orthodox teachings, those orthodox teachings are entirely heterodox. Elsewhere, they are difficult to see but easy to recognize;
here with me, they are easy to see but difficult to recognize. Question: "What is Zhaozhou? The Master replied: "The East Gate, the West Gate, the South Gate."
The Northern Gate:
Master Shibei’s Three Phrases (*Sengbao zhuan*, Vol. 4). The Great Master Xuansha Zongyi of Fuzhou was named Shibei.
He was a native of Min County in that province, surnamed Xie. Because the Great Dharma is difficult to uphold and those of superior capacity are rarely encountered, his students...
Relying on words to produce understanding leads to following after appearances and losing the fundamental principle. Therefore, the essential tenet is shown in three statements:
"The first statement is for you to personally take responsibility for yourself; it is already fully present and complete, for throughout the entire ten directions there is nothing else.
It is simply you—so who else could see or hear? All that comes forth is the activity of your own mind-king, entirely established as immovable."

Wisdom. It lacks only one thing: self-acceptance. This is called "opening the gate of skillful means" to lead you to believe that there is a portion of true permanence flowing through, spanning from antiquity to the present, which has never not been so and never not been otherwise.
However, this statement merely establishes a state of equality. Why? Because it is simply using words to dispel words and using principles to pursue principles; it remains level.
It is merely that the constant nature connects with objects to benefit sentient beings. Furthermore, regarding the fundamental tenet, this still clarifies what precedes but not what follows;
it is called "one flavor" and "level reality. It is the measure of partial realization of the Dharma-body, yet it contains no phrase that transcends the ordinary.
One dies beneath the words and lacks any portion of freedom. If one knows the measure of transcendence, one will not be driven by the demons of the mind.

Entering into the midst of the level, one immediately undergoes a transformation and descends with full presence. This is called "penetrating the Great Way" without falling into the view of a settled, ordinary state;

this is what is termed the first phrase of the fundamental principle. The second phrase involves turning the cause toward the fruit, without clinging to the principle of the ordinary, suchness, or uniformity.
This expedient means is called "shifting positions to meet the occasion," wherein birth and killing are exercised with mastery, and bestowing and taking away are performed with freedom.

Acting according to what is appropriate, one enters birth and death to extensively benefit all beings. Completely transcending the realms of form, desire, attachment, and views, this expedient means is called the Buddha-nature that suddenly surmounts the three realms.
This is termed the simultaneous illumination of two principles and the concurrent manifestation of two meanings;
it is not moved by the two extremes, and its wondrous function is manifest before us. This is called the second sentence of the fundamental tenet.
The third phrase reveals the possession of great wisdom. Its nature and characteristics penetrate the fundamental source, transcending all limited views.

It is luminous in the yin and penetrating in the yang, pervading the entire dharma-realm. This single true essence manifests great function before us, responding and transforming without fixed direction.
"Fully employed and fully not employed; fully arising and fully not arising. This expedient means is called the gate of the samādhi of compassion.
This is what is known as the essential principle of the third phrase.
Yuan'an of Luopu in Lizhou (the sixth patriarch in the *Huiyuan*, the successor of Yanguan Qisheng).
One day he said to his disciples: "I shall depart at any moment. If anyone asks you a question, answer it;
if you can respond correctly, I will entrust you with my bowl and robe. He continued: "If you say this is it, you are placing a head upon a head. If you say it is not..."
He immediately cut off his head, seeking to live. The first seat in the hall replied, "The green mountains do not lift their feet;
beneath the sun, one does not pick up the lamp. An said, "Go! You cannot support my school.
Yancong, from the upper seat, said, "Setting aside these two paths, I ask the Master not to question me. An said, "Not yet—speak further. Yancong said, "Yancong."
"Your Way is not exhaustive," [Nanquan] An said. Yancong replied, "I do not concern myself with whether your Way is exhaustive or not.

He continued, "Yancong has no attendant; I am here solely to respond to the Master. Nanquan An then returned to his quarters. That night, he summoned Yancong and said, "Today you have responded to this old monk quite reasonably.
According to you, you ought to have grasped the essential intent of the former master. The former master said: 'The eye...'"
"Before there was any dharma; the intent lies right before one's eyes. It is not a dharma of the present moment, nor is it something reached by the ears or eyes.
Now tell me: which phrase is the guest, and which is the host? Yancong was utterly bewildered and did not know how to answer. An said, "Kū! Kū! (Suffering!)
At the third watch, the assembly requested that Dao’an respond on their behalf to inquiries. Dao’an said, “The Compassionate Boat does not sail upon the vast blue waves;
at Jianxia, it is in vain to release the wooden goose. Having spoken thus, he passed away in stillness.
Fayuan (of Mt. Guishan Fayuan) was a monk whose demeanor was stern, cold, austere, and simple; the monks revered him.
When Fushan Yuan and Tianyi Huai were still among the assembly, they went specifically to visit and question him. It happened to be a time of bitter snow and cold;
Xing scolded and drove them away, even splashing water on them until their robes and bedding were all soaked. As for the others...
The monks were all angry and departed. Only Huiyuan remained; he folded his bedding together, adjusted his robes, and sat back down in the guest quarters.
Xingshao arrived and rebuked him, saying, "If you do not leave immediately, I shall beat you.

Huiyuan stepped forward and said, "We two have come from thousands of miles away specifically to study the Chan of the Master. How can we simply depart because you splashed us with a bucket of water? If..."
"Even if you beat me to death, I will not go. He said with a wry smile, "If you two wish to practice Zen, you should instead go to hang the memorial tablets [at the monastery].
Daowu of Guannan in Qunzhou (from *Huìyuán*, Vol. 4). A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master took his tally-stick (a *jiǎn*, which is a *hù*) and bowed, saying, "Yo! Yunding Mountain.
Master Defu composed a verse on the general meaning of past and present [cases], saying: "Dowu brandishes his ritual tablet; those who understand are like him. Shigong draws his bow;
those who know are the true practitioners. (Chuan Deng Lu 29) Bimoye held up a staff (a successor of Lingtan;
Chuan Deng Lu 10). The Song Dynasty biography states: His name was Changyu, his surname Yin, and he was a native of Fanyang.
He left the household life at An Guo Temple in northern Yan. He came to reside at Bimora Rock on Mount Wutai, which is the very place where Mañjuśrī subdued the dragon;
it was named for that reason. He constantly carried a wooden fork.

Whenever he saw a monk coming to pay his respects, he would immediately thrust the fork across the monk’s neck and say, "Which demon or spirit taught you to go forth from the household life? Which one..."
The demon-possessed one taught you how to travel on foot. "If you can speak, you die under the staff; if you cannot speak, you die under the staff.
Speak quickly! Few among the students were able to respond. Only Jingtong of Mount Huo in Jinzhou (who was later known as Dachenfo) did so:
as soon as he arrived, he leaped into the Master’s embrace and sat there. The Master patted him three times on the back, and Huoshan immediately ran out.
Yunmen said, "From three thousand *li* away, you have deceived me into coming.
Yunyan (the Dharma heir of Yaoshan Yan) felt for his pillow. Daowu asked Yunyan, "Of the thousand hands and eyes of Great Compassion, which one is the true eye?
Yunyan replied, "It is like a person at night feeling for their pillow with their back turned. Daowu said, "I understand."
Yan asked, "How do you understand this? I replied, "My whole body is hands and eyes. Yan said, "You have spoken quite well;
you have only spoken to eighty percent of it. I asked, "What about you, Elder Brother? Yan replied, "My entire being is hands and eyes."

Nanquan Points to a Flower (Chuan Deng Lu 8). While Master Lu Xun was conversing with Nanquan, the Master said, "Dharma Master Zhao said, 'Heaven and earth share the same root as I; the myriad things are one body with me. How extraordinary!"
Nanquan pointed to the peony flowers in the courtyard and called to the Grand Master, saying, "When people of this age see this single stalk of flowers, it is like being in a dream.
Caoshan Qingrui (a dharma heir of Liangjie;

*Chuan Deng Lu*, Case 17) asked: "I am solitary and poor; I beg the Master for [instruction]. Caoshan Baijiu (a dharma heir of Liangjie; *Chuan Deng Lu*, Case 17). Caoshan Qingrui asked: "I am solitary and poor; I beg the Master [for instruction]."
Zhengji said, "Master, Acharya Rui, come forward. Rui approached. The Master said, "Three cups of Bai family wine from Quanzhou.
Rui replied, "I have not even wet my lips yet. Xuangjue asked, "Where is it? Give him some wine to drink."
**True Ultimate Pure Tea (Chuan Deng Lu 10)** Zhaozhou asked a monk, "Have you been here before? The monk replied, "I have. Zhaozhou said, "Go drink tea.
He asked another monk, "Have you been here before? The monk replied, "I have not. Zhaozhou said, "Go drink tea.
The head of the monastery asked, "It is understandable that one who has been here should go; but how can one who has never been here go to drink tea?"
The Governor summoned the head monk of the monastery. The monk responded with an assent. The Governor said, "Go drink tea.

(Xuánquán Zǎojiǎo [a successor of Yántóu; *Huìyuán* 8]). Chán Master Huìjī Chāohuì of Hánglóng Mountain first visited Yántóu and asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Yántóu said, "Can you even save your own rice-cakes? Huìjī—
He said, "I understand. Huizhou said, "For now, let us save the rice cakes. Later, he went to Xuánquán and asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
Xuánquán picked up a stalk of soapberry (*sòjiǎo*) and asked, "Do you understand? Huì said, "I do not understand. Xuánquán set down the soapberry and made a gesture of doing laundry.
Huì then prostrated himself and said, "I now know that the Buddha-dharma has no other [essence]. Xuánquán said: [The text ends here.]
"What principle have you seen? Huì said, "I once asked Yantou [Guishan]. Yantou said, 'Can you still untie rice cakes?
Untying rice cakes is merely untying what is stuck. When the Master raised up the soapberry brush, that too was untying what is stuck.
That is why it is said there is no difference. Quan laughed heartily, and Huì subsequently attained realization.
Dongshan Liangjie and Guishan Lingyou (Chuan Deng Lu 11): When Yangshan was traveling with Guishan, they arrived at a stone platform where Guishan sat.
As Yangshan stood in attendance, a crow suddenly dropped a red persimmon before him. Guishan picked it up and gave it to Yangshan. Yangshan—
Having received it and washed it, he presented it to Muzhou. Muzhou asked, "Where did you get this? Yangshan replied, "This was moved by the Master’s virtue.
Muzhou said, "You shall not be without your share," and he immediately divided it in half and gave a portion to Yangshan.
Xuansha remarked, "Great Muzhou was pinned down by Yangshan with a single sitting; even to this day, he cannot rise."
From Zhandu Gua (Seventh Generation of the Dharma Lineage of Xuefeng; *Huiyuan* 7). Following the occasion when Baofu was selecting melons, Dayuan Fu arrived.
The Master said, "If you can say something, I will give you a melon to eat. Fu replied, "I have brought one here alone. The Master handed him a slice. Fu took it and immediately departed.
The Master Jinshuo (Huayuan III) said: "The Dharma is fundamentally without mutual obstruction; the three periods of time are likewise so.
Even for one who is unconditioned and without affairs, there remains the difficulty of the golden chain."
The Elephant-Bone Iron Collar (Huìyuán 15): Yúnmén went to visit Xuěfēng. At that time, Xuěfēng was sitting cross-legged atop a stack of firewood, preaching the Dharma to the assembly.
Yúnmén stepped forward and, looking at him intently, said, "There is a three-hundred-jin iron collar upon your neck; why do you not take it off?"
Feng said, "For what reason have you come to such a state? Yunmen wiped his eyes with his hand and hurried out. Feng was struck by this as extraordinary.
The next day, ascending the seat, Feng said, "There is a turtle-nosed snake on Nanshan; everyone, look well when you go in and out.

**Ancient Worthies’ Fire-Scraps (Huìyuán 9): Master Bǎoyún of Lǔzú Mountain in Bāzhōu.** Whenever a monk came to see him, he would simply face the wall. Hearing of this, Nánquán said, "I usually tell monks to try to understand [the Way] before the Buddha appeared in the world; yet I still cannot find even one or half of one who succeeds. For him to act in such a way will take him as long as a donkey’s years. *Commentary:* The Master of Lǔzú was a man of great capacity. When people come seeking the Way, they must first sever their attachments to all things. If one has not yet severed these attachments, how can one possibly encounter the Way? Therefore, he faced the wall to cut off all external entanglements. However, his method was too extreme; it lacked the skillful means of a true teacher. Nánquán’s words were intended to show that while the Way is indeed beyond words and beyond thought, one must still rely on the teacher’s guidance to enter its gate. If one relies solely on one's own power, it will be like a donkey’s years—never reaching the goal. This is why the ancients said, "If you do not meet a true teacher, you will never attain the Way. One must know that the Way is not something to be grasped through intellectual understanding; it is only attained when one’s own mind is exhausted and one returns to the source. This is what is meant by "understanding before the Buddha appeared in the world. It is not that there is no Buddha, but rather that the Buddha is not something to be sought outside of oneself. If one seeks the Buddha elsewhere, one is already far removed from him. This is why Nánquán said, "I cannot find even one or half of one. This is the meaning of the ancient worthies’ fire-scraps. *Verse:* The wall faces the wall, blocking all paths; The donkey’s years pass, yet the road is not reached. If you wish to see the Ancient Buddha, Do not seek him in the realm of speech. When the mind is exhausted and the source returned, Then the Way is naturally present. Lǔzú’s single-minded devotion is vast; Yet he lacks the skillful means of a true guide. Nánquán’s words are like a sharp sword; They cut through delusion and reveal the truth. If you can understand this in an instant, You will transcend the three periods of time. Do not look for the Buddha in the ten directions; The Buddha is right here within your own heart. *Song:* The wall faces the wall, blocking all paths; The donkey’s years pass, yet the road is not reached. Línshù Fēngchē (Chúndēng XI): Zen Master Rúmǐn of Línshù in Shàozhōu. A monk asked: "What is..."
[The monk asked about] the meaning of the Westward Transmission. The Master said, "Child, do not act like a rustic. The monk said, "I beg for instruction.
The Master said, "You have come from Qianzhou; what is it that makes this so difficult to understand? The Master said, "A wind-chariot atop the head of the Fire Official."
*Chanyuan Mengqiu*, Volume Upper; *Chanyuan Mengqiu*, Volume Middle.
The Twin Ankles of the Able One (*Nengren*).
(From *Chuandeng Lu*, Case 1). In Sanskrit, he is called Śākyamuni; here, it is translated as "The Able One" (*Nengren*). In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, at that time...
Kāśyapa and his disciples were dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain, having entered into right concentration (*samādhi*).

While in that state of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), their hearts were suddenly startled and their entire bodies trembled with anxiety. Emerging from concentration, they saw that the mountains and the earth were all shaking violently;
they immediately knew that the Tathāgata had already entered *nirvāṇa*. Thereupon, leading his disciples, he traveled swiftly along the road.
Filled with grief, he quickly proceeded until exactly seven days had passed. Upon reaching the city of Kuśinagara, he circumambulated the precious coffin seven times to the right.
With tears streaming from his eyes, he spoke verses of praise, which said: "O World-Honored One, I now suffer great anguish; My mind is disordered, fainting, and clouded with confusion.
I now prostrate myself before the crown of the World-Honored One’s head; Or rather, out of sorrow, I pay homage to the Tathāgata."
"Is it that you pay homage to the shoulders of the Great Sage? Or do you sorrowfully pay homage to the waist of the Tathāgata? Or do you pay homage to the navel of the Tathāgata?
Or do you, with a profound mind, pay homage to the feet of the Buddha? For what reason do you not see the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa?

I only pray that you will show me the place where I may pay my respects. Out of great compassion, the World-Honored One then manifested the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel, which emerged from outside the coffin.
He replied to Kāśyapa: "From the thousand-spoked wheel, a thousand rays of light were emitted, illuminating all worlds throughout the ten directions;
thereafter, they returned and entered the coffin, which was sealed as it had been before."
*Dharma’s Single Shoe* (Chuan Deng III): After the First Patriarch had personally transmitted the Dharma and the robe, nine years passed before he manifested his entry into *nirvāṇa*.

He was buried at Wuban on Mount Xiong’er. Three years later, the Wei envoy Song Yun was returning from a mission to the Western Regions when he encountered the Patriarch at the Pamir Mountains (*Congling*).
The Patriarch was holding a single shoe in his hand and said to Song Yun, “Your Lord... [is well]...”
"Since I have grown weary of this world, I shall return to the Western Land. Yun initially did not understand these words. After he returned, the Emperor indeed passed away.
He subsequently reported this to Emperor Xiaozhuang of the Later Wei dynasty, who then ordered the stupa to be opened. Inside, they found only a single sandal;
it was subsequently taken by imperial decree to be enshrined as an offering at Shaolin Temple. In the twelfth year of the Kaiyuan era, it was stolen and brought to Taihua Yan Temple.
Later, it too was lost. Lu Neng sold firewood (*Chuan Deng Lu 5*). Master Huineng’s secular surname was Lu. He lost his father at the age of three;
his mother maintained her resolve to raise him. Upon reaching adulthood, his family remained exceptionally poor. The Master provided for them by gathering firewood. One day, he went to sell...
While selling firewood in the marketplace, he heard a guest reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* until reaching the passage: "One should give rise to the mind without dwelling anywhere.
Startled, he attained a profound realization. He went directly to Huangmei, where the Fifth Patriarch of Dongshan saw him and held him in high esteem.
Lanrong Carries Rice (The Dharma Heir of the Fourth Patriarch; *Huìyuán*, Vol. 2). Chan Master Fǎróng of Niútóu Mountain was a native of Yánlíng in Rùn Prefecture.
His surname was Wéi. At the age of nineteen, he had mastered the Confucian classics and histories; he subsequently studied the extensive *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras.
Having attained profound realization of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), he one day sighed and said, "The classics of Confucianism and Daoism are not the ultimate Dharma;
the correct contemplation of Prajñā is the vessel for transcending the world. He subsequently retired to Mount Mao, where he shaved his head under a master.

Later, he entered a stone chamber on the northern cliff of Youqi Temple at Mount Niutou, where the marvel occurred of hundreds of birds offering him flowers. This took place during the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty.
The Fourth Patriarch observed the atmospheric signs from afar and knew that there was a person of extraordinary character on that mountain.

He went in person to seek him out and asked the temple monks, "Is there any practitioner of the Way here? They replied, "Among those who have left the household life, which one is not a practitioner of the Way?"
The Patriarch said, "Which one is the man of the Way? The monk had no reply. Another monk said, "About ten li from here in the mountains there is a Lazy Rong.
He does not rise when he sees people, nor does he join his palms. Could he be the man of the Way?"
The Patriarch then entered the mountains and saw the Master sitting upright and composed, seemingly unconcerned with anything around him. The Patriarch asked, "What are you doing here?
The Master replied, "I am observing the mind. The Patriarch asked, "What is it that observes? What is this mind? The Master was unable to answer.
He immediately rose, paid his respects, and asked, "Great Virtue, where is your lofty tower? The Patriarch replied, "This poor monk has not decided where to stay;
I may go east or west. The Master asked, "Do you know Chan Master Daoxin? The Patriarch asked, "Why do you ask about him?"
The Master said, "I have long admired your virtue and hope to pay my respects to you. The Patriarch replied, "I am that very Dharma Teacher Daoxin.
The Master asked, "For what reason have you come here? The Patriarch said, "I have come specifically to visit you; do you have another place for rest?
The Master pointed to the area behind him and said, "There is a separate small hermitage. He then led the Patriarch to the front of the hut and circumambulated it.
He saw only tigers and wolves. The Patriarch then raised both hands in a gesture of fear. The Master said, "There is still this one remaining.
The Patriarch asked, "What is this? The Master was speechless. After a short while, the Patriarch then wrote the character for "Buddha" (佛) upon the stone where he sat in meditation.
The Master looked at it and stood in awe. The Patriarch said, "There is still this one remaining. Not yet.
Dawn then bowed his head and requested that the Patriarch preach the essential truth. The Patriarch said: "The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates all return to the single square inch of the mind.

The wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all rooted in the source of the heart. All gates of precepts, gates of concentration, and gates of wisdom, as well as supernatural powers and transformations, are entirely and inherently complete within you, never departing from your own mind. All afflictions and karmic obstructions are, from the very beginning, empty and still."
All causes and effects are like dreams and illusions. There is no triple world from which to escape, and there is no Bodhi to be sought.
Sentient beings and non-sentient beings are equal in their essential nature. The Great Way is vast and empty, transcending thought and deliberation.
Such a Dharma you have now attained; it lacks nothing. How is it different from that of the Buddha? There is no other dharma apart from this. You need only act as you please.
The mind is sovereign. Do not practice contemplative exercises, nor do you need to clarify the mind. Do not give rise to greed or anger, nor harbor sorrow or anxiety.
Vast and unimpeded, move freely as you wish. Perform no good deeds and commit no evil deeds.

Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, whatever meets the eye and whatever encounters the conditions—all are the wondrous functioning of the Buddha. Joyful and free from worry, it is for this reason called "Buddha."
The Master said, "Since the mind is already complete, what is the Buddha and what is the mind? The Patriarch said, "If it is not the mind, one does not inquire about the Buddha;

if one inquires about the Buddha, it is not apart from the mind. The Master said, "Since you do not permit the practice of contemplative cultivation (*vipaśyanā*), when objects arise, how should the mind counteract them?
The Patriarch said, "The conditions of objects have neither good nor evil; good and evil arise in the mind. If the mind..."
This is merely a provisional name. From where does deluded sentiment arise? Since deluded sentiment does not arise, the true mind is free to exercise universal knowledge.
You need only follow the mind with sovereign ease and no longer apply antidotes; this is called the eternally abiding Dharmakāya, which is without change or variation.
I have received the sudden teaching of the Great Master Can and now transmit it to you. You must now receive my words with deep sincerity. Only—
He resided on this mountain. Later, there would be five men who attained realization and would carry on your profound transformation.
Having completed the transmission of the Dharma, the Patriarch returned to Shuangfeng, where he passed away. From that time on, the Master’s dharma seat flourished greatly.

During the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty, when the assembly lacked grain, the Master went to Danyang to seek alms. He traveled eighty li from the mountain, carrying a *shí* of rice upon his own back.
Bādòu went out in the morning and returned by evening; he provided for three hundred monks at the two meal times without fail for three years.

[Zhaozhou] held up his whisk. Baizhang said, "Does it function only when in contact with this [whisk], or does it function apart from this? The Master hung the whisk back in its original place.
After a long silence, he said, "In the future, when you open your two flaps of skin, what will you use to save people? Baizhang also raised his whisk.
The Patriarch said, "Just touch this function; leave this function. Baizhang hung it back in its original place. The Patriarch then shook his authority and let out a single shout.

Baizhang attained great enlightenment, to the point that he was deaf for three days. Later, when Huangbo came to study with him, [Baizhang] brought up this incident, whereupon Huangbo heard it and stuck out his tongue.
**Danxia Covers His Ears (Chuan Deng Lu 14)** Chan Master Danxia Tianran of Dengzhou first visited Shitou, and their karmic conditions were in accord.
He personally performed menial labor, such as tending the hearth, for three years. One day, Shitou addressed the assembly, saying, "Tomorrow, you must clear the weeds in front of the Buddha Hall.
When the next day arrived, the great assembly and the novice disciples each prepared spades and mattocks to clear them.
"Grass! Only you, Master, may use a basin to wash your head before the Upādhyāya while kneeling on your haunches.
When Shitou saw this, he laughed and shaved his hair. When the Dharma Master was about to preach the precepts, the man covered his ears and departed.
Later, he went to visit Mazu. Upon entering the Sangha hall, he mounted the neck of the Holy Monk. The assembly all cried out in alarm. Seeing him, Mazu said, "My son!"
"Natural. [The Master] descended from his seat. The Teacher descended and prostrated, saying, "I thank you for bestowing my name.
Longya clenched his fists. (A successor of Wufeng; *Chuan Deng Lu*, fascicle 27). A monk asked Longya, "How should one apply effort throughout the twelve periods of the day?
The Master said, "It is like a person without hands who wishes to throw a punch; only then does it work."
**Juzhi Shuzhi (Tianlong’s Dharma Heir; *Chuan Deng Lu* 11)** Master Juzhi of Mount Jinhua in Wuzhou initially lived in a hermitage.
It was through the exhortation of the nun Jiaji that his resolve was stirred, and he first conceived the aspiration for the Great Way.
Shortly thereafter, Tianlong arrived at the hermitage. Juzhi then related the circumstances of Jiaji’s visit to the hermitage. When he questioned Tianlong, Tianlong simply held up one finger.
He pointed it out to him, and the Master immediately attained realization. In the autumn before his passing, he said to the assembly, "I obtained the 'finger-pointing Chan' of Tianlong;
I shall not exhaust its use throughout my entire life. Having spoken these words, he suddenly passed away.
The Fifteenth Patriarch, the Great Being Kāṇadeva (Blue Cliff Record 2). After first attaining the Dharma, he went to the city of Pāṭaliputra.
Hearing that various non-Buddhists intended to obstruct the Buddha-dharma, and having waited for them there for some time, the Great Being took up a long banner and entered their assembly.
That banner had a shaft eight *chi* long and was twelve *zhang* in height. There, in that...
He stood there without moving a step. The outsider asked, "Why do you not come forward?
He replied, "Why do you not stay behind? The outsider said, "You seem like a lowly person. He replied, "You seem like a man of noble standing. The outsider said, "What Dharma do you understand?
He replied, "You do not understand anything at all. The outsider said, "I wish to attain Buddhahood. He replied, "I have certainly attained it. The outsider said:
"You do not deserve to attain it," [Āryadeva] said. The outsider replied, "I certainly attained it; you truly have not. Āryadeva asked, "Since you have not attained it, why do you say you have?
He replied, "Because you possess the notion of a self (*ātman*), you have not attained it. Since I am without the notion of a self, I shall naturally become a Buddha.
When the outsider was thus defeated in argument, he asked, "What is your name? He replied, "My name is Deva."
The non-Buddhists, having long heard of his reputation, repented their errors and offered their apologies. *Tian* (天) is the Chinese translation for the Sanskrit *deva*.
Regarding "Xuansha’s Blank Paper" (*Huiyuan*, vol. 7): Xuansha ordered a monk to deliver a letter. When the monk arrived at Xuefeng, Xuefeng ascended the hall;
opening the seal, he saw three sheets of blank paper. He presented them to the assembly and asked, "Do you understand? After a long pause, he said, "No."

When the Master saw the gentleman on the Way, they shared the same breeze across a thousand *li*. When the monk Guī reported this to Xuánshā, Xuánshā said, "The old fellow at the mountain head has missed it;
he does not even realize it. Mòyuán covered his nose. (Xìngkōng’s successor; *Fǎtēng* 15). Zen Master Pútàn of Píngtián, Tiantái, once visited Shè...
When Master Wuyuan of Zhuzhou was about to rise to welcome him, Xuedou stepped forward, seized him, and said: "To open your mouth is to lose it; to close your mouth is to perish.
Aside from these two paths, I ask you, Master, to speak otherwise. Wuyuan covered his nose with his hand.
Xuedou let go and said: "The first step is easy; the second step is difficult. Wuyuan said: "Why such a desperate hurry? Xuedou said: "If..."
It is not that this master could escape being scrutinized by those from all quarters.
