The master then bit his teeth to indicate it. The monk did not understand. Later, he asked Jiufeng about the intent behind the former master's biting of his teeth.
"How is it? he asked. Feng replied, "I would rather cut out my tongue than violate the national taboo. He then questioned Yungai.
Yungai said, "What grievance or enmity do I have with my late master?"
The Six Disciples of Fenyang (Huìyuán 11): Chan Master Shànzhào of the Tàizǐyúan Monastery in Fénzhōu.

The monastics and laypeople throughout the world admired and looked up to him so much that they did not dare call him by his name, but simply referred to him as "Fénzhōu. Because Bingfén and Chí were bitterly cold, the Master had discontinued the night assemblies.
One day, a strange bhikṣu arrived, shaking his monk’s staff, and said to the Master, "There are six great beings (mahāsattvas) within your assembly; what will you do?"
He did not preach the Dharma. Having finished speaking, he ascended the hall and departed. The Master secretly recorded this in a verse:
"The foreign monk with the golden staff's radiance Sought the Dharma at Fenyang. Six men shall become great vessels; I entreat you to proclaim it forth."
Dongshan’s Three Sons (Yunyan Tansheng succeeded [to him]; the ninth case of the *Biyan lu*). Dongshan said: "Greed, anger, and delusion—how utterly ignorant they are!
Fortunately, today I have come to recognize them. When they walk, I strike; when they sit, I beat them. I entrust this to the Mind-Prince for careful investigation.
For immeasurable kalpas they have remained unliberated. I ask you three: do you know or not?"—Shending Yan.
He said: "The ancients spoke thus, but Shending does not agree. Greed, anger, and ignorance truly have no conscious agent;
throughout the twelve hours of the day, let them be as they will. When walking, they go; when sitting, they follow. What can the Mind-King do with them?
Since beginningless kalpas, one has been fundamentally liberated; why need one further ask whether there is knowing or not?"
At the Tea Service at Zhaoqing (The Dharma Heir of Daoxian; *Chuan Deng Lu*, Case 22): When Imperial Tutor Wang entered, Zhaoqing was hosting a tea service.
At that time, the senior monk Lang and Mingzhao were holding the tea kettle. Lang turned the kettle over. Seeing this, the Imperial Tutor asked the senior monk, "What is that under the tea stove?
Lang replied, "It is the Spirit Who Supports the Stove. The Imperial Tutor said, "Since it is the Spirit Who Supports the Stove, why..."
"What has overturned the tea kettle? Lang said, "To serve as an official for a thousand days and lose it all in a single morning.
The Grand Tutor (Taifu) shook his sleeves and departed. Mingzhao said, "Lang, you Senior Monk! After eating at Zhaoqing, you went outside the river to gather firewood.
Lang asked, "What about you, Master? Zhao said, "The wrong person found the opportunity."
Yunyan Sweeps the Ground (Yaoshan Yan’s Dharma heir; *Chuan Deng Lu* 14). While Yunyan was sweeping the ground, Daowu said, "You are far too busy.
The Master said, "You must know that there is one who is not so busy. Daowu said, "If that is so, then there is a second moon.
The Master held up his broom and asked, "Which moon is this? Daowu then walked away. When Xuansha heard of this, he said: [...Xuansha’s verse follows...]
This is precisely the "Second Moon.

Chanjian fulfills the prophecy recorded in the *Qingzhou Yingji* (The Successor of Dayang Xuan; the lower fascicle is in the Qingxu section of the *Dayang*). Andoh supplements this by citing the *Sengbaozhuan*, fascicle...
Seventeenth: Chan Master Toudi Yiqing was a native of this district and the son of the Li family. He moved his residence to Toudi, and so forth.
When the founder, Ciji, first established the mountain, he left a record saying: "If my stupa turns red, it shall be my rebirth."
The local people happened to refurbish his stupa, making it the color of agate. Before long, he was appointed to the post of *qingling* (administrator) at the monastery.
Regarding Shoushan Guangyao (a dharma heir of Fengxue; *Sengbaozhuan*, vol. 3): Chan Master Shoushan Shengnian of Ruzhou.

His verse on the essential principles of the school says: "Alas, you clumsy young man! (Fenyang’s commentary: 'Naturally pure and upright. No one recognizes your cleverness. (His movement of the pivot is not of the face. Strike! (He strikes.)
Breaking through the Fenglin Pass (completely exhausting the crystalline nature). Standing on the water wearing boots (dust and mud are naturally distinct).

"Alas, you clever girl! (Fenyang said: "Subtle wisdom and principle are fused. Dropping the shuttle without knowing how to weave (uninterrupted skill cannot be established). Look at that man fighting cocks (observing from the sidelines their soaring and pecking; competing for merit without injuring oneself).
Even the water buffalo does not recognize him (capable of bearing all power, yet showing no horns or head).

**The Essential Teachings of Ming’an** (Liangshan Lingguan, successor in the *Sengbaozhuan*, volume 13). Ming’an said: "Those who lose the essence while pursuing the marvelous become stuck on the path of words;
those who lose the essential principle in their phrases remain mired in the mechanism [of expression], their understanding of the beginning and end obscured.

They dwell only within the words, and thus the essential principle is not perfected. Every phrase must contain that which is expressed within the words and that which is unexpressed within the words; it must contain that which is expressed within the unexpressed."
Thus, one finally attains the subtle, profound, and perfect essence.
Regarding the *Lotus Sūtra* Master’s attendance at a vegetarian feast (Sengbao, vol. 20): as for the Great Being known as Fahuazhi, no one knows where he came from.
I first beheld him at the Seven Koṭi Hall of Jingde Temple. His features were strangely ancient;

he gazed straight ahead without blinking, his mouth moving rapidly as if chanting, though its form was indiscernible. It was said that he recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and thus he was given this name.
In the third year of Zhìhé, Emperor Rénzōng first fell ill, and as no successor had yet been established, the whole realm was filled with anxiety. That night, the Emperor burned [incense].

The Emperor prayed silently, saying: "Tomorrow, at the Hwa-seong Hall, a vegetarian feast shall be prepared to reverently invite the Great Being of the Lotus Sūtra (Dharma Flower Bodhisattva) to grace us with his presence;
let there be no refusal. At dawn, he donned his ceremonial robes and stood solemnly, waiting.

Suddenly, a messenger arrived to report that the Dharma Flower [Bodhisattva] had come directly from the right armpass gate straight to the inner palace. The attendants tried to stop him with cries of protest, but the Emperor laughed and said, "I invited him, and..."
He arrived. After a short while, he ascended the imperial dais and sat in the full lotus posture.

When he had finished receiving the offerings and was about to depart, the Emperor said, "I have not yet established an heir to the succession. My high ministers all speak of this. As I am approaching old age, I wonder whether or not there will be an offspring.
May the Dharma Master decide this for me. The Master took up his brush and, drawing paper, wrote in continuous strokes: "Thirteen, ten. (130)
In total, there were over thirty lines. He threw down his brush without further words, and none could fathom their meaning.
Later, when Emperor Yingzhong ascended the throne, it was revealed that he was indeed the thirteenth son of King An-yi; thus, his previous words were proven correct.

**De Pu Yu Si (from the *Sengbao zhuan*, fascicle 29; successor of Jia Shan Shan Hui)** On the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month in the fifth year of the Yuanyou era, Chan Master De Pu of He Shan addressed his attendants, saying:
"When the venerable elders of various quarters pass away, the monastic communities invariably perform memorial rites."
"I consider this to be merely a hollow formality. If I were to die, you all should perform the first sacrifice; therefore, I order that sacrifices be prepared from now on.
Because the assembly considered him old and fond of humorous speech, they asked again, "When will the Master pass away?
He replied, "I shall go when your offerings cease. Thereupon, he screened off his chamber and sat within it. The Master placed the offerings in the center, read the liturgical texts, and knelt.
The Master accepted the prostrations and partook of the food with natural composure. From the chief disciples down to the laborers, each took turns performing the duties day after day.
On the first day of the following year, when the offerings were concluded, he said, "Tomorrow, when the snow clears, we shall depart. When the time came, the clear sky suddenly turned to snow.
Once the snow ceased, the Master sat peacefully, burned incense, and passed away.

Longsha Menghu (Dharma heir of Nanquan; *Chuan Deng Lu* 10). While Zen Master Jingcen of Changsha in Hunan was gazing at the moon with Yangshan, Yangshan said, "Everyone possesses this very thing, yet they simply cannot use it. The Master said, "That is exactly it!
I ask you, how would you use it? Yangshan asked, "How do you use it? The Master stepped forward, kicked him in the chest, and knocked him down. Yangshan—[remained lying there].
Baizhang rose and said, "You are, in every respect, like a great tiger. From then on, he was known throughout all quarters as "Tiger Cen.
Regarding Baizhang’s Wild Fox (Huiyuan III): Whenever Master Baizhang ascended the hall, there was always an old man who followed the assembly to listen to the Dharma.
One day, when the assembly had withdrawn, the old man alone did not leave. The Master asked him, "Who are you? The old man—
He said, "I am not a human being. In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, I once dwelt on this mountain.
When a student asked whether one who practices great cultivation still falls within the realm of cause and effect, I replied, 'They do not fall within cause and effect.'"

Consequently, for five hundred lifetimes he fell into the body of a wild fox. Now he requests that the Master provide a turning phrase on his behalf, so that he may be precious in escaping the wild fox body.
The Master said, "Ask. The old man asked, "Does a person of great cultivation still fall within the realm of cause and effect?
The Master said, "Not obscuring cause and effect. At these words, the old man attained great enlightenment. He prostrated himself and said, "I have already..."
Having shed its body as a wild fox, it remained behind the mountain. [The master] dared to request that it be sent off according to the rites for deceased monks.
The Master ordered the *vinaya-dhara* (Vina) to strike the gavel and announce to the assembly: "After the meal, we shall escort a deceased monk. The great assembly gathered and deliberated:
"The entire community is at peace, and there is no one ill in the Nirvana Hall; why is this so? After the meal, the Master led the assembly to the base of a cliff behind the mountain.
Using a staff, he pulled out a dead wild fox and cremated it according to the Dharma. That evening, the Master ascended the hall and recounted the preceding circumstances.
Huangbo then asked, "The ancients fell into the body of a wild fox for five hundred lifetimes because they gave one wrong response;
if they had not made a single mistake at each turn, what would they have become? The Master said, "Come closer, and I will tell you."
Dao. Huangbo stepped forward and struck the Master with his palm. The Master clapped his hands and laughed, saying, "I thought the beard was red;
it turns out there is also a red-bearded barbarian. Miaoyan brought this up and asked Yangshan. Yangshan said, "Huangbo constantly employs this device.
Miaoyan asked, "Do you say he obtained it by natural birth, or did he receive it from another? Yangshan replied, "It is both received through the transmission of a teacher, and it is also [natural]."
Regarding the "Patriarchal Lineage of Essential Nature" (*svabhāva-yāna*), Guishan said, "So it is, so it is. At that time, Guishan was serving as the head cook (*karmadāna*) in the assembly.
The Dharma Master Sitong (Sima Tuo) raised the story of the wild fox and asked the head cook, "How would you handle this?
The cook shook the door panels three times. Sitong said, "That is quite crude. The cook replied, "The Buddha-dharma is not a matter of such things."
Fenyang Shizi (Huìyuán 11). Fenyang ascended the hall and said to the assembly:
"In the gate of Fenyang there sits a West River Lion, crouching right at the entrance. As soon as anyone approaches, he bites them to death.
What skillful means (*upāya*) is there by which one may enter Fenyang’s gate and see Fenyang’s man? If you can see Fenyang’s man, you are worthy to be a successor of the Patriarchs."
The Buddha is the Teacher. It is not seen that among the people of Fenyang there are any who are "dead men standing on the spot.
Jiangxi’s Majo (from *Huiyuan* 3) was Master Mazu, whose name was Daoyi. He was born in Shifang, Hanzhou, and his surname was Ma.
The Sixth Patriarch said to Nanyue, "In the future, the Buddha-dharma shall proceed from your side; you shall give birth to a 'horse colt'."
The Master trod upon and killed all people under heaven. He practiced the Way in Jiangxi, and people of the time called him Mazu.
Purple-Hu’s Fierce Dog (a dharma heir of Nanquan; *Huìyuán*, vol. 4). Chan Master Lìzōng of Zihu Rock in Quzhou once ascended the hall and said:
"Zihu has a dog that takes people's heads above, takes people's hearts in the middle, and takes [them] below."
If a person hesitates, they immediately lose their body and life. A monk asked, "What is the one dog of Zihu?
The Master said, "Bark! Bark!
Sansheng the Blind Donkey (a dharma heir of Linji; *Huìyuán*, vol. 11). When Linji was about to pass away, he sat upright and said, "When I am gone..."
Jiandou said, "In the future, you must not extinguish my treasury of the true Dharma-eye.
Sansheng stepped forward and said, "How would we dare extinguish the Master’s treasury of the true Dharma-eye? Jiandou said, "If someone asks you hereafter, what will you say to them?
Sansheng then gave a shout. Jiandou said, "Who knew that my treasury of the true Dharma-eye would be extinguished by this blind donkey?"
Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away.
Lǎn'ān Báigǔ (the Dharma heir of Bǎizhàng Hǎi; *Chúndēng* 9). Chan Master Chángqìng Dà'ān of Fúzhōu was styled Lǎn'ān.
He was the son of the Chen family of that commandery. He received his monastic training at Mount Huángbò and studied the Vinaya vehicle. He once said to himself:
Although I have exerted myself with diligent toil, I have not yet heard the principle of the profound ultimate. Thus, carrying my solitary staff, I travel to various regions;
on my way to Hongjing, I pass through Shangyuan and encounter an old man who says to me, "Master, when you go to Nanchang, you shall surely attain something.
The Master then proceeds to Baiyang, pays his respects, and asks: "A student wishes to come and recognize the Buddha—what is it?"
“Is that so? [Zhaozhou] said, “It is very much like riding a cow while searching for the cow. The Master asked, “After you have recognized it, what then?
Baizhang said, “It is like a person riding a cow home. The Master asked, “I do not yet understand how to maintain this from beginning to end.

Baizhang said, “It is like a cowherd who holds his staff and watches over the cow, not allowing it to trample the crops. From that time on, the Master understood the essential meaning and no longer wandered about.
Seeking. Chan Master You, a fellow practitioner, first established his residence at Mount Mí. The Master personally plowed the fields to assist in the Way.
When You passed away, the assembly requested him to succeed him as abbot. Entering the hall, he said: "All of you who have come here to seek from Anqiu—what is it that you seek?"
If you wish to become a Buddha, you are yourself already a Buddha. Yet you carry this "Buddha" about with you as you run from house to house, like a thirsty deer chasing a mirage;
when will you ever attain true realization? If you wish to become a Buddha, simply abandon these many inverted attachments, delusive thoughts, and evil perceptions.
The very mind of sentient beings—whether defiled or pure—is itself the initial awakening of the Buddha. Furthermore...
Where else would he go to seek it? This is why he settled at Mount Gui. For thirty years, he has eaten Mount Gui’s rice and defecated Mount Gui’s dung;
he has not studied Mount Gui’s Chan, but has merely watched a water buffalo.
If it strays onto the path or enters the grass, he pulls its nose back; as soon as it trespasses upon the crops, he whips and tames it. Thus it is.
For a long time, you pitiable fellow have been subject to the interpretations of others' words. Now you have transformed into a white ox in the open air;
it is always before you, standing wide-eyed all day long, yet you cannot drive it away.
Fozhai Huannu (Dharma heir of Mazu; *Chuan deng lu* 8). The Monk of Fozhai in Wenzhou was asked, "What is a being of a different species?
The Master struck a bowl and said, "Huannu, Huannu, come and eat!"
Nanshan Bi-ji (Chuan Deng Lu 16) was seen previously at the place of Xianggu and Tiejia;
Donghai Liyu (Yunmen Lu) was seen previously beneath the "One Path" of Qianfeng.

The Stupa Model of National Teacher Huizhong (Sixth Patriarch’s Dharma Heir; *Huiyuan*, Vol. 2). National Teacher Huizhong of Guangzhai Monastery in the Western Capital, sensing that his period of transforming beings was nearing its end and that the time for his nirvana had arrived, took leave of Emperor Daizong.
The Emperor said, "After the Master passes away, upon what shall your disciples rely?
The Master replied, "Inform the donors to construct for me a 'seamless stupa' (*wuseng ta*). The Emperor asked, "How shall it be made? The Master said, "Just as the Master [is]."

"Please take this model of a stupa. After a long silence, he asked, "Do you understand? He replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "After I have passed away, my attendant Yingzhen will know this matter.
After the Master’s passing, Emperor Daizong summoned Yingzhen to the inner palace and questioned him regarding the previous dialogue.
Yingzhen remained silent for a long time and then asked, "Does Your Majesty understand? He replied, "I do not understand. Yingzhen then recited a verse: Xiang’s...
South of the pond, in its northern reaches, lies a land filled with gold. Beneath the shadowless tree, the vessels are joined together;
atop the lapis lazuli palace, there is no one who knows.

At the Guǎngzhàn Guóhǎichāng Chányuàn in Yánguān, Hángzhōu, Chan Master Qí'ān (a Dharma successor of Mázǔ; *Huìyuán*, vol.
3), one day called his attendant and said, "Bring me the rhinoceros fan. The attendant replied, "The fan..."
The fan was broken. The Master said, "Since the fan is broken, bring me back the rhinoceros. [Yangshan] had no reply.
Yangqiao presented a pearl (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp, Vol. 9). Dongyi asked when Yangshan arrived for an audience, "Where are you from?"
Shan said, "I am from Guangnan. Mingyi asked, "Is there a 'bright pearl in the sea' in Guangnan?
Shan replied, "There is. Mingyi asked, "What shape does this pearl take? Shan said, "It appears during the bright moon and hides during the dark moon.
Mingyi asked, "Will you bring it here? Shan replied, "I will bring it. Mingyi said, "Why then do you not present it to this old monk?"
Shan said, "Yesterday when I arrived at Mount Gui, I also sought this pearl from Huiji. It left me with no words to respond and no principles to advance.
Yiyue said, "A true cub of the lion makes the great roar of the lion."
Changqing’s Gold-Digging (The Successor of Xuefeng; Huìyuǎn 7). A monk asked Changqing, “When sentient beings dig for gold, who is it that obtains it?
The Master said, “It is those who possess skillful means. The monk asked, “Does this student obtain it as well? The Master said, “It is still far off.”
A letter from Mount Funiu at Yque addressed to Chan Master Zizai of Mount Funiu, sent by Daji to National Teacher Zhong.
The National Teacher asked, "With what dharma does Master Ma instruct his disciples? He replied, "It is 'this very mind is Buddha.
The National Teacher said, "What kind of talk is that? After a long silence, he asked again, "Beyond this, what else is there?"
[The Master] asked about this teaching. The Teacher said, "Neither mind, nor Buddha," or alternatively, "Not mind, not Buddha, not a thing.
The National Teacher asked, "Master Mazu speaks thus; I wonder, how is it here with you, Reverend?
The Teacher replied, "The three dots are like flowing water; the curve is like a sickle for reaping grain. Later, the Master lived in seclusion at Mount Funiu.
These two phrases concern the word "mind.
Huìrán Penetrates the Net (*Chúndēng luò* 12). Zen Master Huìrán of Sāṅshèng Monastery in Zhènzhōu asked Xuěfēng:
"What does the golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net eat? Feng said, "I will tell you once it has passed through the net.
The Master said, "Even as a teacher of fifteen hundred people, you do not even recognize the critical pivot of the teaching."
Xiyun stroked his beard (Huìyuán 11). Having seen the previous instance [of Huangbo’s] single blow, Chuánmíng dispersed the assembly (a dharma successor of Chuánzǐ;
*Fǎtēng* 15). Chan Master Jiashan Huì was posthumously titled Dàshī Chuánmíng. The account of dispersing the assembly is found in the section concerning Chuánzǐ’s "catching the scales."

Cishou Qitu (Huìyuán 16): Chan Master Huishen of Huilin in Dongjing, surnamed Cishou. Four years after shaving his head, he went abroad to seek the Way and relied upon Jingzhao at Zisheng Temple in Jiahe.
When Jingzhao raised the kōan concerning Liangsui’s meeting with Magu, asking, "What is the place where Liangsui knows?
the Master immediately attained thorough clarity. He subsequently left and took up residence [at Huilin].

At Zifu Monastery, the shoes were so numerous they filled the space outside the door. When Chan Master Fojian Qin of Jiangshan arrived there while traveling for alms, the Master led him on a tour of the quarters until they reached the section for the thousand monks.

Fojian asked, "Since this is the section for a thousand monks, why is there only one person here? The Master replied, "Much emptiness is not as good as little reality. Fojian said, "Is that so? The Master was abashed.
At one time, the imperial court designated Zifu as the Shenxiao Palace (a Daoist monastery). Consequently, [Changsha] abandoned his post and went to Jiangshan, where he stayed at Xiaman.
He requested instruction from Dayuan Jian, saying, "At Zifu, I understood that such matters simply come to an end. The Master said, "I am truly not yet settled;
I hope the Venerable will not dismiss me. Jian brought up the story of the "Divided Soul of the Clever Woman" and interrogated him on it repeatedly until his mind was completely opened.
Feeling obstructed by doubt, he presented a verse, saying: "It is merely the place where I used to walk in the old temple;
yet to casually mention it is already a source of confusion. A sudden gale rises at midnight, blowing down the peach blossoms—how many must there be?
Zhaojian struck the desk and said, "Is this not the living meaning of the Patriarchs? Not long after, he received an imperial decree to reside at Mount Jiao.
*Sanfeng Yuguan* (Huìyuán 11): When Linji was traveling on pilgrimage, he arrived at the place of Master Sanfeng Ping.
Ping asked, "Where have you come from? Linji replied, "I have come from Huangbo. Ping asked, "What words or phrases did Huangbo have for you? Linji said:
The Ox of Gold met with calamity last night; even until now, no trace remains. Ping said, "The golden wind blows through the jade flute;
who is the one who knows this sound? Ji said, "It penetrates straight through ten thousand layers of barriers, never dwelling within the blue heavens."
Yunping said, "Your question, my son, is far too lofty. Linji said, "A golden phoenix born of a dragon breaks through the azure lapis lazuli.
Yunping said, "Sit for a moment and drink some tea."
Elder Brother Jinchu (Qinglin Qiansi Huiyuan 13): Chan Master Xianyun of Shimen in Xiangzhou. He was a native of Jingzhao.
Initially, he asked Qinglin, "How can one apply the mind so as to become equal to all the sages? Qinglin looked up for a long time and said, "Do you understand?
The Master said, "I do not understand. Qinglin said, "Go; there is no place for you to apply the mind. The Master then paid his respects.
Having attained realization, he no longer wandered elsewhere and subsequently became the head gardener. One day, while returning to stand in attendance, Lin asked, "What have you been doing today?
The Master replied, "I have been planting vegetables. Lin asked, "Since the entire world is the Buddha-body, where have you gone to plant them?
The Master said, "The golden hoe does not move the soil; the sacred sprouts grow wherever they are. Lin was delighted.
"However, tomorrow when you enter the garden, call for Dharma Master Yun. The Master assented.
Lin said, "I have planted an extra tree without a shadow, to leave for later generations to behold. The Master said, "If it is a tree without a shadow, how could it be planted?
Lin said, "Setting aside for a moment that it cannot be planted, have you ever seen its branches and leaves? The Master replied, "I have not seen them. Lin said, "Since..."
"Since one has never seen [it], how can one know it does not receive planting? The Master said, "Precisely because one has never seen it, it does not receive planting.
Lin said, "So it is, so it is. Initially, he resided at a *aranya* (hermitage) on Mount Nanyue; before long, he moved to Jiaoshan.
While traveling through Tanzhou, the Prince of Chu, Lady Ma, came out of the city to welcome him and asked, "What is the Patriarch's [Dharma]?"

Regarding the Great Meaning of the Western Arrival, the Master said: "Good brother! The imperial carriage with its six dragons is a marvel of a thousand ages; the jade-staffed procession emerges from the Golden Gate.
The King was greatly pleased and invited him into the Tiance Palace, where he provided him with offerings for several days.
Only then did he arrive at Jia Shan. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Western Arrival? The Master said: "The jade seal does not leave the hand of the Son of Heaven. Gold...

"How could this chest ever be allowed for outsiders to know? [The student] asked: "Please speak directly, Master, on that which does not fall into the trap. The Master said: "The profound moon reflects the mechanism;
there is nothing to compare it with. How many people have you questioned until now? He replied: "I am questioning the Master right now. The Master said: "Good brother!
When the clouds part, there is no need for the nine-tailed comet to fall; your angry life-force is exhausted, so return quickly to the silken thread. The Master... [continued].
Because the Man and Yi tribes rose in rebellion, he left Jia Mountain. Arriving at Xiangzhou, he founded Shimen Temple and once again revitalized the profound Dharma.
A monk asked, "When the moon rises above the horizon, what is it like? The Master said, "Three grandchildren embrace a flower drum."
"Good brother! Do not come to block my path to the ball gate. The Master frequently responded to the occasion by saying, "Good brother," and was thus known at the time as "Brother Monk.

(Recorded in *Chuan Deng Lu*, fascicle 15). Regarding Chan Master Xuanjian of Deshan in Langzhou: whenever he saw a monk enter the gate, he would strike him with his staff. (From *Chuan Deng Lu*, fascicle 15). Chan Master Xuanjian of Deshan in Langzhou: whenever he saw a monk enter the gate...

[He] struck him with the staff. ○ The *Hewubuji* says: The *Chuan deng lu*, volume fifteen, states that the Master (Deshan) usually struck monks who came for an audience with his staff. When Linji heard of this, he sent an attendant to visit him. [The attendant said,] "If Deshan strikes you, simply take hold of the staff and strike him right in the chest. When the attendant arrived, he first performed a prostration, whereupon [Deshan] struck him. The attendant then bowed again, and [Deshan] struck him once more. The attendant then bowed yet again, and [Deshan] struck him a third time. The attendant then departed. Deshan later told Linji, "That fellow has great spirit; he is fit to be my successor. Linji replied, "I will go and see him myself. Deshan said, "If you go there, do not speak a single word. If he strikes you, you must strike him back. Linji went to see him. Before he had even finished bowing, Deshan struck him. Linji struck him back. Deshan struck him again. Linji struck him back once more. Deshan then said, "What is it? Linji said, "The old man has no eyes. Deshan struck him, and Linji left. Deshan called out, "Wait! Wait! Linji turned his head. Deshan said, "Later on, when you encounter people, you must not say that Deshan has no eyes. Linji said, "I will not say it. Deshan said, "Why would you not say it? Linji said, "If I were to say it, I would surely lose my life. Deshan said, "You have great spirit; you are fit to be my successor. Linji returned and reported this to Huangbo. Huangbo said, "That fellow has great spirit; he is fit to be my successor. Linji said, "He is not my successor; he is your successor. Huangbo said, "How so? Linji recounted the entire sequence of events. Huangbo said, "You have great spirit; you are fit to be my successor. Linji said, "I am not your successor; I am Deshan’s successor. Huangbo said, "How so? Linji recounted the entire sequence of events. Huangbo said, "You two have great spirit; you are both fit to be my successors. Later, when Linji was about to leave, Huangbo said, "Where are you going? Linji said, "To see Deshan. Huangbo said, "If you go there, do not say I sent you. If he asks why you have come, you should answer, 'Because I could not bear to see the old man's staff. Linji went to see Deshan. Deshan asked, "Where have you come from? Linji said, "From Huangbo. Deshan said, "Did Huangbo send you? Linji said, "No. Deshan said, "Why have you come? Linji said, "Because I could not bear to see the old man's staff. Deshan immediately struck him. Linji seized the staff and struck Deshan. Deshan said, "This fellow has great spirit; he is fit to be my successor. He then gave him the robe and bowl. This is recorded in the *Chuan deng lu*. It is also stated therein that when Linji was about to leave, Deshan said, "Where are you going? Linji said, "To see Huangbo. Deshan said, "If you go there, do not say I sent you. If he asks why you have come, you should answer, 'Because I could not bear to see the old man's staff. Linji went to see him. Before he had even finished bowing, Huangbo struck him. As he was about to receive the staff, Linji gave him a blow. The Master returned to his quarters; the attendant went back and reported this to him.
Linji said, "From the beginning, I have suspected this fellow."
Linji’s Shout (The Eyes and Ears of Humanity and Heaven). Whenever Linji saw a monk enter the gate, he would immediately shout. Hebo said:
*The Eyes and Ears of Humanity and Heaven* states that the Master said to a monk: "At times, a single shout is like the Vajra King’s precious sword."
"Sometimes a single shout is like a lion crouching on the ground; sometimes a single shout is like a probe-staff and its shadow-grass;
sometimes a single shout does not function as a single shout. How do you understand this? When the monk hesitated, the Master shouted.
Zhaozhou’s Cloth Shirt (*Chuan Deng Lu* 10). A monk asked Zhaozhou, "All dharmas return to One; where does that One return?
The Master said, "When I was in Qingzhou, I made a cloth shirt that weighed seven *jin*."
Puhua’s Straight-Sleeved Robe (*Chuan Deng Lu* 10). One day, Puhua went among the people in the marketplace to beg for a straight-sleeved robe (*zhiduo*).
Everyone gave him one, yet the Master would not accept any of them. Linji ordered the monastery steward to purchase a coffin.
When the Master returned, Linji said, "I have made a straight-sleeved robe for you. Thereupon, the Master himself carried it away and walked around the streets.
He shouted to the townspeople, "Linji has finished making my *zhidu* (monastic robe) for me; I am going to the East Gate to pass away.
The townspeople vied with one another to follow and watch him. The Master said, "I will not go today;
I shall go to the South Gate to pass away tomorrow. For three days, no one believed him. By the fourth day, no one followed to watch; he departed alone.
Outside the city, he entered the coffin himself and requested a passerby to nail it shut. News spread immediately, and the townspeople vied with one another to go there.
Upon opening the coffin, they saw that his entire body had vanished; only the faint sound of bells ringing was heard as he departed into the air.
**Foji Benchan (Huìyuán 13): Chan Master Fobenkong of Foji Temple in Hangzhou.** While traveling on pilgrimage, he arrived at Jiashan.
One day, during a communal work session (*pǔqǐng*), the Rector (*wéinà*) ordered the Master to deliver tea. The Master said, "I have come for the sake of the Buddha-dharma;
I have not come to deliver tea. The Rector said, "The Abbot has requested you, Venerable Sir. The Master said, "The Abbot..."
He immediately understood. The Master then took the tea to the place where work was being done. Seeing Jia Shan there, he shook the tea bowl to make a sound.
Jia Shan paid him no heed. The Master said, "Three or five bowls of strong tea; the intent lies at the edge of the hoe.
Jia Shan said, "The bottle has the potential to pour tea; how many bubbles are in the basket? The Master said, "The bottle has the potential to pour tea; there is not one bubble in the basket."
"O! he said, and then he poured out the tea. The entire assembly gazed at him with their eyes. The Master said, "The assembly looks up with crane-like anticipation; we beg for a word from the Master.
Yunmen said, "If you encounter a dead snake on the road, do not strike it; carry it away in a bottomless basket.
The Master said, "Holding a night-bright talisman in one's hand, how many know when the dawn breaks? Yunmen called to the assembly, "There is already someone here."
"Go back! Go back! Then he stayed for the communal labor (fujō).
The Chan Master Zong was a man of unknown origins; he traveled between Shu and Qi and frequently stayed at Touzi. By nature he was fond of wine and was never sober.

The villagers loved and respected him, always providing him with plenty to eat. *Linjian Lu, Vol. 2* [Note: The source text provided contains a mix of Chinese characters and romanization. The translation above renders the Chinese characters into standard English prose.]
He kept a vessel of pure wine. One day, just as he was about to enter the bathhouse, he heard someone seeking his master.

Judging that the visitor must have brought a wine jug with him, he hurried out, obtained the wine, and went straight away. Everyone laughed loudly, yet Xuanzong remained haughty and paid them no mind.
Once, while walking down the mountain with his robes disheveled, someone met him and asked, "What is the 'family style' of a man of the Way? He replied, "The *kāṣāya*..."
[He] wrapped his robes and wore straw sandals. What was the meaning of this? [Zhaozhou] said, "With bare feet, go to Xiangcheng.
When Chen Tuifu first went to the provincial examination, he passed by the temple and jokingly asked, "Guan, do you think you can become the Grand Marshal (Zhuangyuan) on this trip?
Zong stared at him intently and said, "You will get it when there is no time. Tuifu did not fathom these words, yet he indeed finished third.
At that time, Shiyan was the leader; only then did he realize the meaning of the "timeless" (wu-shi) expression. Zong saw Xuedou and became liberated and self-possessed;
he was said to be of the lineage of Fahua.
Xianglin Yideng (Dharma heir of Yunmen; *Chuan Deng Lu*, fascicle 22). Chan Master Chengyuan of Xianglin Monastery in Qingcheng, Yizhou.
A monk asked, "What is the single lamp inside the room? The Master said, "Three people testify that a tortoise becomes a turtle."
The Three Objects of the Virtuous Woman (Huìyuán 1): Seven virtuous women and sisters traveled together to the Śītavana forest.
One sister pointed to a corpse and said, "The corpse is here; where is the person? The sisters contemplated this intently, and they all attained enlightenment.
Śakra, the Lord of Devas, moved by this, sent down a rain of flowers and praised her, saying: "Sisters, what do you require? I am able to bestow it upon you. The women replied:
"In our home, the four requisites and the seven treasures are all complete; we only require three things: first, a single tree without roots;
second, a patch of ground where neither sun nor shade exists; third, a valley where one's cry goes unanswered. Śakra said: "First—"
"I possess everything that is required; however, I truly do not have these three things. They then went together to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "My disciples do not understand this meaning; only the Bodhisattvas understand this meaning."

**Stone and Cobblestones (Qingyuan’s Dharma Heir; *Chuan Deng Lu*, Case 14)** Chan Master Shitou Xiqian of Nanyue was invited to the Southern Monastery on Mount Heng during the Tianbao era of the Tang dynasty.
To the east of the monastery was a rock shaped like a platform, upon which he built a hut.
He was then known as "Master Shitou. A monk asked, "What is Chan? He replied, "Cobblestones. The monk asked again, "What is like [the nature of]..."
"What is the Way? The Master said, "A wooden block.
Yunmen said, "A piece of dried dung" (*Yunmen Lu*). A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "A dry piece of dung."
Two Monks and the Curtain (Chuan Deng Lu 24). Once, when a monk came to pay his respects before the midday meal, Master Fayan pointed at the curtain with his finger.
At that moment, two monks went together to roll up the curtain. The Master said, "One has gained; one has lost."
**The Three Elders Admire the Moon (Huìyuán III)** Mazu, Baizhang, Xitang, and Nanquan were once admiring the moon together.
Mazu asked, "At this very moment, what is it? Xitang said, "It is precisely the time for cultivation. Baizhang said, "It is precisely the time for making offerings.
Nanquan shook his sleeves and walked away. Mazu remarked, "The Sutras have entered the Canon; Zen has returned to the sea. Only Nanquan remains alone."
Transcending the mundane world.
Master Huiman of Ryūkeiji Temple in Sagami Province (Recorded in *Dengyō Daishi Den Tōdai San*). Master Huiman maintained a life of frugality and kept only two needles.
He would beg for thread to repair his robes in winter and discard them in summer. He said of himself: "Throughout my life, my mind has never known fear."
He was fearless; his body was free of lice; he slept without dreaming; he constantly practiced begging for alms and never stayed overnight in the same place twice;
and wherever he went to a monastery, he mended his purple-dyed sandals.
The Three Pairs of Ancient Worthies (Huìyuán III) and Bǔ’s Commentary: One day, Cān Master Yàoshān Wéiyǎn was asked by Mǎzŭ, “How is it that you have perceived things recently?
The Master replied, “All skin and flesh have fallen away; only the single reality remains.
Mǎzŭ said, “What you have attained may be called being in accord with the essence of the mind and manifesting it throughout the four limbs. Since—
It was thus: he bound his belly with three strips of bamboo splints and went to dwell wherever he pleased.
Master Yan—Chan Master Fa Yan of the Five Patriarchs—was at his monastery of ordination, reciting the Lotus Sutra while prostrating to each character.
One night, he encountered the character for "excrement" (shi). As he was about to perform his prostrations, he suddenly felt doubt.
He said to the elder masters, "How can even the character for 'excrement' be called a Treasure of the Dharma? My prostrations have reached this point, yet my doubt remains unresolved.
An elder master said, "Based on what you have asked, you may travel south to seek instruction; you are truly a vessel of the Lineage School. Thereupon, the Patriarch traveled south.
A Monk Spits at the Buddha (Huìyuán 6). A certain attendant monk followed a Dharma Master into the Buddha hall. The attendant turned toward the Buddha and spat.
The Dharma Master said, "Attendant, you have little sense of propriety; why do you spit at the Buddha?
The attendant replied, "Bring me a place where there is no Buddha, and I shall come there. The Master had no response.
Dongpo Unties His Girdle (The Sixteenth Assembly of Donglin’s Disciples, Huiyuan).
One day, while Chan Master Liaoyuan Foyin of Yunju Mountain in Nankang Commandery was in his inner quarters with his disciples, the layman Dongpo arrived before him. The Master said:
"There are no seats here. Layman, why have you come? The layman replied, "I shall temporarily borrow the Buddha-seal of the four great elements as my seat.
The Master said, "I, this mountain monk, have a question. If you can answer it, I will invite you to sit."
"If you cannot say it, you shall forfeit the jade belt from your waist. The scholar joyfully replied, "I request it at once.
The Master said, "The layman just now said he would temporarily borrow the mountain monk’s four great elements as a sitting mat.
But since the mountain monk’s four great elements are fundamentally empty and the five aggregates are non-existent, where will the layman sit? The scholar was unable to answer and remained there.
The Jade Girdle. The Master, in turn, presented him with a *yunshan* (cloud-mountain) *nà* robe. The scholar then composed a verse, saying: "A hundred thousand lamps form a single lamp’s light;
All are the wondrous Dharma Kings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Therefore, Dongpo dares not begrudge it; I borrow your four elements to serve as a meditation seat.
This sickly frame cannot endure the girdle of jade; My dull faculties still fall short of the 'arrow-point' pivot."
I shall surely beg for alms at the courtesans’ quarters; I will seize back my old monastic robes from the clouds and mountains.
This sash has seen many pass through it like travelers in an inn; its transmission reaching me is also full of leisure. Though the brocade robe is tattered, it still suits me well;
I shall give it to the mad old man Wan-hui to wear.

Pei Xiu Presents His Official Tablet (*Cánlín lèijù*, Vol. 17; Disciple of Huangbo). When Prime Minister Pei arrived at the abode of Chan Master Shishuang, the Master picked up Pei’s official tablet and asked, "In the hands of the Son of Heaven, it is called a *gui* (jade tablet);
now that it is in my hands, tell me, what do you call it? Pei had no reply. The Master then kept the tablet.
Shun Laofu (from the *Dongshan Cong* lineage; in the *Sengbao Zhuan*): While Shun Laofu resided at Qixian, the local prefect was corrupt and greedy.
The Master could not bear to use the property of the monastery to cultivate personal ties and secure his position. Consequently, he composed a panegyric for the prefect.

The people clothed him, and he resided at Taiping Hermitage. When King Inmyeong heard of his spiritual practice, he honored him with monastic robes and a silver alms bowl, appointing him once again as the abbot of Qixian Temple.
Upon entering the monastery, he composed this verse: "Without cause, I was praised; in vain, I have met with misfortune."
Having been a layman for more than half a year, today he returns once more to Sanxia Temple. How many will praise him, and how many will scold him?
(Regarding "Furong Shuofa" [Touzi Qing’s Dharma heir; in the *Sengbaozhuan*], the supplementary commentary states: Master Chan Teacher Dao Kai of Furong was great.)

In the first year of the Yuan year, Li Xiaoshou, the Governor of Kaifeng, submitted a memorial stating that Huikai’s spiritual practice was preeminent among the monastic community and that he should be honored accordingly.

Thereupon, the Emperor bestowed upon him a purple *kāṣāya* robe and conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Dingzhao (and so forth). Later, having incurred punishment, he donned the *fengyi* scholar’s robe and tied up his hair.
After Huikai had burned incense to express his gratitude for the imperial favor, he submitted a memorial to decline it, saying: "I humbly receive the grace of Your Majesty..."

By Imperial Command, Tan Zhen, Attendant of the Changshan Pavilion, was specially dispatched to confer upon me, the Chan Master Dingzhao, the title of *Dingzhao Chanshi* and a diploma for the purple robe.
Grateful for this profound imperial grace, I have immediately burned incense, ascended the seat, and offered prayers for the longevity of the Emperor’s reign.
Having completed these rites, I humbly reflect that my religious practice is clumsy and my spiritual power is meager; I have long made a vow not to accept...

I have long maintained this intention over many years, hoping that the Dharma might be transmitted to future generations in this way, so that people would devote themselves exclusively to the Buddha-dharma.
Even though I have received the grace of the Wu state, should I instead allow myself to be negligent, I would be violating my own original vow;
how then could I teach others? How could I possibly look up to and honor the intent of Your Majesty in commanding me to preside over this monastery?
I do not dare to accept the aforementioned imperial edict of grace. I prostrate myself before Your Majesty’s compassionate benevolence to examine my humble sincerity;

it is not that I am merely using flowery words, but rather I pray for your special grant of permission. I shall devote the rest of my life to practicing the Way, so as to repay the heavenly bounty from above and bring peace to the people below.
Having heard this, [the Emperor] entrusted it to Li Xiaoshou to personally go and convey the imperial intent of honoring the virtuous. However, Kai remained resolute and would not yield.
The Governor of Kaifeng reported the matter in full detail. The Emperor was incensed and handed the case over to the judicial authorities.

Aware that Hui-kai was a man of loyalty and integrity, yet had just offended the imperial majesty, the officials asked him, "Elder, are you emaciated and exhausted from illness? Hui-kai replied, "I have been ill in the past, but at present I am truly not.
They asked again, "If you say you are ill, you shall be exempted from punishment. Hui-kai said, "How could I dare seek such an advantage?"
Yet he sought release from the punishment. The official sighed deeply as he was sentenced to wear the *fengye* robe and be exiled to Liuzhou;
Du Cheng, a monk and layman who witnessed this, was moved to contemplate the Great [Master] who could have swallowed the Buddha.
(From the biography of Huìyuán, a disciple of Huíwén of the Northern Qi, concerning Sīdà). Bǎozhì sent someone to deliver a message to Sīdà.
[The monk] said, "Why do you not descend the mountain to transform sentient beings? Why do you gaze at the Milky Way?
The Master said, "I have swallowed all the Buddhas of the three periods of time in a single mouth; what sentient beings are there to be saved?"
The Great Being Preaches the Sūtra (Chuan Deng Lu 27). Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty invited the Great Being Fu to preach the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
As soon as the Great Being ascended the seat, he struck the lectern once with a ruler and then descended.
Emperor Wu was startled. Master Zhigong asked, "Your Majesty, do you understand? The Emperor said, "I do not understand. Zhigong said, "The Great Being has finished preaching the sūtra."

The Old Lu’s Banner Moves (Huìyuán 7). After the Sixth Patriarch himself transmitted the robe, in the early years of the Yífēng era, he arrived at Nǎnhǎi and encountered Dharma Master Yìnzōng preaching the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at Fǎxìng Temple. The Patriarch stayed in the corridors and eaves;
there, as the wind blew the banner atop the flagpole, he heard two monks debating it—one saying the banner was moving, and the other saying...
The wind moved. After several rounds of discussion, he had still not attained realization. The Patriarch asked, "May a layman be permitted to join in this high discourse?
The monk said, "Please try to explain it for me. The Patriarch said, "It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving. It is your own mind moving.
At these words, the monk attained great enlightenment. Master Yinzong overheard these words in secret and was struck with awe and wonder.
The Monastic Bell Chimes (Huìyuán, Vol. 11). When Gayāsata first met the seventeenth patriarch, Saṃghanandin, he held a precious mirror and hurried forward to welcome him.
Saṃghanandin asked, "What do you intend to do with this round mirror?
The youth Gayāsata then replied in verse: "The great round mirror of all Buddhas is without interior or exterior..."
"Flaws and obscurations—both men perceive them alike; their eyes and minds are similar.
Because his responses differed from those of Nanda, his parents sent him forth to leave the home life. Nanda accepted this and took him back to the monastery.
Later, when the wind shook the copper bells of the hall so that they rang out, he asked again: "Is it the bell that rings, or is it the wind?"
He replied, "It is neither the wind nor the bell; it is my own heart that is ringing.
Magu (a successor of Mazu; *Chuan Deng Lu* 5) arrived at Zhangjing carrying his staff.
He circled the meditation seat three times, struck the ground once with his staff, and stood there motionless. Zhangjing said, "So, so. Magu then went to Nanquan.
He circumambulated the meditation platform three times, shook his staff once, and stood there resolutely. Baizhang said, "It is not so, it is not so.
Magu said, "At that time, Zhangjing said it was so; why does the Master say it is not? Baizhang said:
"Zhangjing is this; you are not. This is turned by the power of the wind and will ultimately end in ruin.
Puhua shook his bell (from *Chuan deng lu*, fascicle 10). As for the Venerable Puhua of Zhenzhou, it is unknown where he was from.
He served Panshan as his master, receiving the true instructions in secret while feigning madness; his speech was unrestrained.
When Panshan passed away, he began to propagate his teachings at this site, whether in the city or among the graves, shaking a single bell and saying:

"If it comes from the bright side, strike the bright side; if it comes from the dark side, strike the dark side; if it comes from the four quarters and eight directions, strike with a whirlwind. Empty...
Coming from empty space, he struck the frame of the gate. One day, Linji ordered a monk to seize him and asked, "What if one does not come in this manner at all?
The Master pushed him away and said, "Tomorrow there is a vegetarian feast at Dayi Monastery. The monk returned and reported this to Linji.
Linji said, "I have always suspected this fellow. Whenever he saw anyone, regardless of their status, he would shake his staff.
He was known at the time as Master Puhua. Sometimes he would take a metal gong and shake it against people’s ears, or pat them on the back;
if anyone looked back, he would immediately open his hands and say, “Give me a coin.

The Master once stood shaking his gong and singing among the crowds in the marketplace, saying, “I seek a place to go, but cannot find one. At that time, Daowu encountered him and grabbed hold of him.
The questioner asked, "Where do you intend to go? The Master said, "From where have you come? The questioner was speechless. The Master clapped his hands and departed.
Yishan Huizhe (a successor of Mazu; *Chuan Deng Lu*, fascicle 8), the Chan Master of Longshan in Tanzhou, was also named Yishan. He lived in seclusion in a cave.

When Chan Master Shanjia was first traveling to seek teachers, he journeyed together with a monk named Mipo. Passing beneath Longshan in Changsha, they saw vegetable leaves floating in a mountain stream.
Shanjia looked back at the peaks and ridges with deep insight and said to Mipo, "There must be a hidden practitioner here.
They then proceeded along the stream for about ten li, where they encountered an elderly monk who appeared very emaciated and was using his hand—
Raising his eyebrows, he called out, "There is no path here; how have you all arrived? Jia said, "As for there being no path, let that be;

but from where did you yourself enter, Master of the Hermitage? He replied, "I am not one who wanders as a cloud or water. Jia asked, "How long has it been since you, Master of the Hermitage, have lived on this mountain?
He replied, "I have not been involved with spring or autumn. Jia said, "Did you live here first? He replied, "I do not know. Jia [continued].
[The Master] asked, "Why do you not know? [Yunju] replied, "I have never come from the human or celestial realms.
Jia said, "What principle have you realized that allows you to dwell in the mountains thus? [Yunju] said, "I saw a clay ox fight its way into the sea; even until now, there has been no news."
Jia immediately stepped down from the platform and bowed to him, asking, "What is the guest within the host? He replied, "Green mountains shrouded by white clouds.
He asked again, "What is the host within the host? He replied, "Never leaving the door for many years. He asked again, "How far apart are the host and the guest?
He replied, "Waves upon the waters of the Long River. He asked again, "When the guest and host meet..."
"What words can describe it? he asked. "It is the clear breeze brushing against the white moon. Jia bowed twice and requested to become his attendant. The old monk smiled and said:
"I have lived for long in this three-bay thatched hut; / A single path of divine light leaves all phenomena at rest. / Do not come with notions of right and wrong to judge me;
/ This floating life’s forced interpretations are irrelevant. Thereupon, he set fire to his hermitage and retreated deep into the layered peaks.
Dongshan Removes His Name (Dharma heir of Tanmeng; *Chuan Deng Lu*, fascicle 15). As Dongshan was about to pass away, he said to the assembly, "I have a name that has long been known to the world;
who can remove it for me? No one in the assembly could respond. At that time, a novice monk stepped forward and said, "Please tell us your Dharma-name, Reverend.
The Master replied, "The name I have long held has already ceased."
The Price of Rice in Luling (Huìyuán V): A monk of Qingyuan asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
The Master said, "What is the price of rice in Luling?"
The Sound of the Yanxi Water (Huìyuán 7). Once, when Jingqing came to visit Xuansha, he asked:
"A student who has newly entered the monastic community requests that the Master point out a way of entry. Xuansha said, "Do you hear the sound of the Yanxi water? Jingqing replied, "I hear it."
Sāhu said, "He enters from within. At this, Qing suddenly attained great enlightenment.

According to the *Chuan* (Biography) of Shuanglin: When the Great Being Shanhui was invited by Emperor Wu to preach the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra of the Threefold Wisdom* in the Chongyun Hall, some among the princes and nobles noticed that the Great Being’s sitting posture was not upright, and they asked him:
"Why do you not sit upright? He replied, "The upright person has no fixed nature; the slanting person has no slanting mind. The Way is traversed crosswise.
(From *Deshan Yuan*, a successor of Deshan Yuan, *Huiyuan* 15). Chan Master Shixian of Kaishan on Mount Lu was a native of Linjiang Commandery. His conduct was pure and austere;
he traveled extensively among the seats of various masters, making awakening his primary goal. He visited Deshan.
Upon seeing this, Shanshan ascended the hall and looked out at the assembly, saying, "The lion stretches; the elephant king turns his gaze. At these words, the Master suddenly attained realization.
He entered the room to present his understanding, whereupon Shanshan asked, "How do you understand this? The Master turned around and said, "The donkey in the back garden is eating grass.
Shanshan approved. Later, he went to Xuedou; when Xuedou spoke with him, he was delighted by his transcendent insight and [bestowed upon him] the title...

The Kitchen Steward and the Birth of Insects (Chuan Deng Lu 15). When Chan Master Shishuang Zhu first arrived at Da Mei, he volunteered for manual labor, working diligently with pestles and mortars for a very long time.
When Yanhui saw him winnowing grain, he said, "The offerings of the donors must not be scattered or wasted.
Shishuang replied, "I dare not. Yanhui stooped down, picked up a single grain, and said, "Is this not what was being scattered? The Master [was struck silent].
[The monk] attempted to counter him. Huìyǒu said, "Do not underestimate this single grain; hundreds of thousands of grains are born from this one grain.
[The monk] asked, "If that is so, from what is this grain born? Huìyǒu laughed heartily. The next day, he ascended the seat and said, "Great assembly!"
"There are worms in the rice.
Huik'e understood clearly (*Chuan deng lu* 3). When the First Patriarch first resided at Shaolin Monastery for nine years, he preached the Dharma for Huik'e, instructing him only by saying:
"Cease all external conditions; let the inner mind be without gasping. Let the mind be like a wall or a fence; thus you may enter [the Way]."
The Master [Nanyue Huairang] explained the principle of the nature of mind in various ways, yet he did not yet accord with the Way.

The Patriarch merely refuted his errors but did not explain the essence of the non-conceptual mind. The Master said, "I have already stilled all conditions. The Patriarch asked, "Does this not result in annihilation?
The Master replied, "It does not result in annihilation. The Patriarch asked, "How do you verify that it is not annihilated? The Master said:
Because it is known with constant clarity, it cannot be reached through words. The Patriarch said: "This is the essence of mind transmitted by all Buddhas;
do not doubt it further.
Master Yan of Ruiyan in Taizhou was ever-vigilant throughout his life and constantly sat in meditation, calling out, "The Host!"
He then responded for himself, saying, "Be clearly aware; hereafter, do not be deceived by others. Later, a monk went to Xuansha and recounted this incident to him.
Xuansha said, "They are equally spirits—how truly extraordinary! Xuansha then asked, "Why did you not remain right there?
The monk replied, "He had already passed away. Xuansha asked, "If you were to call out to him now, would he respond?"
The monk had no reply. Sanda cried out, "Heaven! Heaven! (Dafu Shouzhi succeeded him;
*Sengbaozhuan*, Vol. Lower). Zen Master Wenyue of Yunfeng sat behind the rack. The rack collapsed.
As he descended, a bucket and basin fell from the rack below him. Suddenly, he attained awakening and immediately saw the practical application of Dongshan’s former teachings.
He ran, donning his *kāṣāya*, up to the dormitory hall. Dongshan met him with a smile and said, "Venerable Vinaya Master, rejoice! Your great matter is now concluded."

The Master bowed twice, and sweat poured from him; he departed without uttering a single word. He served with diligence for eight years, during which time thousands of officials brought peace and security to the solitary commoners.
The Ten Vows of Qingliang (The Patriarch of the Fourth [Patriarch] of the Avataṃsaka). Supplement: National Teacher Qingliang Chengguan, courtesy name Daixiu, was a native of Kuaiji.
His surname was Xiahou. He exhorted himself with ten matters, saying: "In my conduct, I shall not damage the outward appearance of a śramaṇa;
in my mind, I shall not contravene the regulations of the Tathāgata; in my sitting, I shall not turn my back on the sūtras of the Dharmadhātu; and by nature, I shall remain unstained."
Regarding the realms that obstruct his emotions: his feet did not tread upon the dust of a nunnery; his side did not touch the couch of a layman;
his eyes did not gaze upon colors that were not righteous; his tongue did not taste delicacies served after noon; his hands did not let go of the perfectly luminous pearl;
and he did not sleep apart from the side of his robes and bowl (and so forth). This is seen in the *Biographies of Monks of the Six Studies*.
The Four Practices of Bodhidharma (from *Chuan deng lu*, Vol. 30). Master Bodhidharma briefly distinguished the four practices for entering the Way according to the Mahāyāna.
Now, there are many paths for entering the Way; to summarize them, they do not exceed two kinds: first, entry through principle (*lirù*); second, entry through practice (*xingrù*).

Entry through principle means awakening to the fundamental source by relying on the teachings. It involves deep faith that all living beings share the same true nature, yet [are obscured] merely because...
Covered by adventitious delusions, one cannot manifest clarity. If one abandons delusion to return to the truth, remaining steadfastly in wall-contemplation, there is neither self nor other;
ordinary beings and sages are equal as one. Abiding firmly without wavering, one no longer follows the teachings of words and texts.
This is precisely in accord with the principle; it is free from discrimination, quiescent, and unconditioned—this is called "entry by principle.
As for "entry by practice," this refers to the four practices, into which all other practices are fully subsumed. What are these four? First, the practice of requiting grievances;
second, the practice of following conditions; third, the practice of seeking nothing; and fourth, the practice of conforming to the Dharma. What is meant by "requiting"?
The Practice of Resolving Enmity: This means that when a practitioner on the path of cultivation undergoes suffering, they should reflect to themselves:

"Throughout countless kalpas in the past, I abandoned the fundamental for the peripheral and wandered through the various realms of existence, giving rise to infinite enmity, hatred, and harmful opposition.
Although I have committed no offense now, this is the ripening of the fruit of my own past calamities and evil karma; it is not something caused by gods or humans."
One perceives and understands this; with a willing heart, one endures it without any resentment or complaint. As the Sutra says: "When encountering suffering, do not accept it.

Why is this? Because of thorough understanding. When this mind arises, it accords with principle; by taking offense as the catalyst for advancing on the Path, it is called the "Practice of Retribution for Offenses.
Second is the "Practice of Following Conditions": sentient beings lack a self, being merely transmitted through the conditions of karma; thus, suffering and joy are equal.
All sensations arise from conditions. If one obtains superior retributions such as honor and fame, these are induced by causes from one’s past lives;
they are now obtained, but when the conditions are exhausted, they return to nothingness. What cause for joy is there? Gain and loss follow conditions; the mind neither increases nor decreases.
Like the true wind that does not stir, one remains in profound accord with the Way. Therefore, it is said: "Acting in accordance with conditions."
Third, regarding the practitioner who seeks nothing: worldly people are long deluded, greedily attached to everything everywhere; this is called "seeking.
The wise person awakens to the True Principle and turns away from the mundane. They settle their minds in non-action (*wuwei*) while their bodies follow the turning of destiny.
All phenomena are empty, and there is nothing to desire or delight in. Merit and darkness constantly pursue one another; dwelling long within the three realms is like being in a fire.

Dwelling: Since all that has form is suffering, who could find peace therein? Having thoroughly realized this point, one abandons all states of existence (*bhava*), ceases conceptualization, and becomes free from seeking.
As the Sūtra says: "All seeking is suffering; non-seeking is bliss. One discerns that non-seeking and the pursuit of truth constitute the practice of the Way;
therefore, it is called the "practice of non-seeking. Fourth, regarding the "practice in accordance with the Dharma": this refers to the principle of the purity of intrinsic nature.
This is the Dharma. This principle is empty of all characteristics; it is without defilement, without attachment, and without "this" or "that. As the Sūtra says:
"The Dharma has no sentient beings, because it is free from the defilement of sentient beings; the Dharma has no self, because it is free from the defilement of the self.
If a wise person can believe and understand this principle, they should act in accordance with the Dharma. The essence of the Dharma is without stinginess regarding body, life, or wealth.
One practices the giving of alms with a mind free from stinginess. Having realized and understood the three kinds of emptiness, one does not rely upon or cling to them;

one acts solely to remove defilements. While transforming sentient beings according to their needs, one does not grasp at signs. This constitutes both self-cultivation and the benefiting of others, and it also serves to adorn the path to Bodhi.
As it is with the perfection of giving, so it is with the other five perfections; they are practiced to eliminate deluded thoughts.
To practice the six perfections while having nothing to practice—this is called practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
Regarding the "Account of the Merit of Master Changzhao Kuang" (from *Chuanteng lu*, vol. 14): When Master Changzhao Kuang first visited Shitou, Shitou asked, "Where have you come from?
He replied, "From the top of Mount Dayu. Shitou asked, "Has the one set of merit at the summit of the mountain been completed yet?"
[The Master] said, "He has accomplished it; he only lacks a touch of the eye. [The Master] asked, "Shall I not give him a touch of the eye? [The Master] said, "Then please do so.
Shitou lowered one foot. The Master then prostrated. [The Master] asked, "What principle did you perceive that you prostrate? [The Master] replied, "Like a single drop of snow on a red-hot furnace."
**Huangmei Foxing (Chuan Deng XIII): The Fifth Patriarch, Great Master Daman** There was once a layman surnamed Lu and named Huineng who came from Qizhou to seek an audience with the Master.
The Master asked, “Where have you come from? He replied, “From Lingnan. The Master said, “What do you seek?
He replied, “I only seek to become a Buddha. The Master said, “People of Lingnan have no Buddha-nature; how could you possibly become a Buddha?”

He attained Buddhahood. [Nanquan] said, "People have north and south, but how could the Buddha-nature be like that? The Master knew he was an extraordinary person, so he rebuked him, saying, "Go to the fodder shed!
He was able to prostrate at his feet and withdraw, then entered the space between the pestle and mortar to perform manual labor.
*Śāriputra Collects Medicine* (Huìyuán 2). Mañjuśrī instructs Śāriputra to collect medicine, saying: "Bring this medicine here.

"This medicine can both kill people and bring people to life."
Daci Huanzhong Chanshi (the fourth patriarchal lineage record of Baizhang’s dharma heirs). Master Daci Huanzhong of Hangzhou addressed the assembly, saying:

Yinfeng said, "I ask the Master to withdraw your feet. Mazu replied, "Once spread, they do not contract.
Yinfeng said, "Once advanced, one does not retreat," and he pushed the cart, crushing Mazu’s feet. Mazu returned to the Dharma Hall holding an axe and said, "Just now..."

(Lu You kicked over the jar; *Huìyuán*, Case 9. Zen Master Baizhang Hai was once visited by the itinerant ascetic Sima Tuo from Hunan.
Lai said to Baizhang, "Recently, while in Hunan, I found a mountain named Dayue (Great Mui).
It is the dwelling place of a teacher of one thousand five hundred people. Baizhang asked, "Can an old monk like me reside there?
Daowu replied, "It is not a place for the Master to dwell. Baizhang asked, "Why? Daowu said, "The Master is a man of bone; that is a mountain of flesh."
The resident disciples did not number more than a thousand. The Master asked, "Is there anyone among my assembly who can abide [in this state]? Dadao replied, "I shall observe him closely.
At that time, Hualin Jue was serving as the First Seat (Dìyīzuò). The Master ordered an attendant to invite him to his presence and asked, "What is this man like?
Dadao requested that he cough once and walk a few steps. Dadao said, "He cannot. The Master then...
He summoned Chan Master Lingyou; at that time, the Master was serving as the head cook (diànzuò). Upon seeing him, Baizhang said, "This is truly the master of Mount Gui.
That night, Baizhang summoned the Master into his room and instructed him, saying, "My karmic conditions for transformation end here."
"Mount Gui is a supreme realm; you should dwell there, continuing my lineage and extensively guiding future students.
When Hualin heard this, he said, "I am respectfully serving as the head monk; why should I, the kitchen steward, take charge of the monastery?

Baizhang said, "If you can utter a single phrase that transcends the ordinary before the assembly, I shall grant you the position of abbot. He then pointed to a water pitcher and asked, "Is it not..."
"It can be called a 'pure vase' (*śuci-ghaṭa*). What do you call it? Lin said, "It cannot be called a wooden bucket. Baizhang then asked the Master.
The Master kicked over the pure vase and went out. Baizhang laughed and said, "The First Seat has lost to Shanzzi.
The Master then departed for that mountain. It was steep and precipitous, utterly devoid of human habitation, with only monkeys and apes there.
He sustained himself on acorns and chestnuts for five or seven years, with no one coming at all. The Master thought to himself, "I originally took up residence here to benefit others.
Now that all contact has ceased, how can my own virtue alone provide salvation? He immediately abandoned the hermitage and intended to go elsewhere.
As he reached the mountain pass, he saw snakes, tigers, wolves, and leopards crossing his path. The Master said:
"You beasts, do not block my path. If I have a karmic affinity with this mountain, you may each disperse;
if I have no such affinity, there is no need for you to move. I shall pass along the road as I please; feel free to eat me.
Having spoken these words, the insects and tigers dispersed in the four directions, and the Master returned to his hermitage. Less than a year had passed when An Zuo (An the Elder) arrived.
(He was Lan’an. Several monks came from Baizhang to assist the Master. An said, "I shall serve as the *dianzuo* (steward) for the Master;
I will provide meals for five hundred monks regardless of the season, and I shall not prepare congee. He then dismissed them, saying, "Leave me alone.
Afterward, the local residents at the foot of the mountain gradually learned of this and led the community in jointly providing offerings.
Minister Li Jingrang submitted a memorial requesting that the temple be renamed Tongqing Temple. The Chancellor, Lord Pei Xu, once consulted him on its profound mysteries;

Jizang Breaks the Mirror (Yangshan’s name was Huiji; *Chuan deng lu*, fascicle 11). Once, when Yangshan received a mirror sent by Guishan, he ascended the hall and said:
"Tell me, is this Guishan’s mirror or Yangshan’s mirror? If you say it is Guishan’s..."
Furthermore, it was in Yangshan’s hand. If one says it belongs to Yangshan, it was actually sent by Guishan.
"If you can speak [the truth], I shall not break it; if you cannot speak it, I shall break it. He asked this three times, but the assembly had no response. Thereupon, he smashed it to pieces.
Awakening to the Source at the Pickaxe (Tánshèng’s Dharma Heir; *Huìyuán*, 13). Dōngshān and Mì Shībǎi were hoeing a tea garden.
The Master threw down his pickaxe and said, "Today I have not a single bit of strength. Mì said, "If you have no strength, how could you say such a thing?

The Handle of the Ink-Bean Ladle (Mazu’s Dharma Heir; *Huìyuán*, Vol. 3). Master Wugu (Ujū) asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk replied, "Dingzhou.

The Master said, "If it is no different, then go back there! and he struck him. The monk said, "There are eyes upon the staff; do not strike so recklessly."
The Master said, "Today I have struck one. He struck three blows. The monk then went out.
The Master said, "It turns out there is someone here to eat the staff. The monk replied, "But the handle of the ladle is still in the hands of the Master.
The Master said, "If you want it, I shall give it back to you. The monk stepped forward, snatched the staff, and struck the Master three times. The Master—
The Master said, "Beng! Beng! The monk replied, "There is someone eating. The Master said, "In a flurry, I have struck this fellow.
The monk bowed; the Master said, "And yet you go away like that? The monk laughed loudly and departed. The Master remarked, "He is worthy of such treatment."

The Woman’s Emergence from Samādhi (Huìyuán 1): *The Scripture on the Essential Assembly of All Buddhas*.

Mañjuśrī wished to see the assembly of the Buddhas, but he was unable to reach it, as each of the Buddhas had returned to their own respective places. Mañjuśrī then went to the site where the Buddhas had gathered.

A certain woman sat near that Buddha and entered into samādhi. After Mañjuśrī had entered and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "Why is it that this woman is able to sit near the Buddha while I am not?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "Awaken this woman and cause her to arise from samādhi; you should ask her yourself."
Suśīla snapped his fingers to awaken him, but he could not be awakened. He called out with a loud voice, yet still could not awaken him.
He struck him with his hand and pulled at him, but still could not awaken him. Furthermore, he shook the trichiliocosm with his leg in meditative concentration, yet [the man] still did not awaken.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "I did not intend for him to awaken. At that moment, the Buddha emitted—
A great radiance illuminated the world below. Within it was a bodhisattva named Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, who immediately came from the lower direction to the place where the Buddha was.
He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side.
The Buddha said to the bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, “Awaken this woman. Immediately, he snapped his fingers, and the woman arose from her samādhi.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha: "By what cause and condition was it that although I shook this trichiliocosm, I could not cause this woman to arise?
Yet the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin caused her to rise from samādhi with a single snap of his fingers.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "It is because of this woman that you first resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Di. This woman, because of her encounter with the Bodhisattva Qi zhige (Discarding All Veils), has resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, you were unable to awaken her. Regarding the verse, it refers to the Bodhisattva Gangming;

however, this is recorded in the *Chuandeng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) and its source in any sutra or śāstra remains unclear. A search through the Tripitaka and the various vehicles of scripture reveals no such citation. (From the *Zuting shiyuan*, entry titled "Wenming")
