Whenever he asked about his own spiritual progress, his peers—seeing his coarse appearance and awkward demeanor—would all mock and deride him.

One day, while walking through the temple courtyard, he suddenly tripped and fell; at that moment, he attained sudden and perfect enlightenment. He composed a verse and had an attendant write it down.
On the wall he wrote: "This one exchange, this one exchange—ten thousand taels of gold would hardly suffice to repay it. A hat upon the head, a bundle at the waist;
the clear breeze and bright moon are carried upon the tip of the staff. That very day he departed from Donglin.

When the news reached Zhaojue, Zhaojue was greatly delighted and said, "If a monk’s investigation of the Way is such as this, no greater excellence could be added. He then ordered someone to trace his calligraphy.
Wherever one goes, in the end, there is no one who knows [it].
(Zhaojue, Elder of Donglin Temple) The Abbot of Gushan asked Upādhyāya Fu: "Before your parents were born, where was your nose?
Fu said, "Teacher, you go first. Gushan said, "Even now, in this very life, where is your nose?"
Deshan asked, "How about you? Huo said, "Bring me the fan in your hand.
Deshan passed the fan to him. Deshan asked again; Huo pointed at it and set it down. Deshan then gave him a punch.
Cuiyan Maimao (Dharma heir of Xuefeng Cun; *Huiyuan* 8). At the end of the summer retreat, Cuiyan addressed the assembly, saying:
"Throughout this entire summer, I have been speaking for you, my brothers. Look: are Cuiyan’s eyebrows still there?"
Shanshan Holds Up a Ruler (from *Chanlin Leiju*, Volume 17). One day, while Master Shanshan was sitting with Layman Pang, the Master picked up a ruler and said, "Layman, do you see it?
The Layman replied, "I see it. The Master asked, "What do you see? The Layman said, "Shanshan.
The Master said, "You must not say that. The Layman asked, "Why can I not say it? The Master threw the ruler down.
The Master said, "Son, the layman says there is a head but no tail; that is detestable.
The Master said, "It is not that this old fellow today still says he cannot reach it. Where? The Master said, "In the place where there is a head but no tail.
The Layman said, "One may find weakness within strength, but one finds no strength within weakness. The Master seized him and said, "This old man has nothing within him!"
"In the place where there is life, there is no place for life.
(Huìyuán 7) One day Dōngshān asked Xuěfēng, "What have you been doing? Fēng replied, "I have been hewing a trough.
Shān asked, "How many blows of the axe did it take to complete it? Fēng said, "It was completed with a single blow. Shān remarked, "That is still..."
"This matter here—what about that matter there? Feng stopped. Fenyang spoke on his behalf, saying, "I am but a simple fellow.
(The Patriarch’s Hall Collection, Case 16). Once, a monk who was a lecturer came to visit Master Yanguan. The Master asked him, "Lecturer..."
"What work do you perform? He replied, "I lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. The Master asked, "How many kinds of dharmadhātu are there?
He replied, "To speak extensively, they are infinitely layered; to speak briefly, there are four kinds of dharmadhātu.
The Master held up his whisk and said, "Which of these four is this? The presiding lecturer hesitated and pondered slowly for an answer. The Master—
It is said: "To know through thinking and to understand through deliberation is the livelihood of ghosts—a solitary lamp beneath the sun.
Indeed, the light is lost; indeed, the light is lost.
The Phoenix Nest on the Cliffs (Lóngtán Xìn’s Dharma heir; *Chúndēng Lù*, Case 16). Master Yuǎn'ān of Lèpǔ Mountain in Lǐzhōu arrived.

Jiashan was staying at a hermitage atop a tomb. Upon receiving a letter from Jiashan, Xuanze sent it to An and instructed his messenger, "If this monk does not open the letter upon receipt, he will come tomorrow;
if he opens it, he will not come. When An received the letter, he indeed set it aside and gave no reply.
The messenger reported this fully to Jiashan, who said, "He will surely arrive by dawn or dusk. Shortly thereafter—
Baoguan arrived. Seeing him from afar, Jiashan scolded him, saying, "A rooster nesting in a phoenix’s den—this is no match for its kind.
Get out! Baoguan then asked, "I have come from afar to pay my respects; I pray the Master will grant me an audience. Jiashan said, "Before my eyes there is no monk;
here there is no old monk. Baoguan said, "Wrong! Jiashan said, "Stop, stop! Do not be so hasty and reckless."
Chuang said, "Clouds and moon are the same; streams and mountains are each different.
It is not that one cannot cut off the tongues of all under heaven, but can you, O Acharya, save a tongueless person from speaking? An was at a loss and did not know how to answer.
Jia Shan struck him with his staff, and from this point on, An devoted himself to his teachings for several years.
Letang Mugua (Dharma heir of Longtan Xian; *Chuan deng lu* 15). Master Baofeng of Letang in Hongzhou had a newly arrived monk.
The Master said to him, "The matter within [the realm] is easy; the matter that does not fall within [the realm] is difficult from beginning to end."
The monk said, "While I was on the road, I already knew there would be this question.
The Master said, "Even if you had traveled for another twenty years, it would not have made much difference. The monk asked, "Is it that you do not approve of my intent?
The Master replied, "A bitter gourd is no fit host for guests."
Xianglin Chengyuan (Chuan Deng 11):
While Linji was working in the fields during a communal labor session, he saw Huangbo approaching and stood with his hoe resting on his shoulder.
Huangbo asked, "Is this fellow tired? The Master replied, "The hoe hasn't even been lifted; what is there to be tired about? Huangbo—
He struck him. The Master caught the staff and gave it a shove, sending him tumbling down. Huangbo called out, "Venerable Steward, Venerable Steward, help me up!
The steward approached and supported him, saying, "How can you, Master, tolerate this madman’s impertinence?
As soon as Huangbo rose, he struck the steward. The Master, working with his mattock, said, "Everywhere else they perform cremations; here, we bury them alive all at once."
Huiji Plants His Hoe (Chuan Deng Lu 11). Master Guishan suddenly asked Master Yangshan, "Where have you come from?
Yangshan replied, "From the fields. Guishan asked, "How many people are in the fields? Yangshan stood there planting his hoe.
Guishan said, "Today on South Mountain there are many people cutting thatch. Yangshan raised his hoe and departed.

The True Testament of Lingyuan (the sixth in the lineage of Puding, dharma heir of Huanglong Zuoxin): Chan Master Huanglong Fushou, whose name was Weiqing, courtesy name Juetian, and sobriquet Lingyuan Srou.
Ten days before his passing, he composed the "Inscription on the True Return to Unborn Permanence," which states:
"The forty-eighth generation directly descending from Śākyamuni Buddha, the fourth honored one of the Bhadrakalpa."

The great-great-grandson, Weiqing, although born from the response to conditions through fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), realized that conditions are themselves empty and have never possessed inherent nature (*svabhāva*).

His ancestral lineage and native place cannot be detailed with certainty; he simply takes the single thought of the true cause (*tathatā-hetu*) as his primary lineage, thereby constituting a distant descendant of Śākyamuni.
He was styled the Elder Lingyuan, based on what is realized through the factor of self-realization (*svayambhū-hetu*).
Within the wondrous nature that is devoid of names, designations are merely shown for the sake of reference. This "True Person of No-Station" from Linji is akin to the "King of Mind" of Master Fu;
it is also the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the Wondrous Mind of Nirvana—something known only through personal realization, which others cannot fathom.
Thus, when the Sixth Patriarch asked Reverend Rang, "Where have you come from? he replied:
He came from Mount Song. The Patriarch asked, "What thing comes in such a manner? He replied, "To describe it as a thing is not to the point.
The Patriarch asked, "Is there still cultivation and realization? He replied, "Cultivation and realization are not absent, yet it cannot be defiled.
The Patriarch said, "This very state of being undefiled is that which all Buddhas protect and keep in mind. Since you are thus, so am I."
Thus it is. This passage singles out the pure *dharmakāya* alone to follow the tradition of the "special transmission outside the teachings.

It distinguishes [the other bodies] by stating that the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* are not the true Buddha, nor are they the speakers of the Dharma. However, this does not mean that the great function and great utility of the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* do not exist.
It is said that if one understands the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* but fails to suddenly perceive the *dharmakāya*, one will remain stuck in the conditions of defilement.

This surely deviates from the intent of [the Buddha’s] protective mindfulness; in principle, one must certainly exercise vigilance and self-reflection. Now, as for the practice of the Shaoshi lineage, its light soared through successive generations:
there was Yunmen Wenyan, who raised a heroic voice and an unprecedented chant within the realm; and Linji Yixuan, who shook forth great function and great capacity throughout the world.
Both attained the authentic transmission, and the world universally revered them. Only Qingwang [remains] of the ninth generation of Linji.

This is the work of Sun. Nowadays, the religious teachings have declined and fallen into ruin; of those that have not yet been entirely extinguished, only faint traces of two schools remain here and there.
Yet their reputations often fall short of their actual substance, and they find themselves in precarious and strange circumstances.

My own life is as transient as morning dew, and the conditions of my existence are so urgent that I am on the verge of withering and falling away due to illness. Therefore, I have left the secular world to follow the Truth, recording the matters above for the sake of my two or three disciples.

After I have entrusted [my affairs] to the Truth, you should rely upon and follow the contemplative investigation; thus you will not contravene the Dharma-gate of the former sages and will personally perceive profound benefit.

Be careful not to follow the prevailing trends of the Final Dharma (mofa), begging for empty texts from those in office or seeking to have inscriptions and monuments composed, using flowery rhetoric to defile me.
My most earnest exhortation! My most earnest exhortation! Therefore, he wrote of his own accord: "Unborn and Eternal."

I, Zhuzhen, offer this address and bind it with an inscription. The inscription says: In the boundless, profound sea, a single bubble momentarily arises; spanning a hundred years, what floats and what rests?
Across the vast, empty Milky Way, a fragment of cloud suddenly appears; how can existence and non-existence, arising and ceasing, or concealment and manifestation be distinguished?
To comprehend these two is to perceive the true mark (*dharmatā*). Throughout the ten ages of past and present, from beginning to end...
Direct Perception: I inscribe this principle to proclaim it clearly to you all. "The mud is deep, so the Buddha is great; the water is long, so the boat is high.
This is the "Song of Mount Tai" (Shishuang’s Dharma heirs, *Chuan Deng Lu*, Vol. 16). Nan-nie of Tai resided at a hermitage on the eastern side of Mount Heng, known as Qibao Terrace.
He vowed never to establish formal disciples, yet those from all quarters who came to rely upon him were all treated with [the same] respect.

Regarding the etiquette of friendship: [The Master] once observed that Mount Heng was frequently ravaged by mountain dwellers who cleared the land by felling timber and burning the fields (*miántián*), causing immense harm.
He therefore composed the "Ballad of the Burnt Fields" (*Yeshānyáo*), which spread far and wide until it reached the Imperial Court. An edict was subsequently issued prohibiting the practice;

consequently, the monasteries within the sacred peaks were no longer subjected to fire. This was due to the Master’s efforts. The Ballad of the Burnt Fields: The child of the burnt fields (*yeshān’ér*) has no...
It is known: year after year the green peaks of Mount Mei are hewn down. Among them, the colors of Mount Heng are the most exquisite;
yet the sharp axes destroy the steadfast branches of the cypresses and pines. The numinous birds and wild cranes have no place to rely; white clouds avoid the rising blue smoke.

The paths for monkeys and apes are cut off as they emerge from the cliffs; the roots of *zhi* and *shu* herbs are lost as the marsh grasses flourish. Year after year, once the felling is done, they are planted again.
The hoe—after a thousand years, it is ultimately difficult to restore the original state. It is further said: "This year’s planting was not much;
next year we shall clear even more of the slopes facing the sun. If the life-mountain of the nation were like this, one knows not how such a principle could be sustained.
Master Shaoxian of Tanzhou Aohua (a dharma heir of Xian of Beichan, among the Jewel of the Sangha) established a monastic hall.
At that time, the reputation of Master Nan of Nanchan was flourishing, and monks from the Jinghu region were flocking into Jiangnan.
Within a hundred li of Changsha, there was no place to lodge, and many were plundered by bandits; consequently, the roads became impassable. Master Shaoxian was nearly fifty years old.
He established a guest house and invited the *śramaṇa*-master to preside over its reception, enabling travelers to stay, eat, and depart. People from all quarters held him in high esteem;
he protected the state and repaired bridges.
The Sixth Patriarch Carries Gold (The Lamp of the Dharma, Volume 5). Zen Master Zhiche of Jiangxi was a native of Jiangxi. His secular surname was Zhang and his given name was Xingchang.
In his youth, he was a man of chivalric spirit. Since the division between the North and South, although the two patriarchs had ceased all notions of "self" and "other,"...
Meanwhile, his disciples vied with one another in their likes and dislikes. At that time, the followers of the Northern School established Master Xiu as the Sixth Patriarch;
they resented the fact that Master Neng had transmitted the robe, which became widely known throughout the world. However, the Patriarch was a Bodhisattva who foresaw these events.
He immediately placed ten taels of gold in his quarters. At that time, Xingchang was a follower of the Northern School.
Following these instructions, Xingchang entered the Patriarch’s chamber with a blade, intending to do him harm. The Patriarch extended his neck toward him;
though Xingchang struck three times, the blade did not cause the slightest injury. The Patriarch said, "A true sword is not crooked; a crooked sword is not true. I owe you only gold, not my life.
Startled, Xingchang collapsed and only regained consciousness after a long time. He then begged for mercy and repented his transgressions.

"I wish to leave the household life. The Patriarch then gave him gold, saying, "Go for now. I fear that the assembly might instead bring harm upon you. You may come another day in a different guise; I shall then receive you.
Xingchang followed these instructions and fled under the cover of night. Later, he captured a monk, ordained him as a full monk, and he practiced with great diligence.
One day, remembering the Patriarch’s words, he traveled a long distance to pay his respects. He engaged in a dialogue with the Master.
The karmic conditions were in harmony. The Patriarch said, "You have now attained thorough penetration. You should be named Zhiche (Thoroughly Penetrated). The Master bowed in thanks and departed.
Shenguang repaid his debt [to the Dharma] (*Huiyuan*, 1). As for the Second Patriarch, he was a native of Wulao. His surname was Ji, and his father was JI.
Before he had a son, the father used to think to himself, "My family honors what is good; how could we be without offspring? After he had prayed for a long time...

One night, he was moved by a supernatural light that illuminated his room; his mother consequently became pregnant with him. When he grew up, she named him Guang (Light) after this auspicious sign of the light filling the chamber.
From childhood, his aspirations were extraordinary; he studied the *Shi* and *Shu* classics extensively and was particularly adept at the profound principles of the *Xuanxue* (Dark Learning).

Yet, he did not concern himself with family property, preferring instead to roam among mountains and waters. Later, upon reading Buddhist scriptures, he attained a state of transcendent self-realization. Immediately—
He arrived at Mount Xiangshan in Longmen, Luoyang, where he took ordination under Master Shijing.

He received full precepts at Yongmu Temple and traveled among lecture halls to study the doctrines of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. At the age of thirty-two, he returned once more to Mount Xiangshan.
He sat in meditation throughout the day for another eight years. Amidst his silence, he suddenly beheld a divine being who said to him, "You are about to receive the fruit [of enlightenment];
why do you linger here? The Great Way is not far from Nan. The Patriarch, knowing this was divine assistance, changed his name to Shenguang (Divine Light).
The following day, he felt a headache as piercing as thorns. His master wished to treat it, but from the air—
A voice said, "This is the extraordinary pain of changing one's bones. The Patriarch then informed his master of what he had seen.
The master examined his cranial bone and saw that it rose up like five peaks; he then said, "Your marks are auspicious and you shall surely attain realization.
That the spirit commanded you to go south refers to the Great Master Bodhidharma of Shaolin; he must be your [teacher]."
He was his teacher’s disciple. His master received the teachings and traveled to Mount Shaoshi. Bodhidharma consequently changed his name to Huikē and transmitted the dharma to him.
Later, at the Triple Gate of Kuangjiu Temple in Guancheng County, he expounded the Unsurpassed Way.
The audience was like a forest gathering. At that time, Dharma Master Bianhe was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at that monastery.

When his disciples heard that their master was expounding the Dharma, they gradually drifted away. Unable to contain his indignation, Bianhe raised a slander against the community and sent it to Zhi Zhongkan.

Zhongkan was deluded by these claims and imposed illegal debts upon the Master. The Master accepted them with serene composure and submitted to his fate; those who recognized him [praised him for this].
The "Real" is called "repaying a debt. ○ When the offering-master Haoyue asked Changsha Cen, [the Master said]:
"When one has realized it, karmic obstacles are originally empty; when one has not yet realized it, one must repay past debts.
Why did the Venerable Siṃha and the Great Master the Second Patriarch, however, repay their debts? Cen said: "Virtuous One, you do not recognize original emptiness. What is this 'original'?"
Changsha said, "Coming is emptiness. The attendant asked, "What is meant by 'karmic obstacles are [emptiness]'? Changsha replied, "'Karmic obstacles are' means that they are originally empty.
The attendant was speechless. Changsha then presented this verse: "Provisionally existent, yet fundamentally not existent; Provisionally extinguished, yet also not non-existent.
The meaning of Nirvana as the settling of debts— In its single nature, there is no further distinction."
Luopu Throws Himself Before the Master (Chuan Deng Lu 16): At the site where the phoenix nestled among the cliffs at Jialing. The *Huiyuan* (Compendium of the Source), fascicle six, states:

After the Master had finished his travels, he went directly to Jiaoshan and established a hermitage there. For a year he did not visit Jiaoshan. Jiaoshan then composed a letter and dispatched a monk to deliver it.
Upon receiving it, the Master simply sat down and placed it aside; when the messenger extended his hand again to request it, the Master [remained seated].
The monk had no reply. The Master struck him and said, "Go back and report this to your Upādhyāya.
When the monk returned and reported it, Shanshan said, "If this monk opens the letter, he will surely come within three days. If he does not open the letter, this man cannot be saved.
The Master indeed arrived three days later; seeing Jia Shan, he did not prostrate, but instead stood with his hands joined before him.

The Master stood up. Yaoshan said, "A rooster nesting in a phoenix’s nest is not of the same kind. Begone! The Master hurried from afar to seek an audience with the teacher, saying, "I request the Master to grant me an interview.
Yaoshan said, "Before my eyes there is no *śrāmaṇera*; here there is no old monk. The Master then gave a shout. Yaoshan said, "..."
Stop, stop! Do not be so hasty or impatient. The clouds and moon are the same; the streams and mountains differ.
(From *Chuan Deng Lu*, Case 14: The Novice Seeking Precepts). When the novice Gao first visited Yaoshan, the Master asked, "Where have you come from?"
[The monk] said, "I have come from Mount Nanyue. Dongshan asked, "Where did you go on that mountain? He replied, "I went to Jiangling to receive the precepts.

Dongshan asked, "What is the purpose of receiving the precepts? He replied, "To escape birth and death. Dongshan said, "There is a person who does not receive the precepts and yet also escapes birth and death;
do you know of such a one? He replied, "If that is so, then what use are the Buddha's precepts? Dongshan said, "They still hang from your lips and teeth."
While there, he summoned the *vinaya-dhara* and said, "This lame śrāmaṇera is unfit for monastic affairs; arrange it so that he is sent to the rear hermitage.
Then the Mountain Master said to Daowu and Yunyan, "That śrāmaṇera who just came actually has a significant background."
Daowu said, "One must still be examined before it is acceptable. Deshan then asked again, "It is said that Chang’an is very busy.
Daowu replied, "In my country, all is peaceful. Deshan said, "Are you merely reading sutras and seeking instruction?
Daowu said, "Not at all like that. Deshan said, "There are many who cannot manage even this. Daowu said, "I do not say they lack [the capacity]; it is simply..."
He was unwilling to accept [the responsibility].
At Mount Jiangshan, there was Chan Master Zanyuan (a dharma heir of Ciming Huiyuan; *Chuanteng lu*, fascicle 23).

When Imperial Prince Shu first mourned for his late grandmother, he went to the mountains to recite the sutras and associated with Chan Master Zanyuan of Mount Jiangshan like brothers. He questioned him regarding the essential meaning of the Patriarchs.
The Master did not answer. The King pressed him further. The Master said, "Your Majesty has three obstacles to Prajñā and one quality that approaches the Way.

After one or two more lifetimes, you will likely attain full maturity. The King said, "I wish to hear the explanation of this. The Master replied, "Your Majesty’s temperament is robust and grand, yet your worldly conditions are deep.
Because of this robust and grand temperament meeting such deep worldly conditions, you must inevitably take responsibility for the welfare of others through your person."
The world is grave and weighty. To harbor the ambition for economic and political governance while being unable to determine whether one will be employed or set aside leaves the mind unsettled.
To maintain the will to govern the world with such an unsettled mind—how could one ever achieve "a single thought spanning ten thousand years"?
First, there is excessive anger; second, a preoccupation with intellectual learning over principle, which constitutes a delusion regarding the Way; third, these are the three [obstacles].
He regards fame and profit as if shedding his hair; he carries his burdens with the lightness of a dhūta practitioner. This is to draw near to the Way.
Furthermore, it is appropriate that you cause the teachings of the Śāstras to flourish. The King bowed twice and received the instruction.
Huazang’s Fourth Case: The Radish of Zhenzhou (from *Huiyuan*, Case 4). A monk asked Zhaozhou, "I have heard that you, Master, personally met Nanquan—is this true?
Zhaozhou replied, "In Zhenzhou, they grow large radishes."

Puhua Eating Raw Vegetables (Chuan Deng X). One day, while Puhua was eating raw vegetables in front of the Sangha Hall, Linji saw him and said, "You look very much like a donkey. Puhua immediately brayed like a donkey. Linji said, "This thief!
Puhua replied, "Thief! Thief! and then went out.
Yongjia Yisuo (Huìyuán II): Chan Master Xuánjué of Wenzhou went to Caoxi.
Upon his arrival, he shook his staff, carried his water jar, and circumambulated the Patriarch three times, then stood firm and upright.

The Patriarch said, "A śramaṇa possesses three thousand dignified demeanors and eighty thousand subtle practices. From what direction have you come, Venerable Sir, that you display such great arrogance? The Master—
[The monk] said, "The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. The Patriarch said, "Why do you not realize non-arising?
Why do you not understand that there is no swiftness? [The monk] said, "Realizing it is non-arising; understanding it is fundamentally without swiftness. The Patriarch said, "So it is, so it is.

At that time, the great assembly was struck with astonishment. The Master then assumed his full dignified demeanor to pay his respects. After a short while, he took his leave. The Patriarch said, "Returning too..."
"Quick! The Master said, "Since it is fundamentally non-moving, how can there be speed? The Patriarch said, "You have thoroughly grasped the meaning of non-arising.
The Master said, "If there is no arising, how can there be meaning? The Patriarch said, "If there is no meaning, who would make distinctions?
The Master said, "Even making distinctions is not meaning. The Patriarch sighed and said, "Excellent, excellent! Stay for one night. At that time, this was called...
This was his first awakening. The following day, he returned to Yongjia.
Yun’gai [was there] for half a year (Shishuang’s Dharma heirs; *Huiyuan*, vol. 6).
Chan Master Yuanjing Zhiyuan of Mount Yungai in Tanzhou, while traveling, asked Yunju: "When Zhiyuan is at a loss, what then? Yunju said: "Only..."
The Master said, "It is because the power of my *ācārya* has not reached him; thus, the teacher does not prostrate. He went straight to Shishuang and asked as before.
Shishuang said, "It is not only you, *ācārya*, that I cannot do anything about; even I, this old monk, am helpless. The Master asked, "Why, Preceptor, are you helpless?
Shishuang replied, "If I were able to do something about it, I would have already set you aside from your helplessness. The Master then prostrated.
He paid his respects. A monk asked Shishuang, "I do not ask about the time when all ten thousand doors are closed; what is it like when all ten thousand doors are open?
Shishuang said, "What is the matter within the hall? The monk had no reply. After six months, he finally uttered a single phrase: "No one can receive him; the Master has gone.
He then prostrated himself, requesting that the Master provide an explanation for him. Shishuang was unwilling. The Master [recounted this].
He then took Master Fangchang by the arm and said, "If you, Preceptor, do not speak, I shall strike you! Fangchang replied, "I am willing.
The Master prostrated repeatedly, and Fangchang said, "No one recognizes him. At these words, the Master attained sudden enlightenment.
Wang Yue’s Four Mysteries:
The Samādhi of Miu and Yang (from *Rendayanmu*). Regarding Master Gudai of Langzhou: When Yangshan arrived to pay his respects, Gudai said, "Go."
"You have no Buddha-nature. Mount folded his hands, stepped forward three paces, and responded.
Daitō laughed and said, "From where did you obtain this samādhi? Mount replied, "I received my name from Tanyuan; I obtained the ground from Weishan.
Daitō asked, "Are you not then a son of Weishan? Mount said, "In terms of worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is not that I am not; however, as for the Buddha-dharma..."
He did not dare. Mount [Shishuang] then asked, "Where did you, Master, obtain this samādhi?
Di replied, "I obtained this samādhi from Zhangjing. Mount sighed, "Inconceivable! Those who come here find it difficult to match you. Yihai:
Once while Yangshan was seated, a monk came and paid his respects. Yangshan did not look at him. The monk...
He then asked the Master, "Do you know how to write characters? The Master replied, "I do so to the best of my ability. The monk circled him once clockwise and asked, "What character is this?
The Master wrote the character "十" (ten) on the ground in response. The monk circled him once counter-clockwise and asked, "What character is this?
The Master changed the "十" into the character "○" (circle). The monk then drew the *svastika* symbol (卍) and pressed his two palms against it.
As the asura grasps the sun and moon with his palms, he asks, "What character is this? Shanshan then draws the *svastika* (*wan*) facing him.
The monk then assumes the posture of Louzhide. Shanshan says, "So it is, so it is. This is that which all buddhas protect and keep in mind.
You are thus, and I am thus. Guard and maintain it well for yourself. The monk bows in gratitude.
He ascended into the air and departed. At that time, a certain practitioner saw this. Five days later, he asked Master Shanshan, "Did you see him?
Shanshan replied, "Did you see him? The practitioner said, "I saw him leave the gate and ascend into the air.
Shanshan said, "This was an Arhat from Western India who came specifically to test my Way. The practitioner said, "Although I witnessed this samādhi..."
He did not discern its principle. The Mountain Master said, "I shall explain it for you according to its meaning. This refers to the eight kinds of samādhi;

it is the ocean of awakening that transforms into the ocean of meaning. Their essence is identical. This meaning necessarily involves cause and effect, whether simultaneous or sequential, general or particular, yet they are never separate from the *guptikāya-samādhi* (the samādhi of concealing the body)."
Tongfeng Husheng (a Dharma heir of Linji; *Chuan deng lu*). A monk approached the master of Tongfeng and asked, "What should one do when suddenly encountering a tiger here?

**Qinghuo Returns to the Mountains (Successor of Zen Master Shuilong Pu of Quanzhou; recorded in the *Denglu* as number twenty-three)** Zen Master Qinghuo of Baofu Monastery in Zhangzhou, shortly before his passing, relinquished the assembly and intended to enter the mountains to await his death. Upon crossing the Stone Bridge at Zhuxi, he left behind this verse:
"Let the people of the world cease speaking of the difficulty of the road; The bird-path and the sheep’s-gut trail are but a few inches apart. Take care, O Zhuxi!"
"By the stream, by the waterside; you return to the vast ocean, I return to the mountains. He then went to Guihu to establish a hermitage.
After a short time, he said to his disciples, "After my passing, you shall offer my remains to the insects and ants; do not erect a tomb or stupa.
Having spoken, he entered Mount Hutou and sat upon a flat rock, remaining in solemn stillness until his final departure. His disciple Jieyin subsequently entered the mountain.
Upon investigation, it was found that he had fulfilled his final instructions by remaining for seven days, during which time he was not infested by even a single insect or ant.
He was subsequently cremated, and his remains were scattered across the forests and fields. Today, his memorial hall exists at the Jingtusiyuan (Pure Land Cloister) of Kaiyuan Temple in Quanzhou.

it saves the need for firewood and avoids the excavation of earth. To cast off one's hands and go forth immediately is truly a matter of joy."

Yinfeng’s Inverted Transformation (Dharma Successor of Mazu; *Fodenglu*, Fascicle 8). Before Master Deng Yinfeng was about to manifest his passing, he first asked the assembly: "All of you..."

"Is there anyone who has passed away while standing on their head? the assembly asked. "None yet," they replied.

The Master then stood on his head and passed away, remaining perfectly upright with his robes falling naturally over his body. At that time, the assembly discussed carrying him to the cremation pyre, but he remained motionless and firm.
As he moved, those far and near gazed upon him with unceasing wonder and admiration. The Master had a younger sister who was a nun; she was also there at that time.

Luo Pu Returns to His Hometown (Dharma Heir of Jia Shan; *Huiyuan*, Volume 6). A monk asked Luo Pu, "When a student intends to return to his hometown, what then?

"Resolute in my will, I depart for my native land, Boarding a boat to cross the Five Lakes. Raising the oar, the stars and moon vanish; Pausing the rowing pole, the sun stands solitary.

This refers to Chan Master Fānguì of Xěwū (Case 19 of the *Xuányuán*). When he first resided at Yángqí, his dwelling was an old house with dilapidated rafters that barely shielded against wind and rain.

They submitted their sincerity, wishing to provide the materials for the construction. The Master declined them, saying: "The Buddha has said that this is an age of decline.
High peaks and deep valleys are subject to constant change; how can one expect everything to be perfect and as one wishes? Seek what is sufficient for yourself.

The King did not understand the reason for this. Later, when the King was traveling in a carriage with the Venerable One, he saw the Maṇibhadra youth prostrating before them.
The Venerable One asked, "Do you remember past events? He replied, "I recall events from distant kalpas."
He lived together with his teacher, who was expounding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*; I, meanwhile, was turning the profound *sūtras*.
Today’s events surely accord with our past causes. The Venerable One further said to the King:
"This youth is none other than the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta. After this Sage, two persons shall appear; one will transform the southern region of India."
He was destined for China; within four or five years, he would return to this land. Thus, based on his past causes, he was named Prajñātāra.
Once, while Prajñātāra was attending a vegetarian feast for the Patriarch at the invitation of the King of East India, the King asked:
"Everyone here is reciting sutras; why alone do you not recite? The Patriarch replied: "I am poor..."
The outgoing breath does not fall into the various conditions; the incoming breath does not dwell within the aggregates or realms.
One should constantly recite this scripture in this manner for hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions, and trillions of scrolls—not merely one or two scrolls.
Kuti’s Chanting of Mantras (The Dharma Successor of Tianlong; Section Eight of Huìyuán). Kuti merely recited the Three-Line Mantra, and thus he attained renown as one who surpassed all others.
Shenhui’s Exegesis (Huìyuán II): Chan Master Shenhui of Heze in the Western Capital was a śrāmaṇera at the age of fourteen when he visited the Sixth Patriarch.
The Patriarch said, "My good friend, you have come from afar with great hardship. Do you bring your original nature?
If you possess this original nature, you ought to recognize its master; try to explain it to me. The Master replied, "Taking non-abiding as the foundation, seeing is itself the master."
The Patriarch said, "Stop, you śrāmaṇera! How can you speak so casually? He then struck him with his staff. Under the staff, the Master reflected:
"A Great Good Knowledge (Mahā-kalyāṇamitra) is difficult to encounter throughout kalpas. Now that I have met one, how could I spare my own life? From then on, he served him.
On another day, the Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying: "I have an object that has no head and no tail; it has no name."
"No name. No back and no front. Do you all recognize it? The Master then came forward and said, "This is the original source of all Buddhas;
it is the Buddha-nature of Shenhui. The Patriarch said, "I told you it has no name and no character, yet you immediately call it the 'original source' and 'Buddha-nature'.
The Master bowed and withdrew. The Patriarch said, "In the future, this son shall possess a thatched hut..."

"Covering one's head" (i.e., concealing one's true nature) merely results in becoming a follower of the school of intellectual understanding. (Fayan said: "The ancients' bestowal of predictions was never mistaken.
To establish intellectual understanding as the core tenet today is precisely the approach of Heze.
This is the "True Roar of Shitou. (From *Línjiàn lù*, Vol. 1). Supplement: When the Great Master of Caoxi was about to enter extinction, he finally dared to fully... [text fragment].
As for this proclaimer of the command: when it reached Mazu of Jiangxi, Nanyue, and Shitou, they caused its brilliance to shake and its radiance to flourish.
Therefore, Shitou was titled "True Roar" and Mazu was titled "Complete Proclamation."
Weiyang did not act [for the sake of worldly things] (Huayuan 5). When Yaoshan went to visit Shitou, he secretly grasped the profound essence of the teachings.
One day, while Yaoshan was sitting, Shitou observed him and asked, "What are you doing here? He replied, "I do nothing at all."
Shitou said, "If it is so, then you are sitting idly. [The monk] said, "If one is sitting idly, then one is acting.
Shitou said, "You say that you do not act; yet what is it that you do not act? [The monk] said, "Even the thousand sages do not recognize it. He praised him with a verse:
"From the beginning we have lived together, yet its name is unknown; Spontaneously we go along, just as we are. Since antiquity, the supreme sages..."
[The monk] still did not understand. How could ordinary people in their haste and confusion possibly comprehend this?
Zhenkan said, "It remains as it was" (*Linjian Lu*, Vol. 1). Zhaozhou said, "Do not exert such effort. These are truly excellent words. Why do you not simply remain as you were before?
Even worldly dharmas have their gateways; how could the Dharma lack a gateway? It is precisely because you no longer remain as you were before that [you have failed]."
Old Rang Opens His Chest (Recorded in the *Lao Shan Daoxian Chuan Deng*, Case 23). Zen Master Rang of Nanlan in Jiangxi.
The Elder Liang of Hutang asked, "I have heard that you, Elder Brother, have painted a portrait of our late teacher; I request permission to pay my respects.
The Master reached out both hands, pushed open his chest, and showed it to him. Liang immediately prostrated. The Master said, "Do not prostrate! Do not prostrate! Liang said, "Master..."
"The elder brother was mistaken; I did not pay obeisance to you, Elder Brother. The Master said, "You paid obeisance to the true likeness of the former master.
Liang asked, "Why did you tell me not to pay obeisance? The Master said, "How could there ever have been a mistake?"
*Daofu Suoshou* (Xuefeng’s Dharma Heir; *Huiyuan*, Vol. 7) Jingqing had a monk lead a young boy to him and say, "This child has always loved to question monks about the Buddha-dharma.
We request that you, Master, examine him. The Master then ordered tea to be prepared. When the boy brought the tea, the Master drank it.
After he finished, he passed the cup and saucer to the boy; as the boy reached out to take them, the Master withdrew his hand.
Withdrawing his hand, he said, "Tell me, can you say anything? The youth said, "Ask on. The monk asked the Master, "What is this boy’s understanding like?
The Master replied, "He is merely a monk who has observed the precepts for one or two lifetimes."
Fenggan’s Loquacity (Chuan Deng Lu 27). Lü Qiu Che invited Fenggan to serve as abbot, but Fenggan did not comply.
Lü Qiu said, "If that is so, whom should I pay homage to as my teacher there? Fenggan replied, "There are those known as Han and Shi;
they are emanations of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra. You should pay homage to them. Lü Qiu went to Xingxing Temple on Mount Tiantai and paid homage to Han and Shi.
Hanshan and Shide said, "For what reason do you bow to us? Qiu replied, "Master Fenggan said that Hanshan and Shide are emanations of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.
You should bow to them; therefore, I have come to bow. Hanshan and Shide laughed and said, "Fenggan talks too much!
Fenggan talks too much! Why do you not bow to Fenggan? Do you not know that he is Amitābha Tathāgata?"
Qiehe Duokou (Shao Shan Pufa Si; Huizong, Sixth Generation). Supplement: One day a monk visited Shao Shan.
Shan asked, "Are you not that talkative old fellow? The monk replied, "I dare not say so. The Master said, "How many mouths do you have?"
[The monk] said, "The whole body is it. The Master asked, "Where do you usually defecate? [The monk] said, "I defecate within the words of Shao Shan.
The Master said, "If there are the words of Shao Shan, that is fine; but if there are no words of Shao Shan, where do you defecate?
Because [the monk] was speechless, the Master struck him.
**Yun’gak’s Leftover Soup (Linji’s Dharma Heir; *Chuanteng lu* 12)** A monk came from the Western Capital to visit Master Yunshan.
The Master asked, "Have you brought a letter from the host of the Western Capital? The monk replied, "I dare not arbitrarily transmit any news.
The Master said, "A masterful monk indeed; you naturally possess [the Way]. The monk said, "Who would eat leftover soup and stale rice? The Master said, "Only I."
There was a preceptor who did not wish to eat. The monk then made a gesture of vomiting. The Master called to his attendant, saying, "Escort this sick monk out. The monk then departed.
Letang Suanjiao (Dharma heir of Zhenjing Wen; *Huiyuan* 17). Chan Master Zhantang Wenzhun of Letang in Longxing Prefecture.
A monk asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "Heaven! Heaven! The monk said, "I have come specifically to ask this question.
The Master said, "Blowing a flute at the crossroads; drinking two or three rounds of sour, cold village wine."
Guyuan Banbi (a dharma successor of Fenyang), the Abbot of Nan’ue Bajiao Hermitage, was popularly known as "Quán Dàdào" (Great Way of Quán).
This was because among his songs and verses, "Dàdào" (Great Way) frequently appeared as a title; for instance, the verse on the Six Banbis begins: "The Great Way Banbi."
Questioning while dozing; carrying a gourd on one's back; singing and playing at will—this is the nostril of the "scattered sages.

Performing as the occasion demands; surging east and sinking west; in the southern provinces and northern villages—this is the nostril of the Chan masters. Whether gain or loss; the emerald peaks are steep and lofty;
the dragon strides and the tiger gazes—this is the nostril of the patch-robed monks. A sitting cloth of one foot two inches; do not seek its length or shortness. The wind...
High clouds arise; the Master’s core essence flows like a rushing river without obstruction. A golden lotus springs from the earth; he holds a *cintāmaṇi* in his hand.
The mountain boy’s core essence: gold is tested by fire. A guest asks of dwelling in the mountains: "It is no easy matter to have traveled so far."
Zhenxie Linzou (successor of Danxia Zichun). Huike Severs His Arm (Huìyuán 1).
When the First Patriarch was seated upright and no instruction or exhortation was heard from him, the monk Shen Guang stood in the courtyard.
At dawn, the accumulated snow reached his waist. The Patriarch took pity on him and asked: "You have been here for a long time..."

Standing in the snow, what do you seek? The Master wept with compassion and said, "I only pray that through your compassion, I may hear the gate of the nectar of immortality and extensively deliver all sentient beings.
The Patriarch said, "The unsurpassed, wondrous Way of the Buddhas is difficult to practice even with diligent effort over vast eons;
how could one hope for the True Vehicle with a mind of minor virtue and minor wisdom, or with a frivolous and arrogant mind? Having heard this, the Master took [the staff].
Using a sharp blade, he cut off his own left arm and placed it before the Patriarch. The Master then said, "May I hear the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas?
The Patriarch replied, "The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from another. He asked, "My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the Master to pacify my mind.
The Patriarch said, "Bring forth your mind, and I will pacify it for you. He replied, "I have searched for my mind, but it cannot be found. The Patriarch said:
"I have finished settling your mind for you. He further recorded this, saying: "You need only externally cease all conditions and internally allow the mind to be without agitation;
when the mind is like a wall or a screen, you can enter the Way."
Shenguān Ān Tóuhé wrote a supplement, saying: Zhēnjìng composed a verse to present to the Elder Xiāngchéng Chún, which says:
The western mountain’s colors roll up the curtain; The Chan mind shares in the moon’s radiance. Deep within the temple of Xiāngchéng, Is the dwelling of the noble family of Lìngguān.
The summit altar still remains; the overflowing milk has long since vanished. Now, those who follow the pure path recite the White Lotus Sutra.
Wang Lao Shu-niu (a dharma heir of Mazu, *Chuan Deng Lu* 8). Nanyuan was once asked by a monk: "After the Master passes away for a hundred years, where will you go?"
"Where have you gone? The Master said, "I have gone to become a water buffalo. The monk asked, "May I follow the Master there?
He replied, "If you come, bring back a blade of grass in your mouth."
Master Hongsi of Zhongyi on Langzhou (Dharma heir of Mazu; *Chuan deng lu* 6): Once, when Yangshan was a newly ordained monk, he went to pay his respects to the Preceptor for Ordination.
Seeing him approach, the Master clapped his hands upon the meditation seat and said, "Ha ha!"
Yangshan stood at the eastern side, then at the western side, and then in the center. After he had finished receiving the precepts, he withdrew and stood back.
The Master asked, "Where did you obtain this samādhi? Yangshan replied, "I learned it from the seal left behind at Caoxi.
The Master asked, "Tell me, at Caoxi, what kind of person did they employ this samādhi to receive? Yangshan replied:
Upon meeting [Baizhang], he asked, "Where did you, Master, obtain this samādhi? The Master replied, "I learned it from Mazu.
He then asked, "How does one realize one's nature? The Master said, "It is like a house with six windows. Inside there is a monkey;
when someone calls 'Shanshan' from the east, 'Shanshan' responds. It is the same for all six windows."
Yanshou replied, "Yes. He bowed in thanks and rose, saying, "Having received the Master’s parable, there is nothing I do not understand.
Yet there is one further matter: when the inner monkey is exhausted and asleep, and the outer monkey wishes to meet him, what then?
The Master descended from his meditation seat, took Yanshou by the hand, and danced with him, saying, "Mountain upon mountain, I have already met you. It is like this..."
A tiny mote-insect builds its nest upon the eyelashes of a mosquito and cries out at the crossroads:
"The world is vast, people are rare; those who meet one another are few."
Zhuyou Dingjue (Dharma Heir of Nanquan): The Venerable Master of Mount Zhuyou in Ezhou. Initially, he resided at Huguo Monastery in Suizhou as its first patriarch.
When the Venerable Jinlun Ke guan asked, "What is the Way? the Master replied, "Do not drive a stake into empty space.
Ke guan said, "Empty space itself is the stake. The Master then struck him; Ke guan seized him.
[The monk] said, "Do not strike me; later on, you might strike the wrong person. The Master then desisted.
(Xuange Gengqiu, Huìyuán 7). Xuansha said to Xuefeng, "I am now going to employ the Great Function."
"Master, how about you? The Master threw three wooden balls out at once. Zhaozha made a gesture as if brandishing a shield.
The Master said, "Only because your parents are present at Vulture Peak can you act like this. Zhaozha replied, "This too is my own business."
One day he ascended the seat. Once the assembly had gathered, the Master rolled out a wooden ball. Xuansha then seized it and placed it back in its original position.
Whenever a monk came to seek instruction, the Master would roll it out to show him.

Tanzhu replied, "I am returning this kindness to you. Huang said, "This was brought by you; what fault is there in returning it to you?
Thereupon, Tanzhu attained realization and subsequently left home to become a monk.
(From the *Cuiwei Wuxue Sifu Zhuan Denglu*: "Touzi bought oil... Having realized the fundamental tenets of Cuiwei, Touzi built a thatched hut and [resided there].
While he was living there, one day Zhaozhou arrived at Tongcheng County. Meeting him on the road, Zhaozhou went toward him and asked, "Are you not the Master of Touzi Mountain?
The Master replied, "I beg for a single coin for tea and salt. Zhaozhou was speechless. He then went ahead to sit in the hermitage.
When the Master returned carrying an oil jar, Zhaozhou said, "I have long heard of Touzi; now that I have come, I see only a..."
The Oil Seller. The Master said, "You have seen only the oil seller; you do not yet know Touzi.
What is Touzi? The Master said, "Oil, oil."
Yanyang Fei Fei Fei Raising Tigers (Dharma Heir of Zhaozhou; *Chuan Deng Lu*, Case 11).
When Venerable Yanyang first visited Zhaozhou, he asked, "What is it like when one brings nothing forth? Zhaozhou said, "Put it down.
The Master said, "Since I bring nothing forth, what is there to put down? Zhaozhou replied, "Then carry it away. At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment. Later...
While staying in the mountains, a snake and a tiger would come to his hand to eat from it.
(Chuan Deng Lu 6) Chan Master Huizang of Shigong in Fuzhou was once performing chores in the kitchen when Mazu asked him, "What are you doing?
He replied, "I am tending the ox. Mazu asked, "How do you tend it? He said, "One..."
[The ox] went back into the grass. [Xuansha] suddenly pulled it back by the nose. The Master said, "You truly know how to herd an ox.
Xuansha came out of his bath. (A successor of Longtan; *Chuan deng lu*, fascicle 6). Attendant Shoukuo asked Deshan, "Where have all the sages of the past gone?
Deshan said, "What? What? Kuokuo said, "An imperial decree summons the flying dragon horse."
A lame turtle pokes its head out. Shanshan then stops. The next day, after bathing, Guokuo comes to serve tea to Shanshan.
Shanshan pats him on the back once and says, "What about yesterday’s public case?
Guokuo replies, "This old fellow has only just begun to see clearly today. Shanshan then stops again.
Shi Ding Ascends the Tower (Dharma Heir of Xuefeng; *Chuan deng lu*, Case 19). Shi Ding of Yue Mountain in Zhuji County, Yuezhou, was styled Chan Master Jianzhen.

Initially, he studied under Xuefeng and gained a preliminary understanding. Later, while invited by the Prince of Min to a vegetarian feast at Qingfeng Lou, he sat for a long time and, looking up, suddenly beheld the sunlight.
In that instant, he attained sudden enlightenment and composed a verse, which begins: "The Clear Wind..."
On the day he went to the official vegetarian feast at Lou-shang, his lifelong vision was suddenly opened;
only then did he recognize that the events of the distant Putong era had not been brought from the road of the Pamir Mountains. He presented this to Xuefeng, who approved it.
Yun’an Duoxi (Dharma Heir of Huanglong Nan; *Sengbao Zhuan*, Vol. Lower). Chan Master Yun’an Zhenjing Kewen was twenty-five years old when he tested his mastery of his studies.
He shaved his head and received full ordination (*upasampadā*); in his study of the sutras and śāstras, there was nothing in which he did not reach the pinnacle of excellence.
He repeatedly seized the lecture seats of the capitals of Jing and Luo, acting as both host and guest to expound upon profound meanings on numerous occasions.
Jingzhao followed the boat [to Mount Fushan]. (Fushan Yuan’s Dharma heir; the twenty-sixth in the *Sengbao zhuan*).

Chan Master Jingzhao, whose name was Daozhen and courtesy name was Boxiang, once while traveling along the river, looked at his boat and thought silently to himself: "I shall follow wherever I may dwell; let my karmic conditions be trusted."
He asked the boatman, "May I ride on the stern of your boat? The boatman laughed and said, "Where does the Master wish to go?
My vessel is bound for Bianzhou. The Master replied, "I am traveling to the capital to tour it; therefore, please take me north."
National Teacher [Huizhong] called out three times (Sixth Patriarch’s Dharma Heir; *Huiyuan* II). One day, National Teacher Huizhong of Nanyang called out three times.
The attendant responded three times. The Master said, "I thought I was failing you, but it was actually you who were failing me."
Zhaozhou’s Single Pinch (Huìyuán 4). A nun asked Zhaozhou, “What is the meaning of the profound mystery?
Zhaozhou pinched her with his hand. The nun said, “The Master still has this. Zhaozhou replied, “In fact, it is you who have this.”
Daishū Kabi (Chuan Deng 11): Chan Master Dazui Fazhen of Yizhou had a tortoise beside his hermitage.
A monk asked, "All sentient beings have skin wrapping their bones; why does this sentient being have bones wrapping its skin?"
The Master took up his sandals and placed them over the back of the tortoise;
the monk was speechless. "Wild ducks" (Huìyuán 3). See the section on "Bǎizhàng Rolling Up the Mat" in the first volume. ○ Hébù added:
While Bǎizhàng was walking with Mázǔ, they saw a flock of wild ducks fly by. Mázǔ asked, "What is that? Bǎizhàng—
Baizhang said, "A wild duck. The Patriarch asked, "Where has it gone? Baizhang replied, "It flew away.
The Patriarch then grabbed him by the nose and twisted it. Baizhang cried out in pain. The Patriarch said, "So you say it flew away? At these words, the Master attained realization.
Cao Jiao’s Robe of the Spirit (Dongshan Jue’s Dharma Heir; *Huiyuan* 13). A monk asked Caoshan, “What is it like when the robe of the spirit is not worn?
The Master said, “Caoshan’s filiality is complete. The monk asked, “After the filiality is complete, what then? The Master said, “Caoshan loves to get drunk on wild wine.”
Shushan’s Memorial Tower (Huìyuán, Case 13). Once, when a monk had finished constructing a memorial tower for his master, he informed the master.
The master asked, "How much money will you give to the craftsmen? The monk replied, "Everything is up to you, Master.
The master said, "Will you give three coins to the craftsmen? Or two coins? Or one coin?"

Huineng, Master of the Dharma (*Sengbaozhuan*, Vol. Lower): Huanglong Nan said, "The essential requirement for a monastic administrator is to win over the assembly;

winning over the assembly depends on understanding human sentiments. Our former teacher said, 'Human sentiment is the field of merit for the world,' for it is through sentiment that the Way of principle arises.
Therefore, whether the times are in decline or prosperity, and whether affairs involve loss or gain, must depend upon human sentiment. Sentiment is sometimes open and sometimes obstructed."
Thus, prosperity (Tai) and adversity (Pi) arise. When affairs are sometimes abundant and sometimes meager, diminution (Sun) and augmentation (Yi) follow.
Only the Sage can penetrate the conditions of the world. Therefore, in the hexagrams of the *I Ching*, when Qian is below and Kun is above, it is called Tai;

when Qian is above and Kun is below, it is called Pi. Regarding the symbolism, when the upper is diminished and the lower is augmented, it is called Yi; when the lower is diminished and the upper is augmented, it is called [Sun].
[This results in] Loss. Now, Qian represents Heaven and Kun represents Earth. For Heaven to be below and Earth above is a reversal of their proper positions;
yet it is called Tai (Threatening Peace), because the upper and lower interact. For the host to be above and the guest below is consistent with the proper principle;
yet it is called Pi (Obstruction), because the upper and lower do not interact. Therefore, Heaven and Earth...
If one does not interact with the myriad things, they will not flourish. When human relations do not interact, all affairs fall into discord.
The principles of diminution and augmentation are likewise derived from this. Now, those who stand above others can restrain themselves to enrich those below;

the subordinates will surely rejoice and serve their superiors. Is this not what is called "augmentation"? Conversely, when those above look down upon their subordinates and act with self-indulgence, the subordinates will surely—
To harbor resentment and rebel against one’s superior—is this not what is meant by "diminution"? Therefore, when those above and below communicate with one another, there is prosperity (*tai*);

when they do not communicate, there is stagnation (*pi*). Those who diminish themselves are benefited by others; those who seek to benefit themselves alone are diminished by others. Is the attainment or loss of such emotional states not a matter of no small consequence?
The former sages once used the metaphor of man as a boat and emotion as water: water can carry a boat, yet it can also overturn it.
A boat floats when it follows the current; it sinks when it goes against it. Thus, a monastic administrator prospers when they win the hearts of the people and falls into ruin when they lose them.

If they win them entirely, they prosper entirely; if they lose them entirely, they fall entirely into ruin. Therefore, shared goodness brings abundant blessings, while shared evil brings severe calamity.
Goodness and evil follow one another as consistently as beads on a string; their rise and fall correspond to conduct as clearly as if one were looking at them.

Four Instances of Deceiving People (Chuan Deng Lu, Case 19). Chan Master Baofu Congzhan of Zhangzhou deceived people in four ways.
First, he asked a monk, "What Buddha is in the hall? The monk said, "Wait for the Master to decide. The Master replied, "Śākyamuni Buddha."
The monk said, "Do not deceive people. The Master said, "In fact, it is you who are deceiving me. He asked a second monk, "What karma have you committed to eat such a large portion?
The monk said, "Venerable Sir, you yourself are no small eater. The Master made a crouching gesture. The monk said, "Venerable Sir, do not deceive people.
The Master said, "In fact, it is you who are deceiving me. He asked a third monk, "What is your name?"
"Ma? The monk said, "Xianze. The Master said, "If you suddenly encounter a dried-up [well], what then? The monk said, "Who is the one who is dried up?
The Master said, "I am. The monk said, "Master, do not deceive people. The Master said, "In fact, it is you who are deceiving me. Fourth question:
He asked the bath attendant, "How wide is the cauldron for the hot water? The attendant said, "Please, Master, measure it yourself. The Master then made a gesture.
[The monk] measured the situation. The Master said, "Preceptor, do not deceive people. The Master said, "In fact, it is you who are deceiving me.
(Three times he said *mala*, according to the *Chuan Deng Lu*). Chan Master Shoucheng Jingguo of Huguo Monastery in Suizhou.
A monk asked, "When a crane stands upon a withered pine tree, what then? The Master said, "A scene of utter *mala* for those beneath the ground. He was asked about the King’s assembly.
"Where have the Dharma-protecting benevolent deities gone during the time of the purge? The Master said, "The two before the main gate are both quite embarrassed.
Question: "What is it like when a drop of water freezes? The Master said, "After the sun has risen, there is a scene of great embarrassment."
**Shaoyang’s Nine Nines (Case 3 from Yunmen’s Records)** A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the uppermost aperture?
Yunmen said, "Nine times nine is eighty-one. Another monk asked, "What is the very first phrase? Yunmen said, "Nine times nine is eighty-one.
Yet another monk asked, "The character for 'one' is not it; the character for 'eight' does not form it. I wonder what it is?"
Regarding the character "Mo" (ma): the Gatekeeper says, "Nine times nine is eighty-one.
As for Manjusri, he was the Chan Master Wuzhuo Wenxi of Hangzhou. Initially, he visited Chan Master Xingkong of Mount Daci.
Xingkong said, "Why do you not travel extensively to seek instruction? The Master went directly to Huayan Temple on Mount Wutai.
Upon arriving at the Vajra Cave, he paid his respects. There he encountered an old man leading an ox who invited the Master into the temple.
The old man called out, "Juntai! and a youth emerged from within to receive them. The old man released the ox and led the Master up into the hall; the entire structure was radiant with a golden hue.
The old man sat upon a couch, pointed to an embroidered cushion, and commanded him to sit. The old man asked, "From where have you come recently? The Master—
[The Master] asked about the south. The old man said, "How is the Buddha-dharma maintained in the south?

The Master replied, "In the age of the Dharma's decline, bhikṣus there rarely uphold the precepts. The old man asked, "How many followers are there? The Master said, "Either three hundred or five hundred.
The Master then asked, "How is the Buddha-dharma maintained here? The old man replied, "Dragons and snakes are mixed together; ordinary people and sages dwell side by side."
The Master asked, "How many people are in the assembly? The Old Man replied, "Three times three before, three times three after.
The Old Man called to his attendant boy to serve tea and offer *sukara* (butter and curd). The Master partook of the flavors, and his mind was suddenly enlightened.
The Old Man picked up a glass cup and asked, "Is there such a thing as this in the South? The Master said, "No. The Old Man asked, "What do you usually use to drink with?"
Cha. The Master had no reply. Seeing that the sun was already low, the Master asked the old man, "May I stay for one night?
The old man said, "You still have a mind of attachment; you may not stay. The Master said, "I have no mind of attachment.
The old man said, "Have you ever received the precepts? The Master said, "I have received them long ago. The old man said, "If you have no mind of attachment, why—"
Having received the precepts, the Master took his leave. The old man ordered a youth to escort him. The Master asked the youth, "What is the number of 'three threes before' and 'three threes after'?
The youth called out, "Venerable Sir! The Master responded, "Yes. The youth said, "How many is that?
The Master asked again, "Where is this place? The youth replied, "This is the Prajñā Temple at Vajra Cave. The Master was moved with sorrow.
However, the one who enlightened the old man was none other than Mañjuśrī. Realizing he could not see him again, the old man prostrated before the youth and requested a parting word.
The youth spoke this verse: "A face without anger is the vessel of offerings; A mouth without anger emits wondrous fragrance;
A mind without anger is a precious treasure; Stainless and undefiled, it is the true eternal. Thus he spoke.
Ji-jun-tí and the monastery both vanished. Only five-colored clouds were seen, within which Mañjuśrī, riding a golden-maned lion, came and went.
Suddenly, white clouds arose from the east and covered them so they could no longer be seen. At that time, monks such as Xiu-zheng from Pútí Monastery in Cangzhou arrived;
they still heard the sound of the mountain rocks shaking and roaring. The Master consequently remained there, establishing his residence.
Mount Wutai (see *Huìyuán* II). Niu-nyōu the Rice Barrel (successor of Mazu;
see *Huìyuán* III). Whenever it was time for the midday meal, Master Niu-nyōu would personally take his rice barrel to the front of the Sangha Hall and perform a dance.
He would then laugh loudly, "Ho-ho! Sons of the Bodhisattvas, come and eat!"
Lingzhao’s Vegetable Basket (Transmission of the Lamp, Case 14). When Danxia visited Layman Pang, he saw the girl Lingzhao going out to wash vegetables at the gate.
Danxia asked, "Is the Layman in? Lingzhao set down her vegetable basket and stood with her hands folded.
Danxia said again, "Is the Layman in? Lingzhao picked up her vegetable basket and walked away. Danxia then turned back. From outside, the Layman...
Upon returning, Lingzhao recounted this to the Layman. The Layman asked, "Is Danxia still here? Lingzhao replied, "He has already left.
The Layman said, "It is like smearing red earth on a cow's udder."
Dana Shaofo (Chuan Deng 14): Once, when Danxia arrived at Hui-lin Temple in Luogu, he encountered severe cold and took some of the wooden Buddhas to burn them.
The head of the monastery scolded him, to which Danxia replied, "I am burning for the sake of the *śarīra*. The head said, "Wooden Buddhas—how could they have *śarīra*?
Danxia said, "If that is so, why do you reproach me? Subsequently, the head of the monastery’s eyebrows and beard fell out.
The Old Woman Burns the Hermitage (Huìyuán 6). Formerly, there was an old woman who supported a hermit for twenty years.
She constantly sent a young girl of eighteen to serve him with meals. One day, she ordered the girl to embrace him firmly and asked, "At this very moment, what is it like?
The Master replied, "A withered tree leans against a cold cliff; throughout the three winters, there is no warmth. The girl—
The Master related this to Ba. Ba said, "For twenty years I have been supporting nothing but a worldly fellow.
He then sent him away and burned down the hermitage.
Regarding Yungai’s Discourse on the Meaning (Shishuang Chu’s Dharma heirs; *Huiyuan*, vol. 6): Master Yuan of Yungai, due to Daozheng of Tanzhou...

Upon hearing that the Horse King requested a master for a debate on the Dharma, the King invited the master to ascend the hall to meet him. After tea, the master approached the King and asked for his sword. Grasping the sword, the master asked Dao Zheng: "In your own teachings, it is said: 'Vague and indistinct, yet within it there is something. What thing is this? 'Profound and dark, yet within it there is an essence. What essence is this? Dao Zheng replied: "It is the Way. The master struck him with the sword and said: "If you say it is the Way, then why did you strike me? Dao Zheng was speechless. The master then said: "The Buddha-Dharma is not like this; it is like a bright mirror reflecting all forms—when things come, they appear; when things go, they vanish. It is neither existent nor non-existent, neither eternal nor transient. It is simply the mind-ground of sentient beings. To seek it outside the mind is to wander in delusion. To realize it within the mind is to attain liberation. Dao Zheng bowed in repentance and became a disciple. The master then returned to the capital. Later, he resided at Mount Baizhang, where he established the monastic rules for Chan communities. He passed away in the second year of the Yongxi era (805 CE) at the age of seventy-seven. His remains were enshrined in a stupa at Mount Baizhang. His disciples numbered over a thousand. Among them, Huangbo Xiyun, Linji Yixuan, and Dongshan Liangjie were the most prominent. Their teachings spread throughout the world, and their influence continues to this day. This is known as the Baizhang Huaihai lineage of the Chan school. It is recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* and various historical chronicles. His legacy is preserved in the *Baizhang Huaihai Chanshi Yulu* (The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baizhang Huaihai). His teachings emphasize the direct pointing to the human mind and the seeing of one's nature to become a Buddha. He is revered as one of the patriarchs of Chinese Chan Buddhism. His influence extends beyond China to Korea, Japan, and Vietnam, where his lineage remains vital. His teachings continue to inspire practitioners to seek enlightenment through the cultivation of mindfulness and the realization of the inherent Buddha-nature within. He could not be executed. When Daozheng arrived, he was not executed immediately. Daozheng stood there utterly bewildered, then prostrated himself and repented.
The Master asked the King, "Do you recognize this man? The King replied, "I do. The Master asked, "Who is he? The King said, "Daozheng. The Master said, "It is not so.

Because of this, the Daoists no longer caused further disturbances.

In the *Record of the Transmission of the Lamp* (Volume 15), it is related that when Deshan was giving a small-scale sermon (*xiaocan*) to the assembly, he said: "Tonight’s small-scale sermon will not involve answering questions.
Anyone who asks a question shall receive thirty blows of the staff. At that time, a monk came forward and prostrated; the Master struck him immediately. The monk said, "I..."
The monk had not even finished his greeting when the Master asked, "Where are you from? The monk replied, "I am a man from Silla.
The Master said, "Before you have even stepped onto the ship's railing, thirty blows of the staff would be well-deserved."
The Sublime Song of Master Fuyong Kai (Successor of Touzi Qing; *Rendiantiyanmu*) A verse on the sublime song of Master Fuyong Kai, which does not depend upon the tongue:
"In every land, in every atom, everywhere he speaks; Without a snap of the fingers, Sudhana has visited him. Even Śūnyatā-janman understands the news;
Before the flowering rain on the cliff, the birds do not carry it away. (Śūnyatā-janman is Subhūti.)
*Chángchá Xuántán* (Ten Profound Discourses by Master Chángchá of Tóng’ān; Dharma heir of Jiǔfēng Qián; *Chuándēng Lù*, fascicle 29). 1. The Mind-Seal 2. The Patriarchal Meaning 3.
The Mysterious Mechanism 4. Dust and Difference 5. Buddhist Teachings 6. The Song of Returning Home 7. Shattering the Song of Returning Home 8.
Turning the Position Back to the Source 9. Returning the Function 10. Before the Right Position.
The place where the Second Patriarch, Huik’e, severed his arm to settle the mind is located here.
*Dongshan Sees the Shadow* (Yunyan Cheng’s Dharma heir; *Huìyuán*, vol. 13). Dongshan asked Yunyan:

"After the Master has passed away for a hundred years, if someone should ask whether it is possible to capture the true likeness of the Master, how would you respond? Yunyan said: "The Patriarch would say to him..."
"The Way is precisely this very thing. The Master remained silent for a long time. Yunyan said, "To take responsibility for this matter, one must be extremely careful and discerning.
The Master was still beset by doubt. Later, while crossing a stream, he saw his reflection and attained great enlightenment regarding the previous teaching.
He then composed a verse, saying: "Be most careful not to seek it from others; It would be far removed from me. I shall now go forth alone; Everywhere I find it."
"Meeting him: He is now truly I; I am now not he. You must understand it in this way before you can realize Suchness.
Yao Ling’s Prosperity and Decline (Stonehead’s Dharma Heir; *Huiyuan* 5). One day, Yaoshan was with Daowu, Yunyan, and Gao of Sha.
While traveling through Mount Miyou, [Zhaozhou] saw two trees, one flourishing and one withered. The mountain master asked, "Which is the flourishing one?
Which is the withered one? Zhaozhou said, "The withered one. The mountain master said, "Excellent! Let it go everywhere as withered and bland.
He then asked the cliff. The cliff said, "The flourishing one. The mountain master said, "Excellent! Let it go everywhere as radiant and brilliant."
He asked the śrāmaṇera again. The śrāmaṇera said, "That which withers does so because of another; that which flourishes does so because of another.
Daowu turned back and looked at Yunyan, saying, "Not so, not so."
Jiashan’s Realm (Fifth in the lineage of Huating; *Huiyuan* 5). A monk asked Jiashan, “What is the realm of Jiashan?
Jiashan said, “Monkeys carry their young back behind the green peaks; birds carry fallen flowers before the azure cliffs.”
Xiangyan Climbs a Tree (Dharma Heir of Guishan; *Chuan Deng Lu*, Case 11). One day, Xiangyan ascended the hall to address the assembly:
"It is like a man climbing a tree, with his mouth clutching a branch, his feet not treading on branches, and his hands not grasping branches.
Suddenly, someone asks him the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West. If he answers him, he loses his body and life; if he does not answer him, he violates that person."
Question: At that time, Houtou Zuo stepped forward and said, "I do not ask about the tree;
bring forth a phrase for what is beneath the tree. Yanguan laughed heartily.
Yangshan Emerges from the Well (Chuan Deng Lu 11). Chan Master Xingkong of Mount Shishuang in Tanzhou was once asked by a monk, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey?
Xingkong replied, "It is like a person inside a thousand-foot well who manages to get out without the aid of even an inch of rope.
He continued, "If such a person were here, I would answer you regarding the meaning of the Westward Journey. The monk said, "Recently, Master Ming has emerged from Hunan."
The world also speaks of people who talk east and west; they vainly call out, "Sramana! Drag out this dead man! (This refers to the Sramana of Yangshan).
Later, the Sramana raised this question to Danyuan, asking, "How can one get out of the well? Danyuan said, "Hah! (Du!).
"You fool! Who is in the well? Later, Yangshan asked Miaoshan, "How can one get the person out of the well?
Miaoshan then called out, "Huiji! Huiji responded, "Yes. Miaoshan said, "He is out.
When Yangshan later resided at Mount Yang, he once brought up this previous conversation and said to the assembly, "I attained the essence from Danyuan; I attained the ground from Miaoshan."
Zhaozhou Receiving Guests (Dharma Successor of Nanquan; *Huiyuan*). When King Wang of Zhending led his sons into the monastery, Zhaozhou sat and asked, "Does Your Majesty understand?
The King said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Having observed the fast since my youth, my body has grown old;
seeing you, I lack the strength to descend from my meditation seat. The King especially esteemed him and treated him with great respect. The following day, he ordered an attendant to...

A message was delivered. The Master descended from his meditation seat to receive it. After a short while, an attendant asked, "When the Great King arrived, you did not descend from your meditation seat, Master;
why did you descend today when the General arrived? The Master replied:

"This is not something you can understand. When those of the highest rank come, I receive them upon the meditation seat; when those of middle rank come, I receive them after descending from the meditation seat;
when those of the lowest rank come, I receive them outside the triple gate. The Master then presented the fly-whisk to the Great King, saying: "If he asks where you obtained it, simply say:
'It is something this old monk has used all his life but never exhausted.'"
Jia Lao Inspects the Illness (Dongshan Sheng’s Dharma Heir Yunyan). A monk asked, “Master, among those left behind by you, is there anyone who is not ill?
The Master said, “There is. The monk asked, “Does that one who is not ill come to visit the Master? The Master said, “The old monk has his share of visiting him.
The monk asked, “How can the Master visit him? The Master said, “When the old monk visits, it is precisely...”
[The Master] did not appear to be ill.
Regarding Nanquan’s Oil Cakes (*Cánlín lèijù* 9), Hébǔ said: One day, Chan Master Nanquan Yuan did not go to the hall.
The attendant requested that he attend the hall. The Master said, "Today I have eaten my fill of oil cakes at the manor. The attendant [replied].
The Master said, "The Master (the Abbot) has never gone out. The monk said, "Then you go and ask the steward.
Just as he was about to step out the door, he suddenly saw the steward returning to thank the Master. [And so forth.]
Huping of Shaoyang (from the *Record of Yunmen*, successor of Xuefeng). A monk asked Yunmen, “What is the discourse that transcends Buddhas and patriarchs? Yunmen said, “Huping.”
Deshan Carrying the Alms Bowl (Chuan Deng Lu 15): Xuefeng was serving as the head cook at Deshan’s monastery.
One day, when the meal was late, Deshan took his alms bowl down from the Dharma Hall. Xuefeng then said, "The bell has not yet rung and the drum has not yet sounded;
where is the Old Monk going with his bowl? Deshan returned to his quarters. Yantou, who was in the hall at the time, heard this.
