**Zhanggu Fupo (Chuan Deng Lu 7)** When Xuefeng was serving as the rice steward at Dongshan, while he was washing rice, Dongshan asked, "In washing the sand, you remove the rice;
in washing the rice, you remove the sand. The Master replied, "Sand and rice are removed all at once. Dongshan asked, "What will the assembly eat?
The Master then overturned the rice basin. Dongshan said, "According to your karmic conditions, you ought to be under Master De."
The Mountain. The Nun’s Retinue (*Chuan deng lu* 6). Once, there was a monk who went to visit Mihu. On the road, he encountered a nun living in a hermitage.
The monk asked the nun, "Do you have any followers? She replied, "I do. The monk asked, "Where are they? She said, "The mountains, rivers, and the great earth."
"The plants and trees upon this ground are all my kinsmen. The monk asked, "Are you not coming as a nun?
She replied, "What do you see me as? The monk said, "A laywoman. She said, "Then you cannot be a monk.
The monk said, "Do not confuse the Buddha-dharma, ma'am. She said, "I am not confusing the Buddha-dharma. The monk said, "You..."
"In that case, is this not a confusion of the Buddha-dharma? Ba said, "You are a man and I am a woman;
how could there ever have been any confusion?
(Wang La'er's son [Mazu’s Dharma heir, *Chuan Deng Lu* 8]). Huangbo was serving as the Head Seat at Nanquan. One day, he held up...
Dabo took his seat at the head of the row in Nanquan’s position. When Nanquan entered the hall and saw him, he asked, "Venerable sir, for how many years have you practiced the Way?
Dabo replied, "Before the time of Vairocana Buddha. Nanquan said, "Even so, you are still but a descendant of Old Master Wang.
Dabo then moved to the second seat.
Yunju Sends Pants (Dharma Heir of Lingjia; *Huiyuan* III). Zen Master Daoying of Yunju in Hongzhou once ordered an attendant to deliver a pair of trousers to a practitioner living in a hermitage.
The practitioner said, "I already have trousers from birth," and ultimately refused to accept them.
The Master again ordered the attendant to ask, "Before your mother gave birth to you, what were you wearing? The practitioner was speechless.

Later, after he passed away, there were śarīra relics. When these were presented to his teacher, the teacher said, "Even if one were to obtain eight bushels and four pecks of them, it would not be as good as having uttered a single turning word at that time."
Daowu Obtains a Loincloth (Dharma heir of Yaoshan; *Chuan deng lu*, Case 14). A donor offered a loincloth to Yaoshan.
Yaoshan held it up and addressed the assembly, saying, "Does the Dharma-body possess the four great elements? If anyone can say so, I will give him a loincloth.
Chan Master Zongzhi of Daowu Mountain in Tanzhou said, "The nature-ground is not emptiness; emptiness is not the nature-ground. This is the earth element."
The same applies to the three great [elements]. Because Yaoshan did not go back on his previous word, he gave me my loincloth.
A monk asked Jiufeng, "What is the head? The Master said, "Opening one's eyes, one does not perceive the dawn.
The monk asked, "What is the tail? The Master said, "Not sitting upon the ten-thousand-year bed. The monk said, "There is a head..."
"How is it when there is no tail? The Master said, "The moment it exists, it is not valued. The monk asked, "How is it when there is a tail but no head?
The Master said, "Though full, one has no strength. The monk asked, "What about when the head and tail are joined together?
The Master said, "When the descendants have gained their strength, those within the room do not know."

Dongshan’s Five Ranks (A Successor of Yunyan; Eyes of Humanity and Heaven). Dongshan’s Five Ranks: Xiang (Directing), Feng (Reverence), Gong (Merit), Gonggong (Shared Merit), and Gonggong (Ultimate Merit).
A monk asked, "What is Xiang? Dongshan said, "How is it when you are eating?
The monk asked, "What is Feng? Dongshan said, "How is it when you have your back turned? The monk asked, "What is Gong? Dongshan said, "Put down the hoe."
When asked, "What about when one is at the head? the monk asked, "What is 'shared effort' (*gong-gong*)? Shanshan said, "One does not possess form.
The monk asked, "What is 'effort-effort' (*gong-gong*)? Shanshan said, "Not shared."
Yangqi’s Seven Matters and Yuanjing’s Ten Gates (Fifth Patriarch Yan’s Dharma Successor; *Pudeng* 11). Master Nantang Yuanjing addressed the assembly, saying:
"The most essential point of study does not go beyond the initial phrase and the final phrase. Those who penetrate these throughout their lives..."
The task of studying the Way is now complete. Should you find that this is not yet so, I shall provide you with ten gates, each of which serves as a seal to verify your own mind.

Have you looked into them and seen them with stability? First, you must believe in the separate transmission outside the teachings. Second, you must know that there is a separate transmission outside the teachings.
Third, you must realize that the preaching of the Dharma by sentient beings and the preaching of the Dharma by insentient things are non-dual. Fourth, you must...
1. Seeing one's nature must be as clear and distinct as looking at the palm of one's hand; 2. every stage [of practice] must be kept secret; 3. one must possess the eye that discerns the Dharma; 4.
one must traverse the mysterious path of the birds; 5. one must be equipped with both civil and martial arts; 6.
one must suppress the heterodox and manifest the orthodox; 7. one must possess great capacity and great function; 8. one must act among those of different species; these are the ten gates.

Have you all returned to a state of individual stability and composure yet? If you merely close your doors to attend to your own livelihood and seek only to settle for yourself alone, then you are not included in this category.
If you wish to shoulder the True Lineage and perpetuate the Holy Seed, you must fully clarify these ten essential gates;
only then can you sit upon the curved wooden seat and receive the prostrations of the people of the world.
Prostrations! I dare take the Buddhas and Patriarchs as my teachers. If you do not reach such a state, you will merely be empty and ostentatious;
at some future time, the Old Man Yama will not dare let you go. Is there anyone here? Come forth and let us all bear witness.
If there is none, do not trouble yourself to stand for long.

The Functioning of Old An (Jingde Chuandeng Lu, Case 9): National Teacher Huian of Mount Song was visited by Tanran and Huairang, who asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? An said, "Why do you not ask about your own meaning?
They asked, "What is one's own meaning? An said, "Observe his subtle functioning. They asked, "What is this [subtle functioning]?"
An employed a secret method of action, indicating it by opening and closing his eyes. Thereupon, An attained great enlightenment beneath these words and never again sought elsewhere.
Because the karmic conditions were not yet ripe, he took his leave for Caoqi. At the time of his passing, he was titled National Teacher Old An.

In the *Huìyuán* (Vol. 3), regarding Mazu’s weariness: A monk asked Master Mazu, “Transcending the four propositions and cutting off the hundred negations, I pray that you will directly point out to me the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West. The Master said, “I am weary today and cannot explain it for you;
go ask Zhizang. When he asked Zhizang, [the monk] said, “Why did you not ask the Master? The monk replied, “The Master...”
The monk ventured to come and ask. Baizhang said, "I have a headache today; I will not explain it for you. Go ask Elder Hai.
The monk went and asked Elder Hai. Hai said, "When I reach this point, I do not understand either. The monk reported this to Mazu Daoshi.
Daoshi said, "Baizhang’s head is white; Hai’s head is black."
Jingqing’s Sound of Rain (Seventh in the *Huìyuán*, Dharma Heir of Xuefeng). Jingqing asked a monk, “What is that sound outside the gate?
The monk said, “The sound of raindrops. The Master said, “Sentient beings are inverted; they lose themselves and pursue external things.
The monk asked, “How about you, Master? The Master said, “I have not lost myself. What is the meaning of this? The Master said: “To leave one’s body may still be easy; [but to enter it is difficult].
To manifest the Way in its entirety is surely difficult.

Regarding Xuedou’s “Spiritual Terrace” (a successor of Zhimen Zu, recorded in the *Sengbao zhuan*), the supplementary commentary states: The Master composed a verse titled "Daily Diminution for the Sake of the Way," which says:
Two-thirds of the light of time have already passed; the single point within the spiritual hall has not been polished. Greedily pursuing life, one hastens away in trivial toil;
when called back, one does not turn—what can be done?
Gushan Shengjian (Dharma heir of Xuefeng; *Huiyuan* 7). When Gushan went to attend a request from the Great King, Xuefeng sent him off with a formal escort.
Upon returning to the Dharma Hall, Gushan said, "A single holy arrow has shot straight into the innermost city.
Taoyuan Fu said, "He has not yet reached it. Xuefeng said, "He is a man of thorough penetration. Fu said, "If you do not believe me, wait—"
"Let me go and examine him," [Fufu] said, and he pursued him halfway along the road, where he asked, "Elder brother, where are you going?
Shan said, "I am going to the Ninefold City. Fu said, "What if you suddenly encounter an encirclement by the three armies?
Shan said, "He has his own path that reaches through the heavens. Fu said, "If that is so, then you have left the palace and lost the hall."
Mountan Shān said, "Where would he not be honored? Fú shook out his sleeves and turned back. Mountan Fēng asked, "How was that?
Fú said, "That fine holy arrow was broken in mid-flight," and he then recounted the previous conversation. Mountan Fēng said, "Those words of his were truly excellent.
Fú remarked, "This old fellow still has a bit of local sentiment left in him."

Tie-mian Retires from the Seat (from the *Sengbaozhuan*, lower volume; a dharma heir of Xinghua). After Chan Master Yuan of Jiangshan passed away, Emperor Shu invited Xiu Tie-mian to succeed him on the seat.
When Xiu arrived at the mountain, the Emperor went first to pay his respects, but Xiu was occupied with administrative matters of the monastic community and did not see him immediately.
The Emperor took this as an insult to himself and subsequently departed in displeasure.
Kebin’s Discharge from the Hospital (Huìyuán 11). Xinghua said to the rector Kebin, “Before long, you will become a master who leads the assembly.
Kebin replied, “I will not enter this community. Xinghua asked, “Do you refuse to enter because you understand, or because you do not understand?
Kebin said, “It is neither of these. Xinghua then struck him and said, “This is the Dharma of Rector Kebin.”

In a dharma-battle, he was defeated. He was fined five strings of cash and ordered to provide a meal of "drilled rice" (boiled rice with holes). The next day, Xinghua entered the hall and struck the gavel, saying: "The rector Kebin lost the dharma-battle;
he is fined five strings of cash and must provide a full meal of drilled rice. Furthermore, he must leave the monastery.
Later, Kebin went forth into the world to reside at Mount Daxing, where he succeeded Xinghua as his heir.

*Chiyang Baiken* (The Hundred Questions of Chiyang; *Shi'en*, Vol. 5; *Fudeng*, Vol. 3). Chan Master Ba’en, the first patriarch of Da’hong in Suizhou, once established one hundred questions to interrogate his students.

A brief excerpt states: "Even if one were to not forget the karma created throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, why is it that by reciting 'Namo Buddha' but once, sins are extinguished for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges? He also made this gesture.
It is said: "The myriad phenomena of the universe are all contained therein. Zen practitioners with true eyes, please try to discern this.

Regarding Buddha’s Three Exhortations (*Chuanteng lu* 14): Master Fotu of Famen Temple in Fengxiang Prefecture constantly held a single string of prayer beads and recited three names: first, Śākyamuni; second, Yuanhe; and third, Buddha. From [that time on...]
What else is this? It is but a single *zhanduoqiu* (a bowl-shaped vessel). One ends and then begins; its traces are extraordinary, such that people of the time could not fathom them.
Naturally eradicating the weeds (as recorded in the *Chuanteng Lu*, Vol. 14), it is like the place where Danxia covered his ears as mentioned before.
Devadatta Throws a Needle (Huìyuán 1). When Bodhisattva Devadatta came from Siṃhala Island seeking to challenge him in debate, he arrived at the gate of Nāgārjuna.
Nāgārjuna had long been aware of his reputation; he therefore filled a bowl with water and had a disciple carry it out to show it to him.
Upon seeing the water, Devadatta silently dropped a needle into it. As the disciple was returning, Nāgārjuna highly praised him.
He sighed and said: "The clarity of this water reflects my own virtue; that man came to cast a needle into it to fathom its very bottom.
A person such as this may be discussed regarding the profound and deliberated upon the Way."
Yaoshan’s Long Sigh (Stonehead Qian’s Dharma Heir; *Chuan Deng Lu*, Case 14). One night, as Yaoshan was walking up and down the mountain, the clouds suddenly parted and he beheld the moon.
He let out a great roar, which echoed for ninety li to the east of Liyang. All the residents there claimed it came from their own eastern neighbor.
The next morning, they questioned one another until they reached the disciples of Yaoshan, who said, "Last night, the Master was on the mountain..."
Ding Daoshao. Li Ao presented him with this poem: "Having chosen a secluded dwelling, you enjoy the sentiments of the wild fields; Throughout the year, there is neither seeing off nor welcoming.
At times, you ascend directly to the peak of a solitary mountain, And beneath the moon, part the clouds and let out a single cry."

The Buddha-Fruit: Washing the Mouth and the Old Woman’s Refreshment (Chuan Deng Lu, Case 17). Deshan was a native of the Zhou clan from Jianzhou. He left home at the age of seven and received full ordination according to his seniority.

He studied the Vinaya-piṭaka with great diligence and thoroughly mastered the essential meanings of the various sūtras on the nature and characteristics of phenomena. He frequently lectured on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
The *Jingang jing* (Diamond Sutra). At that time, he was known as Zhou Jingang. He once said to his fellow students: "A single hair swallows the ocean, yet the nature of the ocean is not diminished;
a tiny mote is cast into a bowl, yet the bowl remains unmoved. Whether one is a learner (*śaikṣa*) or one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), only I know this.
Later, hearing that the Zen seats in the South were flourishing, the Master’s spirit was unsettled, and he remarked: "Those who have left the household life study for a thousand kalpas..."
"The Buddha’s majestic deportment—had one not studied these subtle practices for ten thousand kalpas, one could not attain Buddhahood.

Yet this son of Māra from the south dares to speak of 'directly pointing to the human mind to see one's nature and become a Buddha. I shall tear open his den and exterminate his kind, thereby repaying the Buddha's grace.
He then took up the *Qinglong shuchao* (Blue Dragon Commentary) and departed from Shu, arriving at Liyang. On the road, he encountered an old woman.
The son was selling oil-cakes. Taking a rest from his shoulders, he bought some cakes for refreshment. The woman pointed to his carrying-pole and asked, "What kind of writing is this?
The Master replied, "The *Qinglong Shuchao* (Commentary on the Blue Dragon). The woman asked, "Which sutra do you lecture upon? The Master replied, "The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*."
Baoyun said, "I have a question for you. If you can answer it, I will give you refreshments; if you cannot answer it, you must go elsewhere.
He continued, "The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: 'The past mind is unattainable; the present mind is unattainable.'"
The future mind cannot be apprehended. I do not know which mind the Elder is pointing to. The Master remained silent.
He then went to Longtan, a region infested with venomous insects (*Chuan-deng* 17). A monk asked Caoshan: "How should a student preserve [the mind] throughout the twelve periods of the day?"
Ren said, "It is like being in a region of *gudu* (poisonous fungi); not a single drop of water may touch you.

*Benji Shenlou* (The Three Kinds of Leakage by Caoshan; Disciple of Dongshan; *Rendiantiemu*) Caoshan’s Three Kinds of Leakage state it thus: First is the leakage of views (*jian shenlou*), which means that when the faculty of response does not leave its station, one falls into a sea of poison.
Second is the leakage of sentiment (*qing shenlou*), which means that when wisdom constantly turns toward or away from objects, the locus of vision becomes biased and withered.

Third is the leakage of speech (*yu shenlou*), which means that while the essence is subtle, the fundamental source is lost; the faculty of response is dark regarding the beginning and the end. As for the student...
This turbid flow of ignorance revolves; it does not transcend these three types.
Ke-fu’s Verification (Linji Dharma Heir, *Huìyuán* 11). When Linji first arrived at his residence in Hebei, he saw the two senior monks Puhua and Ke-fu and said to them:
"I wish to establish the fundamental tenets of Huangbo here. You..."
"Furthermore, strip me of my robes! The two men respectfully descended.
Three days later, Puhua came back up and asked, "What did you say three days ago, Master? Linji struck him. Three days later, Ke Fu came up and asked.
The Master struck Puhua the day before yesterday; Jie also struck him. Later that evening, he gave a small lecture (xiaocan), saying:
"Sometimes one takes away the person but does not take away the environment; sometimes one takes away the environment but does not take away the person;

sometimes both the person and the environment are taken away; and sometimes neither the person nor the environment is taken away. A monk asked, "What is 'taking away the person but not taking away the environment'?"
Linji said: "The warm sun brings forth life, spreading a carpet of brocade; the infant’s hair hangs down, white as silk.
"What is 'seizing the environment but not seizing the person'? Linji said: "The imperial decree has been issued and reaches all under heaven;
the general is beyond the frontier, where smoke and dust have ceased. "What is 'seizing both person and environment'? Linji said: "In Bing and Fen, all news is cut off; [only] the solitary..."

"Abiding in one place—how can it be that for this person, both the realm and the person are not taken away? Jie said: "The King ascends the precious throne; the village elder sings his song. This perfectly accords with the verse:
"Not taking away the person, but taking away the realm: The conditions themselves carry a hidden paradox. If you wish to seek the profound meaning, To deliberate will only lead to blame.
The pearl of the black dragon shines brilliantly; The shadow of the moon on the cassia tree wavers. Face-to-face, there is nothing..."
Mutually conflicting, one would still be caught within the net. To seize the object but not the person—seeking the truth through words, where is it real?

To inquire about Chan is for Chan to be a delusion; to investigate principle is for principle to be alien. The sun shines upon the pale glow of frost; the mountains lie afar, their verdant hues fresh.

Even if you were to attain a profound realization, it would still be but dust in the eye. When both person and environment are simultaneously seized, the true mandate has been exercised from the beginning.
Whether regarding Buddhas or Patriarchs, to speak of the sentiments of the holy and the ordinary is like attempting to strike a "blowing-hair" sword—it is as if encountering a blind man in the woods.

To advance further in pursuit of a wondrous meeting is to needlessly sever one's own spirit. When person and environment are both unassailable, the scope of conceptual deliberation does not reach them.
When host and guest do not differ in their speech, the principle is complete in both question and answer. Treading upon and shattering the moon in the clear pool, one pierces through...
The Azure Sky (Biluo Tian) cannot clarify its wondrous function; it remains submerged in the absence of conditions.

The Length and Shortness of the Way (Nanyue Ruang’s Dharma Heir; *Chuan Deng Lu*, Case 6). A monk drew four lines before Mazu:
the top line was long and the three below were short. He asked, "One cannot say that one is long and three are short.
Apart from these four propositions, I request you, Master, to provide an answer. The Master then drew a single line and said, "One cannot say it is long or short; this is my answer for you."
It is understood.
Shilou has no ears (Stonehead’s Dharma heir; *Huìyuán*, fascicle 5). Once, a monk asked Master Shilou of Fenzhou, "I do not yet recognize my original nature;
I beg the Master for a skillful means to point it out. The Master said, "Shilou has no ears. The monk said, "I..."
The monk admitted his error. The Master said, "I, the old monk, also have a fault. The monk asked, "Where does the Master’s fault lie?
The Master replied, "It lies in your place of error. The monk bowed, and the Master struck him.
Zhencui Ju’an (the thirteenth patriarch of the Caoxi lineage, Master Rong of Guangli in Chuzhou). When he first resided at Zhencui, a monk came to visit him.
The Master held up his whisk and said, "Does this old man of Zhencui still possess the eye?
The monk replied, "I do not dare to see any fault in the Master. The Master said, "This old monk is dead in your hands."
The monk pointed with his finger to his chest and then emerged. The Master said, "Ācārya, you have seen the former master coming.
When evening came and the Master was drinking tea, the monk picked up the cup and said, "This is the matter concerning the Buddhas appearing in the world.
What is the matter concerning them not yet appearing in the world? The Master brushed the cup away with his hand and said, "It will take until your death for you to reach me, old monk."
[The Master] held it in his hand. The monk said, "The Five Li Signpost is outside the city gate. The Master said, "To cause confusion among the monks without reason.
The monk then rose and thanked him for the tea. The Master said, "I thank you specifically for visiting."

When Chan Master Cuiyan Zhenke visited Master Ciming, Ciming looked at him and asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? Zhenke replied, "Cloudless clouds arise upon the peaks;
the full moon descends into the heart of the waves. Ciming said, "With white hair and yellowed teeth, you still hold such a view! Zhenke...
Truly, he shed tears and sought instruction. Ming said, "You may ask me; you may ask using your previous words.
Ming then said, "No clouds arise upon the mountain peaks; the moon exists within the heart of the waves. At that very moment, he attained sudden enlightenment regarding the Great Dharma under him.
He resided at Cuoyan, which the world esteemed as a Dharma cave for all under heaven.

Deshan Summoning with a Fan (Chuan Deng Lu 16). Chan Master Jiǎn of Gāotíng in Xiāngzhōu first saw Dégshān across the river.
From afar, he joined his palms and called out, "How do you do? Dégshān beckoned him again with the fan in his hand. Jiǎn suddenly opened [his mouth].
Wu (Wumen) then strode off crosswise and did not look back again. Later, he propagated the Dharma in Xiangzhou and succeeded Deshan.

Regarding the "Cāṣa Bird’s Banner Pole" (Case 1 of *Huiyuan*): Ānanda asked Kāśyapa, "Elder brother, besides the golden-brocade *kaṣāya* that the World-Honored One transmitted to you, what else did he transmit?
Kāśyapa called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda responded, "Yes? Kāśyapa said, "Throw it down!"
A banner pole was erected in front of his gate.
Regarding Chan Master Foguang Wunai: he traveled from Yongan in Suzhou to reside at Huilin Chan Monastery in Daxiangguo Temple by imperial decree.
Empress Dowager Huigong once saw him from beneath the palace curtains after he had finished his audience with the Emperor.
He departed through the air. From that time forth, the imperial delicacies presented by the Grand Palace were offered as sustenance to him.

Furthermore, he was ordered to take back to the palace the remnants of the Dhyāna Master’s meal. Additionally, a *dharma-robe* was fashioned from "earth-patterned" brocade (*di-jin*), and a meditation plaque was personally attached and bestowed upon him to manifest his sincerity in honoring the Dharma.
During the winter months, a red silk canopy was granted, along with clothing, ornaments, and utensils.
Regarding items such as these ceramic vessels, Guang subsequently returned the Dharma robes bestowed upon him by the imperial palace to Chan Master Fayun Fozhao.

Fayun, in turn, sent them to Master Zantang of Baofeng in Hongzhou. In his letter, he wrote: "I give these 'earth-patterned' Dharma robes to you, my junior brother, so that you may carry on the Way of our late master.
When Zantang passed away, he left [the robes] at the mountain gate; they remain there even to this day.
Surviving,
he protected the nation with his golden brocade robe until the end of his days on the islands of the sea.
Liang hid himself at West Mountain (Huìyuán 3). Master Liang of West Mountain in Hongzhou abandoned the study of the sutras and śāstras because he went to attend upon Mazu.
Mazu asked him, "I have heard it said that you, Master, lecture extensively on the sutras and śāstras; is this true? Liang replied, "I do not dare."
The Patriarch asked, "With what will you lecture? Huilang replied, "I shall lecture with the mind. The Patriarch said, "The mind is like a performer, and the intellect is like the conductor;
how can you possibly lecture? Huilang raised his voice and said, "If the mind cannot lecture, perhaps empty space can lecture?
The Patriarch said, "Indeed, empty space can lecture. Thereupon, the Master shook out his sleeves and departed. The Patriarch— [continued].
He then summoned Master Yun. As the Master turned his head, the Patriarch said, "From birth until old age, it has been nothing but this.
At these words, the Master attained sudden and great enlightenment, whereupon he prostrated himself. The Patriarch said, "What is the point of this dull-witted monk bowing?
Huilang returned and told the assembly, "I used to lecture on the sutras and śāstras, believing that no one could equal me. Today, I was [defeated] by Mazu..."
Upon this single question, his lifelong efforts were dissolved like melting ice. Thereafter, he withdrew to the Western Mountains (Xishan), where no further news was heard of him.
To this day, those among the people of the Western Mountains frequently see him there. During the Zhenghe era, there was a scholar surnamed Xiong whose personal name is lost;
his family had long been residents of Bangyang. While traveling through the various mountains of Hongzhou, he passed by Cuoyan. At that time, the Elder Si...
Wen was a local of that district. He dispatched two laborers to carry a sedan chair to the location of Kōsō (Kūshō).

As they passed through dense forests and secluded valleys, they suddenly beheld a monk of ancient appearance and serene spirit, with thick eyebrows and a snow-white head, wearing a garment woven from leaves, sitting upon a flat rock like the image of the Buddha Tuo Cheng depicted on a wall.
Wen suspected him to be an extraordinary person, reflecting to himself that he must be Master Liang.
He was hiding in the Western Mountains; it was feared that he might be there. Xiong asked with hesitation, "Could this be Master Liang?
The monk pointed his hand toward the east, and as Xiong turned his head in that direction, he lost sight of where the monk had been. At that time, a light rain had recently cleared.
Xiong stroked the place where he had been sitting, and the stone was still warm. Looking back with hesitation, he sighed deeply and said, "My past affinities are not profound;
even meeting [the Master] is as if I have not met him.

(From the *Sengbao zhuan*, lower volume, on the "Pine Demon of the Great Way" at Fenyang’s lineage). Quandaodao resided at Baozhen Hermitage. This was the case for those from Heng and Xiang... up to [the point where]... the Great Way.

Huangniu Refuses Ordination (Huìyuán 10). As for Huangniu of Zhenghuang: he was a native of Qiantáng who resided at Gōngchén Mountain in Yúháng.
Orphaned at a young age, he served as a novice boy; he possessed extraordinary insight, and his speech always transcended the expectations of others.
His master praised him to others, and a great *dānapati* marveled at him, offering him a monastic certificate (*duòjié*). Huangniu knelt to receive it in gratitude, yet refused to accept it. His...

*Shimen Gouzhui* (Stone Gate Hook and Chisel; Successor of Shoushan Nian; *Huiyuan* 11) Chan Master Shimen Yunchong Cizhao ascended the hall and said:
"Before the fifteenth day, all Buddhas are born; after the fifteenth day, all Buddhas pass away.
Before the fifteenth day, all Buddhas are born—you must not depart from here. If you depart from here, I..."
"The hook hooks you. After the fifteenth day, all Buddhas will have passed away; you shall not remain here with me.
If you do remain here with me, I have an awl to bore into you. Now tell me: on the very fifteenth day itself, is it the hook that is used, or is it the awl?
Thereupon, he spoke a verse: "On the very fifteenth day, The hook and the awl are one."
The breath paused; he intended to ask further how it was so, but turning his head, the sun had already risen.
With nothing left to say, he chanted the Way and composed a poem upon ten thousand hexagrams.
